AI.conclusion: The pipeline demonstrates feasibility and traceability of LLM-assisted patent analysis; testing labels against expert coding and benchmarking against alternative pipelines remain as next steps.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Probabilistic Option Shielding
comment: Accepted at the NEmo workshop @ NeurIPS 2026
summary: Shielding is a safe reinforcement learning technique that provides safety guarantees while learning, by blocking unsafe actions. Traditional shielding relies on a complete model of the environment to provide long-term guarantees. Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) lifts the requirement of having such model, but only considers safety in the short term, typically looking only one or few steps ahead. We propose Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS), which extends PLS to the option level, recovering long-horizon safety without reintroducing the need for a complete environment model. POS learns a model-free critic directly from one-step PLS signals, to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty. We evaluate POS on safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, and show that it achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of standard step-level PLS and other safety related reinforcement learning baselines.

AI.tldr: Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS) extends probabilistic logic shielding from single steps to whole options, using a model-free critic to estimate the probability that an option completes safely, and yields safer training with matched task performance.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) avoids needing a full environment model but only guarantees safety one or a few steps ahead, leaving long-horizon safety unaddressed.
AI.method: POS learns a model-free critic from one-step PLS signals to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty, providing option-level shielding without a complete environment model.
AI.result: On safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, POS achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of step-level PLS and other safety-related reinforcement learning baselines.
AI.conclusion: Option-level shielding recovers long-horizon safety without requiring a complete environment model.

title: Fused-Softmax for efficient quantized attention
summary: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs is growing far faster than vector-arithmetic throughput. Attention therefore cannot realize the available GEMM performance because softmax has become the pipeline bottleneck. We introduce Fused-Softmax Attention, a training-free algorithm that reformulates and approximates softmax to fold its dominant operations into the attention GEMMs, moving work from vector units to matrix cores. Implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture, our MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X GPU, yielding speedups of $2.1\times$, $2.8\times$ and $3.2\times$ over the BF16 attention. Importantly, the additional error introduced by Fused-Softmax remains below the error floor set by quantizing the GEMM operands. On Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule delivers up to $2.05\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving the visual quality of the outputs. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source AITER library, and they powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, which ran $1.7\times$ faster than AMD's previous-round result on the same hardware. Our results show that redesigning softmax to utilize the matrix pipeline enables attention to capitalize on continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.

AI.tldr: Fused-Softmax Attention is a training-free reformulation of softmax that folds its dominant operations into attention GEMMs, reaching about 3.0 to 4.6 PFLOP/s with MXFP8 to MXFP4 kernels on an AMD MI355X and speedups of 2.1x to 3.2x over BF16 attention.
AI.motivation: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs grows much faster than vector throughput, so softmax has become the bottleneck that prevents attention from realizing available GEMM performance.
AI.method: The algorithm reformulates and approximates softmax to move its work from vector units to matrix cores, implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture with MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels shipped in AMD's open-source AITER library.
AI.result: The kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X, giving speedups of 2.1x, 2.8x and 3.2x over BF16 attention; the added error stays below the error floor set by quantizing GEMM operands; on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule gives up to 2.05x end-to-end speedup while preserving visual quality; the kernels powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, 1.7x faster than its previous round.
AI.conclusion: Redesigning softmax to use the matrix pipeline lets attention exploit continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.

title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems
comment: Published in HC_AIxIA_HYDRA 2025, Communications in Computer and Information Science, vol. 2830, pp. 50-63, Springer, 2026. Please cite the published version: doi:https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-16708-8_4
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in high-risks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance, and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables users-such as clinicians-to actively query the system. By fostering an interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a clinical decision support system that pairs predictive models and explainable AI with a retrieval-augmented LLM module that grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge and lets clinicians query them interactively.
AI.motivation: XAI outputs often are not presented in a form accessible to domain experts, and LLM-generated explanations risk hallucination and lack of source traceability in high-stakes clinical settings.
AI.method: A clinical decision support system combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques and a retrieval-augmented generation module that reformulates technical outputs into human-like explanations and supports interactive user queries.
AI.result: The abstract reports only preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology, with no quantitative figures stated.
AI.conclusion: Grounded, interactive LLM explanations are presented as a way for clinicians to explore model decisions and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics, pending further study.

title: MM-DyGraph: A Dataset, Benchmark, and Model for Multimodal Dynamic Graphs
summary: Multimodal dynamic graphs are pervasive in real-world applications, where nodes and edges are accompanied by multimodal signals, including text and images. Despite their practical importance, benchmarks and methods that explicitly study multimodal learning in dynamic graphs remain scarce, hindering the full understanding and effective utilization of multimodal information for downstream tasks. To address this gap, we introduce MM-DyGraph, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for multimodal dynamic graph learning, consisting of diverse real-world datasets with fine-grained temporal graph evolution and rich multimodal attributes. MM-DyGraph provides three evaluation tasks to comprehensively assess model performance in dynamic settings. We benchmark representative state-of-the-art dynamic graph methods and reveal that naive feature concatenation yields target-level inconsistencies: multimodal inputs benefit certain prediction targets while harming others. This observation indicates that the modality informativeness depends on the specific prediction target over time. Building on these observations, we propose a Target-aware Spatial-Temporal Multimodal Fusion (TST-MF) framework, which jointly conditions multimodal fusion on the prediction target and spatial-temporal relations, enabling context-adaptive cross-modal interplay for target-specific representations. Extensive experiments over diverse datasets and tasks show that TST-MF delivers robust and competitive performance, achieving clear gains in multimodal settings.

AI.tldr: MM-DyGraph is the first benchmark for multimodal dynamic graph learning, and TST-MF, a target-aware spatio-temporal fusion framework, conditions cross-modal fusion on the prediction target to achieve clear gains in multimodal settings.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks and methods for multimodal learning on dynamic graphs with text and image attributes are scarce, and naive feature concatenation causes target-level inconsistencies where multimodal inputs help some targets and hurt others.
AI.method: The authors introduce MM-DyGraph with diverse real-world datasets, three evaluation tasks and fine-grained temporal evolution, benchmark representative dynamic graph methods, and propose Target-aware Spatial-Temporal Multimodal Fusion (TST-MF), which jointly conditions multimodal fusion on the prediction target and spatio-temporal relations.
AI.result: Naive feature concatenation shows target-level inconsistencies across prediction targets; TST-MF delivers robust and competitive performance across diverse datasets and tasks, with clear gains in multimodal settings.
AI.conclusion: Modality informativeness depends on the prediction target over time, so target-conditioned multimodal fusion is needed for dynamic graphs.

title: Zero-Query Transferable Pretend Benign Attacks with Amortized Online Generation for Cooperative Perception
summary: Cooperative perception enables an ego agent to acquire information from collaborators beyond its own sensors' reach. Yet, the most beneficial messages are often the hardest to verify from local observations. Pretend Benign (PB) exploits this asymmetry by targeting regions with weak local verifiability and applying multi-objective perturbations, making harmful feature changes appear to be benign assistance. However, PB is victim-dependent: selecting regions and optimizing perturbations require the victim model's architecture, parameters, and gradients, limiting transfer to unseen victims. A transferable attack must capture properties shared across cooperative detection models rather than those specific to one network. We address this by building a victim-agnostic attack from a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models and encoding its capabilities in a reusable dictionary to reduce per-message generation cost. Specifically, Transferable Pretend Benign (TrPB) transfers PB's region selection criterion and multi-objective perturbation strategy across heterogeneous surrogates to construct an offline attack. We further propose RT-TrPB, which encodes transferable regions and perturbation patterns into a region predictor and reusable perturbation dictionary, amortizing per-message attack generation. Experiments on widely used cooperative perception benchmarks show that RT-TrPB bypasses the consensus-based defenses ROBOSAC and FLD with success rates approaching 100% and generates each perturbation in under 56 ms. To counter PB-style attacks masquerading as benign collaboration, we also propose STTrust, which verifies received messages using spatial and temporal consistency and incorporates identity-level trust. STTrust detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores perception performance to near the attack-free level.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces transferable and amortized pretend-benign attacks (TrPB and RT-TrPB) on cooperative perception that transfer to unseen victims and bypass consensus defenses, along with STTrust, a defense that detects over 90% of such attacks.
AI.motivation: Pretend Benign attacks depend on the victim model's architecture, parameters and gradients, which limits their transfer to unseen victims, and existing defenses such as ROBOSAC and FLD can be bypassed.
AI.method: TrPB builds a victim-agnostic offline attack from a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models by transferring region selection and multi-objective perturbation strategy; RT-TrPB encodes transferable regions and perturbation patterns into a region predictor and reusable perturbation dictionary to amortize generation; STTrust verifies received messages using spatial and temporal consistency with identity-level trust.
AI.result: On widely used cooperative perception benchmarks, RT-TrPB bypasses ROBOSAC and FLD with success rates approaching 100% and generates each perturbation in under 56 ms; STTrust detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores perception performance to near the attack-free level.
AI.conclusion: Victim-agnostic, amortized attacks threaten consensus-based cooperative perception, and spatio-temporal consistency with identity trust offers an effective countermeasure.

title: Forecasting cumulative intraoperative hypotension burden: patient-disjoint evaluation of quantile boosting and alert policies
summary: Background: Binary hypotension forecasts do not describe the depth and duration of future low pressure. Burden forecasts may support graded early warning, but better forecast scores need not yield more useful alerts. Objective: To evaluate conditional quantiles of the next 15-minute mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg and distinguish forecasting performance from episode-warning performance. Methods: Public VitalDB numeric arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling. Subject-disjoint training, validation and test splits included 70,402, 14,270 and 15,575 labeled windows. We compared climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without additional MAP-history features. Patient-weighted pinball loss and subject-bootstrap intervals evaluated forecasting. Validation selected alert thresholds before a hash-recorded test evaluation. Results: In the test split, the prespecified residual-versus-persistence comparison at the 90th percentile yielded losses of 2.256 and 2.900 mmHg-min, respectively (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487). Direct prediction achieved 2.196, and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieved 2.193. Episode-warning results were sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold. Conclusions: This retrospective benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance. Findings support further study of direct burden estimation; they do not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates quantile boosting for forecasting the cumulative 15-minute burden of intraoperative hypotension and shows that better forecast scores do not guarantee more useful episode alerts, using a retrospective VitalDB benchmark with patient-disjoint splits.
AI.motivation: Binary hypotension forecasts miss the depth and duration of low pressure, and burden forecasts may support graded early warning, yet forecast skill and alert usefulness need separate evaluation.
AI.method: Public VitalDB arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling; climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without MAP-history features, were compared using patient-weighted pinball loss, subject-bootstrap intervals and validation-selected alert thresholds, with a hash-recorded test evaluation.
AI.result: At the 90th percentile in the test split, residual quantile boosting yields 2.900 mmHg-min versus 2.256 for persistence (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487) as prespecified; direct prediction achieves 2.196 and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieves 2.193; episode-warning results are sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance and supports further study of direct burden estimation, but does not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.

title: Model-based learning for DoA estimation and array calibration via continuous sparse recovery
summary: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, a classical signal processing problem, has experienced renewed interest with the advent of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). While decades of research have yielded highly accurate DoA estimators, hardware impairments have frequently been neglected, despite degrading both DoA estimation accuracy and downstream communication performance in ISAC systems. This work introduces a joint array calibration and DoA estimation method based on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm, following the model-based machine learning paradigm. The proposed method enables the calibration of antenna arrays subject to severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Additionally, DoA estimation is enhanced by extending SOMP to continuous dictionaries via PGD refinement steps. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enables efficient hardware impairment compensation, even without labeled samples, while outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-based machine learning method that jointly calibrates antenna arrays and estimates directions of arrival using continuous sparse recovery, working with or without labelled data.
AI.motivation: Hardware impairments such as gain-phase errors and antenna location errors degrade DoA estimation and communication performance in integrated sensing and communication systems, and are often neglected.
AI.method: The method extends simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) and calibrates arrays with severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), using supervised or unsupervised objectives, and refines DoA estimates on continuous dictionaries with PGD steps.
AI.result: Simulations show efficient hardware impairment compensation even without labelled samples, with the method outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Model-based learning with continuous sparse recovery offers a practical way to compensate array hardware impairments for DoA estimation in ISAC systems.

title: Nudging Decision Models: Do Digital Nudges Steer Fast, Generation-Free AI Agents?
comment: Under Review
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly automate business and consumer tasks but are slow and expensive. Decision models, a new class that chooses among options without generating text, are far faster and less costly. Developers call them "System One models," referencing dual process theory. We ask whether such models can be steered by digital nudges online and whether, as the theory predicts, automatic nudges affect them more than reflective ones. We adapted an online shopping experiment, previously run with humans and LLM agents, to three decision models (Jev, Decision-1, d1). Across 600 runs per model, they chose a preselected default in 97.5-99.9% and a product with social influence information in 75-96% of choices, versus 47-49% in the control. All responded more strongly to the automatic nudge, the opposite of what has been reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents. We provide first evidence that non-generative decision models are susceptible to digital nudges in a System 1 pattern, implying agent-type-specific nudge effects.

AI.tldr: Decision models that choose among options without generating text are susceptible to digital nudges, responding more strongly to automatic nudges than to reflective ones, the opposite of the pattern reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents are slow and expensive, and whether fast, non-generative decision models can be steered by digital nudges, and whether dual-process theory predicts their response, was unknown.
AI.method: An online shopping experiment previously run with humans and LLM agents was adapted to three decision models (Jev, Decision-1, d1), with 600 runs per model comparing a preselected default and a socially influenced product against a control.
AI.result: The models chose the preselected default in 97.5-99.9% of runs and the product with social influence information in 75-96% of choices, versus 47-49% in the control, and all responded more strongly to the automatic nudge.
AI.conclusion: Non-generative decision models show a System 1 pattern of nudge susceptibility, implying that nudge effects are agent-type specific.

title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games
summary: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether an LLM can zero-shot write the weights of feed-forward networks for two-player games of rising difficulty, and finds that exact construction works for cheap-to-verify tactics but collapses on multi-move chess endgame play.
AI.motivation: Weight-space programming sets network weights by hand from an explicit specification without gradient descent or training data, and how far an LLM can carry this practice across games of increasing difficulty was an open question.
AI.method: A four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four difficulty axes was built, with a second structurally unrelated game at each rung to separate difficulty from game-specific effects; ten networks were built and independently verified against independent oracles, six with complete non-statistical proofs of correctness.
AI.result: The chess-endgame rung is exact for move legality and an exact one-ply mate detector in one network, but success falls from 84.1-100% on one-ply tactics to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; a replicate with a shorter plan and exact safety checks shows a collapse an order of magnitude less severe; holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding shallow search on the standard-sized rung shows the gap is an architectural ceiling, reproduced across two unrelated games.
AI.conclusion: The remaining gap in zero-shot weight-space programming reflects an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and the networks, oracles, cost measurements and a cold-prompt protocol are released for future cross-model comparison.

title: PHISHREV+: An ASP-Based Post-Hoc Defeasible Machine Learning Framework for Phishing Detection
summary: Phishing website detection remains a critical cybersecurity challenge. Although machine learning classifiers achieve high accuracy on benchmark datasets, they suffer from a fundamental limitation: once trained, their decision boundaries are fixed and cannot incorporate new contextual evidence without retraining the model. This work presents \textbf{PHISHREV+}, a hybrid framework that instantiates the notion of \textit{post-hoc defeasible machine learning}. This framework does not replace the classifier. It treats the initial classifier predictions as defeasible beliefs and revises them through an Answer Set Programming based non-monotonic reasoning(NMR) layer. The framework operates in two phases. In the machine learning phase, four classifiers (SVM, KNN, DT and RF) are trained on the 87 feature benchmark dataset. In the post-hoc NMR phase, four defeasible rules derived from exploratory data analysis of the training set, and validated through Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, formally revise initial predictions. The proposed framework achieves consistent false positive reduction across all our classifiers SVM (41$\rightarrow$39), KNN (47$\rightarrow$46), DT (62$\rightarrow$61), and RF (52$\rightarrow$51) while maintaining complete false negative parity with zero increase overhead. A comprehensive ablation studies across seven rule configurations confirms that the hierarchical combination of all four defeasible rules is necessary to achieve this optimal balance. Instance level explainability is provided through eXplainable ASP (XASP), which generates formal derivation graphs showing which defeasible rules fired and why the initial belief was retracted, a capability absent from all existing phishing detection approaches.

AI.tldr: PHISHREV+ is a hybrid framework that treats classifier predictions as defeasible beliefs and revises them with answer set programming rules, reducing false positives across four classifiers on phishing detection without increasing false negatives.
AI.motivation: Trained phishing classifiers have fixed decision boundaries and cannot incorporate new contextual evidence without retraining.
AI.method: Four classifiers (SVM, KNN, DT and RF) are trained on an 87-feature benchmark dataset, then four defeasible rules derived from exploratory data analysis and validated with Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests revise their predictions through an answer set programming non-monotonic reasoning layer, with eXplainable ASP providing derivation graphs.
AI.result: False positives drop across all classifiers, SVM from 41 to 39, KNN from 47 to 46, DT from 62 to 61 and RF from 52 to 51, with false negative parity maintained; an ablation over seven rule configurations shows the combination of all four rules is needed for the best balance.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc defeasible reasoning can add explainable false-positive reduction on top of existing classifiers without retraining them.

title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems
summary: Behind the expanding use of large language models (LLMs) across application domains lies a growing dependence on specialized GPU kernel libraries. These libraries underpin the correctness and efficiency of training and inference across diverse GPU platforms, implementing attention, GEMM, quantization, and low-precision operators while managing tensor shapes, memory layouts, code generation, and hardware-specific dispatch. Problems at this layer can silently corrupt outputs, hang GPUs, prevent compilation, introduce deployment incompatibilities, or degrade performance, thereby reducing developer productivity and wasting expensive GPU resources. We present the first comprehensive empirical study of issues in GPU kernel libraries for LLM systems. We manually analyzed 300 high-quality GitHub issue reports, their discussions, and available fixes from seven representative libraries: FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers, and bitsandbytes. The analysis characterizes symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices. Our main findings are: (1) 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions, so validation must cover the deployment and execution stack, not just kernel code. (2) Kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing, and hardware resources. Violations can produce incorrect outputs or launch failures even for supported operations, highlighting the need for explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing. (3) Current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for identifying low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures. We outline research opportunities and tooling directions to support future LLM GPU kernel development.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first comprehensive empirical study of 300 GitHub issues from seven GPU kernel libraries used in LLM systems, characterizing their symptoms, root causes, fixes and testing practices. It finds that 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions.
AI.motivation: GPU kernel libraries underpin the correctness and efficiency of LLM training and inference, yet problems at this layer can silently corrupt outputs, hang GPUs or block deployment, and no comprehensive empirical study of their issues existed.
AI.method: The authors manually analyzed 300 high-quality GitHub issue reports, their discussions and available fixes from seven libraries (FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers and bitsandbytes), characterizing symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices.
AI.result: 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions; kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing and hardware resources; current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures.
AI.conclusion: Validation must cover the deployment and execution stack rather than kernel code alone, explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing are needed, and the authors outline research opportunities and tooling directions for LLM GPU kernel development.

title: Ontology-Driven Control of Conversational Agents with a Use-Case for Job Interview Practice
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely used as conversational agents in both domain-specific and open-domain situations. In domain-specific context, it is often necessary to adapt those LLMs to obtain conversations with desired characteristics, whether those apply at the level of each response (e.g. for tone or style) or more globally (i.e. at the level of a conversational strategy). Such adaptations are, however, generally realized in an ad hoc way, through specific, non-reusable, and non-transparent developments. In this paper, we propose an ontology-based approach to design conversational strategies that rely on the desired and measured characteristics of textual utterances in the conversation. Through a use case related to job interview practice, we show how this approach can be used to control LLMs to follow the strategy defined in the ontology. To this end, we automatically fine-tune the LLM to improve its compliance with ontologically-defined conversation characteristics. Our results show that training the LLM from formally defined concepts effectively enhances alignment with the requested characteristics. Hence, this work demonstrates how ontology-guided conversation control can be achieved while taking into account multiple, concurrent conversation aspects that are formally and transparently defined.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an ontology-based approach to design conversational strategies for LLM agents, demonstrated on job interview practice. Fine-tuning the LLM from ontologically defined concepts improves its compliance with the requested conversation characteristics.
AI.motivation: Adapting LLMs to domain-specific conversations is usually ad hoc, non-reusable and non-transparent, and the characteristics of utterances at both the response level and the strategy level need a formal, transparent specification.
AI.method: Conversational strategies are defined in an ontology over the desired and measured characteristics of textual utterances, and the LLM is automatically fine-tuned to improve its compliance with these ontologically defined characteristics, using job interview practice as the use case.
AI.result: Training the LLM from formally defined concepts effectively enhances alignment with the requested characteristics, and the approach handles multiple concurrent conversation aspects.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-guided conversation control is feasible while keeping multiple conversation aspects formally and transparently defined, offering a reusable alternative to ad hoc adaptation.

title: AutoRefine: Auto-Calibrating Code Judges from Workflow Outcomes
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, prepared for submission to CAIN 2027 industrial track
summary: LLM judges increasingly serve as quality gates for code changes that have no test oracle, but a judge prompt must be calibrated for its task and recalibrated as the system it judges evolves, while hand labels for the calibration are resource intensive and go stale. Development workflows emit outcome labels for free (tests pass or fail, changes land or are abandoned), but these labels are noisy. We present AutoRefine, a loop that rewrites a deployable judge's prompt to reproduce outcome labels, with an informed teacher that sees the judge's input plus the outcome, explains each label it keeps, and abstains when the outcome cannot be explained from what the judge sees. On a held-out dataset with an execution oracle, calibration raised chance-corrected agreement (Scott's $\pi$) from 0.36 to 0.60. On a deployed agent's outcome labels, with 25\% flipped at random to introduce noise, the teacher set aside flipped \textsc{fail} labels at more than twice the rate of genuine ones, cutting overall label noise from 25\% to 20\%. Recalibrating that agent's judge using AutoRefine raised its agreement with merge/abandon outcomes on 17 independently held-out diffs from the current workflow ($\pi$ 0.16 to 0.51); on 16 diffs from older workflows, the previous judge stayed ahead, illustrating the need for recalibration as the agent evolves. By abstaining, the teacher not only removes noisy labels but also flags changes whose outcome the judge's input cannot explain, telling a team when a judge needs better inputs rather than a better prompt.

AI.tldr: AutoRefine is a loop that rewrites an LLM code judge's prompt so that its verdicts reproduce noisy outcome labels from development workflows, using a teacher that abstains when an outcome cannot be explained. On a held-out dataset with an execution oracle, Scott's pi rose from 0.36 to 0.60.
AI.motivation: LLM judges that gate code changes without test oracles need prompts calibrated to their task and recalibrated as the system evolves, while hand labels are costly and go stale; workflow outcome labels are free but noisy.
AI.method: An informed teacher sees the judge's input plus the outcome, explains each label it keeps, and abstains when the outcome cannot be explained from what the judge sees; the loop rewrites the deployable judge's prompt to reproduce the labels the teacher keeps.
AI.result: Calibration raised chance-corrected agreement (Scott's pi) from 0.36 to 0.60 on a held-out dataset with an execution oracle. With 25% of labels flipped at random, the teacher set aside flipped fail labels at more than twice the rate of genuine ones, reducing overall label noise from 25% to 20%. Recalibration raised agreement with merge/abandon outcomes on 17 held-out diffs (pi 0.16 to 0.51), while on 16 diffs from older workflows the previous judge stayed ahead.
AI.conclusion: Abstentions reveal changes whose outcome the judge's input cannot explain, signalling when a judge needs better inputs rather than a better prompt, and recalibration is needed as the agent evolves.

title: Towards an Autonomous AI Steward for Large-Scale Physics Experiments: Integrating Causal Diagnostics, RAG, and Conformal Prediction
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure, 2nd International Conference on AI for Science (AI4Sci2026), 5-9 October 2026, Mainz, Germany (PoS)
summary: Long-term particle physics experiments face critical operational challenges: monitoring non-stationary machine data streams and preserving tacit expert knowledge. We present the "Helmholtz Co-Pilot," a hybrid Multi-Agent System (MAS) acting as an autonomous experiment steward. The system can be triggered interactively by human operators or autonomously by an asynchronous causal diagnostics engine that runs independently of the MAS reasoning core. Continuously monitoring live hardware streams such as data acquisition and slow control, this engine performs dynamic causal discovery to trace cascading alarms back to their root causes and applies adaptive model selection to keep forecasts reliable across shifting machine states; upon detecting an anomaly, it hands a structured diagnostic report to the MAS. The reasoning layer itself relies on a high-throughput C++ core and a Python edge architecture orchestrating a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of specialized ReAct workers. It integrates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) backbone for institutional memory and leverages conformal prediction to bound its evidence-based recommendations with mathematical coverage guarantees. This extended abstract outlines the architecture, the integration of software-enforced Human-in-the-Loop (HitL) guardrails, and ongoing shadow-testing within the KATRIN experiment.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the Helmholtz Co-Pilot, a hybrid multi-agent system that acts as an autonomous steward for a particle physics experiment, combining causal diagnostics, RAG and conformal prediction. The system is undergoing shadow-testing within the KATRIN experiment.
AI.motivation: Long-term particle physics experiments face non-stationary machine data streams and the loss of tacit expert knowledge, which makes monitoring and operation difficult.
AI.method: An asynchronous causal diagnostics engine runs independently, performing dynamic causal discovery on live hardware streams to trace cascading alarms to root causes and applying adaptive model selection; upon detecting an anomaly it hands a structured report to a C++ and Python multi-agent system of ReAct workers arranged as a DAG, which uses RAG for institutional memory, conformal prediction for coverage-guaranteed recommendations, and software-enforced human-in-the-loop guardrails.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results; it outlines the architecture and states that shadow-testing within the KATRIN experiment is ongoing.
AI.conclusion: The work presents an architecture for an autonomous experiment steward with human oversight, and its evaluation is still in progress.

title: AUTEUR: Acoustic Plan Learning for Red-Teaming Text-to-Audio Models
summary: Automated red-teaming of text-to-audio models requires test prompts that pass textual screening and expose harmful acoustic content. The central challenge is to connect the sounds produced by the target model to both reusable test generation and prompt revision. Our key idea is to represent test descriptions as structured acoustic plans that organize foreground sounds, context, and vocal attributes. To this end, we propose acoustic plan learning, a framework that learns and refines these plans using waveform feedback. We train the plan generator through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with audio feedback while keeping the target audio model fixed. At inference time, the same trained model generates initial plans and uses feedback to revise their context and vocal attributes while preserving the foreground. Experiments across four target systems show attack success rates of 79.4% on TangoFlux and 95.6% on Kling. The resulting test prompts also transfer across open-source and closed-source models, indicating shared acoustic vulnerabilities.

AI.tldr: AUTEUR learns acoustic plans that generate test prompts for red-teaming text-to-audio models, refined with waveform feedback through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Attack success rates reach 79.4% on TangoFlux and 95.6% on Kling.
AI.motivation: Automated red-teaming of text-to-audio models needs prompts that pass textual screening yet expose harmful acoustic content, and existing approaches do not connect the sounds produced by the target model to test generation and prompt revision.
AI.method: Test descriptions are represented as structured acoustic plans that organize foreground sounds, context and vocal attributes; a plan generator is trained with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with audio feedback while the target model stays fixed, and at inference it revises context and vocal attributes while preserving the foreground.
AI.result: Attack success rates are 79.4% on TangoFlux and 95.6% on Kling across four target systems, and the resulting test prompts transfer across open-source and closed-source models.
AI.conclusion: The transferability of the prompts indicates shared acoustic vulnerabilities across text-to-audio models.

title: Challenges, Opportunities, and Misconceptions in Neurosymbolic AI
summary: We examine opportunities for neurosymbolic AI alongside increasingly powerful neural models, particularly with regards to efficiency, safety and interpretability. We identify two major challenges: ensuring semantic alignment between neural and symbolic components, and managing the computational cost of symbolic inference and learning. We discuss representative methodological approaches to these challenges and address several common misconceptions concerning differentiability, independence assumptions, and scalability. This paper synthesizes perspectives developed through discussions in the Neurosymbolic Programming and Reasoning (NPR) working group at the 2026 CNRS workshop Neurosymbolic Methods and Their Applications in Data Science, rather than providing an exhaustive survey.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper examines opportunities for neurosymbolic AI in efficiency, safety and interpretability, identifies two major challenges and addresses common misconceptions. It synthesizes discussions of a CNRS workshop working group rather than providing an exhaustive survey.
AI.motivation: As neural models grow more powerful, neurosymbolic AI needs a clear treatment of semantic alignment between neural and symbolic components and of the computational cost of symbolic inference and learning, and several misconceptions persist.
AI.method: The authors discuss representative methodological approaches to the two challenges and address misconceptions about differentiability, independence assumptions and scalability, synthesizing perspectives developed in the NPR working group at the 2026 CNRS workshop.
AI.result: The paper identifies two major challenges, namely semantic alignment and the computational cost of symbolic inference and learning, and clarifies several misconceptions; it reports no experiments.
AI.conclusion: Neurosymbolic AI retains opportunities in efficiency, safety and interpretability if its challenges are addressed, and the paper is a synthesis of perspectives rather than a survey.

title: SafeOrchestrate: Runtime Checked Intent-Driven Orchestration for Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: Modern cyber physical systems (CPS) integrate heterogeneous sensors, actuators, controllers, and services, composed at runtime rather than at design time. Orchestrating such systems through natural language (NL) is attractive, but unconstrained large language model (LLM) tool use is risky because actions must respect device capabilities, runtime state, and safety constraints. We present Safe Orchestrate, a reference architecture for runtime checked, intent driven CPS orchestration. Given an NL intent, it derives atomic goals, generates a runtime checkable specification for each, grounds the specifications to device affordances, and verifies every candidate action against runtime state and safety constraints before execution. In a Web of Things (WoT) instantiation, the architecture produces Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) style specifications from the NL intent, grounds them to Thing Description (TD) affordances exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and checks candidate actions against satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) backed guardrails. We evaluate this instantiation on simulated smart home, greenhouse, and industrial automation tasks against a direct LLM to MCP baseline. Safe Orchestrate maintains 100% required action accuracy on every task and 100% MCP Execution Similarity (MCP ES) on all but one, where MCP ES is 92%. By contrast, the baseline degrades on multi device, event triggered, and ordered tasks, with MCP ES falling to 13%. These results suggest that combining LLM based specification generation with role aware grounding and runtime constraint checking improves reliability for open CPS orchestration without enriched TD annotations or planning domain expertise.

AI.tldr: SafeOrchestrate is a reference architecture that turns natural-language intents into runtime-checked orchestration of cyber-physical systems through LTL-style specifications, Thing Description grounding and SMT-backed guardrails. It keeps 100% required action accuracy on every task, where a direct LLM-to-MCP baseline degrades.
AI.motivation: Unconstrained LLM tool use to orchestrate cyber-physical systems from natural language is risky, since actions must respect device capabilities, runtime state and safety constraints.
AI.method: Given a natural-language intent, the architecture derives atomic goals, generates a runtime checkable specification for each, grounds it to device affordances, and verifies every candidate action against runtime state and safety constraints before execution; in a Web of Things instantiation, LTL-style specifications are grounded to Thing Description affordances exposed through MCP and checked with SMT-backed guardrails.
AI.result: On simulated smart home, greenhouse and industrial automation tasks, the system maintains 100% required action accuracy on every task and 100% MCP Execution Similarity on all but one task, where it reaches 92%; the baseline's MCP ES falls to 13% on multi-device, event-triggered and ordered tasks.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM-based specification generation with role-aware grounding and runtime constraint checking improves reliability for open CPS orchestration without enriched TD annotations or planning domain expertise.

title: KineCouple: Substrate-conditioned residual readout for enzyme kinetic prediction
summary: Accurate prediction of enzyme kinetic parameters can support enzyme engineering and metabolic modeling by complementing experimental characterization. Existing prediction methods often pool residue-level protein features before combining them with substrate features. Such substrate-independent pooling cannot adapt residue weighting to the substrate during aggregation, potentially diluting information relevant to a specific enzyme-substrate pair. Since the contributions of individual residues to catalysis can depend on the substrate, substrate-conditioned aggregation offers a way to emphasize residue features relevant to the prediction. We introduce KineCouple, which uses substrate queries and residue-level keys and values in cross-attention, allowing the substrate to guide residue selection before aggregation. The model preserves the global protein representation and adds a gated correction defined as the difference between the conditioned readout and a uniform readout. ProtT5 and MolT5 remain frozen, and separate models predict kcat and Km on a logarithmic scale. In pooled out-of-fold predictions on the CataPro benchmarks, KineCouple reduces kcat RMSE from 1.333 to 1.330 and increases PCC from 0.492 to 0.496 relative to reproduced CataPro. For Km, RMSE decreases from 0.998 to 0.997 and PCC increases from 0.633 to 0.634. Spearman correlation also improves for both tasks.

AI.tldr: KineCouple predicts enzyme kcat and Km using substrate-conditioned cross-attention over residue features with a gated correction. On CataPro benchmarks it modestly improves on the reproduced baseline, lowering kcat RMSE from 1.333 to 1.330.
AI.motivation: Existing predictors pool residue-level protein features independently of the substrate, which can dilute information relevant to a specific enzyme-substrate pair, since the catalytic contribution of each residue can depend on the substrate.
AI.method: Substrate queries attend over residue-level keys and values in cross-attention before aggregation; the model keeps a global protein representation and adds a gated correction equal to the difference between the conditioned readout and a uniform readout; ProtT5 and MolT5 are frozen, and separate models predict kcat and Km on a logarithmic scale.
AI.result: In pooled out-of-fold predictions on CataPro, kcat RMSE goes from 1.333 to 1.330 and PCC from 0.492 to 0.496 relative to reproduced CataPro; for Km, RMSE goes from 0.998 to 0.997 and PCC from 0.633 to 0.634; Spearman correlation also improves for both tasks.
AI.conclusion: Substrate-conditioned readout gives small gains over the reproduced baseline on both kinetic parameters, and the absolute improvements are modest.

title: Exploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations
summary: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP's potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer. Homepage: this https URL GitHub: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper systematically studies Weight-Space Programming, in which reasoning agents directly edit neural network parameters, across 16 editing trajectories, seven benchmarks and two Qwen3.5 scales. Localized edits give gains of up to 36.72 points, but cross-task transfer and reliability are uneven.
AI.motivation: Weight-Space Programming offers an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation, but its capabilities, cross-task generalization and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood.
AI.method: The authors run 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks on Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B, evaluating full held-out accuracy and the cross-task transfer of edited checkpoints.
AI.result: Accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72 and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval and SciBench, and modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement; a Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18 and 20.10 points without further editing but leaves SciCode unchanged; outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 retain the original weights.
AI.conclusion: WSP enables highly localized model adaptation with promising but uneven cross-task transfer, and intervention discovery, reliability and transfer remain the key challenges.

title: Against All Likelihood
summary: Maximum likelihood is the dominant training principle for large language models, yet likelihood is neither necessary nor sufficient for truth. Unlikely events happen every day, and frequently repeated statements can be false. Drawing on a philosophical tradition that ties objectivity to invariance rather than probability (from Nozick's account of objective facts and Wigner's principles of invariance to the structural realism of Poincaré and Cassirer), we argue that the truth of a statement should be judged not by its probability under a single distribution, but by its invariance across relevant transformations of the environment. We connect this view to machine learning literature on out-of-distribution generalization and invariant learning, sketch how invariance could be tested at inference time with language models, and discuss implications for continual learning.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that the truth of a statement should be judged by its invariance across relevant transformations of the environment rather than by its probability under a single distribution. It holds that maximum likelihood training is neither necessary nor sufficient for truth.
AI.motivation: Maximum likelihood is the dominant training principle for large language models, yet likelihood is neither necessary nor sufficient for truth, since unlikely events happen and frequently repeated statements can be false.
AI.method: Drawing on a philosophical tradition that ties objectivity to invariance, from Nozick and Wigner to the structural realism of Poincaré and Cassirer, the authors connect this view to the literature on out-of-distribution generalization and invariant learning and sketch how invariance could be tested at inference time with language models.
AI.result: The paper reports no experiments; it sketches an inference-time invariance test for language models and discusses implications for continual learning.
AI.conclusion: Truth should be assessed by invariance rather than probability, which has implications for how language models are trained and evaluated, including in continual learning.

title: Travel Cost Calibration for Multi-Agent Target Assignment and Pathfinding
summary: Target assignment and pathfinding (TAPF) is an appealing extension of classical multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF): each agent has a set of targets, and the planner must both assign a target to each agent and plan collision-free paths for them. A trivial approach is to compute an assignment that minimizes the total single-agent shortest-path distance over agent--target pairs, and then solve the resulting MAPF instance. However, this approach falls short because the shortest-path distance remains a proxy that ignores interference among agents. Assigning targets based on the costs agents actually pay, which depend on how every other agent is assigned and routed, would yield a better final outcome. To this end, we propose an iterative TAPF method that improves target assignments by calibrating travel cost estimates from fast, suboptimal MAPF feedback. Experiments show that our method produces solutions close to optimal on small instances and outperforms existing planners in solution quality on larger ones.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an iterative target assignment and pathfinding method that calibrates agents' travel cost estimates from fast, suboptimal MAPF feedback. It yields solutions close to optimal on small instances and better solution quality than existing planners on larger ones.
AI.motivation: Assigning targets by minimizing total single-agent shortest-path distance ignores interference among agents, so the resulting assignment is a poor proxy for the costs agents actually pay once every other agent is assigned and routed.
AI.method: An iterative TAPF method improves target assignments by calibrating travel cost estimates from feedback provided by fast, suboptimal MAPF solutions.
AI.result: Solutions are close to optimal on small instances and outperform existing planners in solution quality on larger instances.
AI.conclusion: Assigning targets according to calibrated travel costs yields better final outcomes than assignment based on single-agent shortest-path distances.

title: PhyCAD: Physics-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
summary: Language-driven computer-aided design (CAD) generation enables the creation of editable parametric models from text, yet geometric correctness alone does not ensure physical feasibility. We present PhyCAD, a framework for physics-aware Text-to-CAD generation that trains language models to produce executable CadQuery programs under geometric and physical constraints. To support this setting, we construct a Text-to-CAD dataset that links parametric CAD models with geometric specifications, loading conditions, and physical constraints. We further develop an automated CAD--CAE verifier that combines program execution, geometric checks, and finite element analysis to provide feedback for model training. A key learning challenge is to prioritize joint satisfaction of geometric and physical constraints while retaining informative feedback on partial progress. A flat aggregation of heterogeneous rewards can obscure this priority, allowing improvements in individual criteria to compensate for unmet design requirements. We therefore introduce a Hierarchical Balanced Advantage for Group Relative Policy Optimization, grouping candidates into levels according to their verification status and combining between-level progress with objective-wise peer ranking within each level. This formulation preserves cross-level priority in the training signal while providing fine-grained feedback for satisfying constraints and improving feasible designs. Experiments across multiple language models show that PhyCAD consistently improves joint geometric and physical constraint satisfaction. These results demonstrate the value of verifiable engineering feedback for advancing language-driven CAD generation beyond geometric reconstruction toward physics-aware design.

AI.tldr: PhyCAD trains language models to generate executable CadQuery programs that satisfy both geometric and physical constraints, using a verifier that combines program execution, geometric checks and finite element analysis. Its Hierarchical Balanced Advantage for Group Relative Policy Optimization consistently improves joint constraint satisfaction across several language models.
AI.motivation: Geometric correctness alone does not ensure physical feasibility in text-to-CAD generation, and a flat aggregation of heterogeneous rewards can let improvements in some criteria compensate for unmet design requirements.
AI.method: The authors build a Text-to-CAD dataset linking parametric models with geometric specifications, loading conditions and physical constraints, develop an automated CAD-CAE verifier, and introduce Hierarchical Balanced Advantage for Group Relative Policy Optimization, which groups candidates into levels by verification status and combines between-level progress with objective-wise peer ranking within each level.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple language models show that PhyCAD consistently improves joint geometric and physical constraint satisfaction.
AI.conclusion: Verifiable engineering feedback, combined with a hierarchical priority in the training signal, moves language-driven CAD generation beyond geometric reconstruction toward physics-aware design.

title: ROAM: Retrieval-Augmented Optimization for Feasible Multi-Day Itinerary Planning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can draft plausible travel itineraries, but the plans they produce are frequently infeasible: attractions are grouped into days without regard for geography, opening hours are ignored, and a single generation pass cannot reliably organize a multi-day trip. We present ROAM, a retrieval-augmented agentic framework for spontaneous multi-day itinerary planning that couples semantic preference retrieval with explicit spatiotemporal optimization. ROAM embeds the natural-language request, retrieves a compact candidate set from a curated point-of-interest (POI) database, partitions candidates into day groups through maximal-clique analysis and K-means, orders each day with a quality-biased simulated-annealing TSP solver, and repairs hard opening-hour violations with greedy exchange. A spatiotemporal retrieval layer injects weather forecasts, real road distances and POI operating hours into the prompt, after which the LLM renders a structured, map-ready itinerary; an interactive ReAct-style replanning agent then supports natural-language edits while re-checking feasibility. Across four Chinese cities and 510 POIs, ROAM produces 27.5 POIs per three-day plan versus 19.3 for a bare LLM and 17.0 for a retrieval-only baseline (+42% and +62%), while reducing route dispersion from 2,101 to 677 (3.1x). Ablations show that spatial optimization is the dominant driver of route efficiency and that hard time-window repair prevents roughly 30% of attractions from violating operating hours.

AI.tldr: ROAM is a retrieval-augmented agentic framework for multi-day itinerary planning that couples LLM generation with spatiotemporal optimization to produce feasible plans. Across four Chinese cities and 510 POIs it yields 27.5 POIs per three-day plan, versus 19.3 for a bare LLM.
AI.motivation: LLM-drafted itineraries are often infeasible, ignoring geography and opening hours and failing to organize a multi-day trip in a single generation pass.
AI.method: ROAM embeds the request, retrieves a compact set of candidate POIs, partitions them into day groups by maximal-clique analysis and K-means, orders each day with a quality-biased simulated-annealing TSP solver, and repairs opening-hour violations with greedy exchange; weather forecasts, real road distances and POI operating hours are injected into the prompt, and a ReAct-style replanning agent supports edits while rechecking feasibility.
AI.result: Across four Chinese cities and 510 POIs, ROAM produces 27.5 POIs per three-day plan versus 19.3 for a bare LLM and 17.0 for a retrieval-only baseline (+42% and +62%), and route dispersion falls from 2,101 to 677 (3.1x); ablations show that spatial optimization drives route efficiency and that time-window repair prevents roughly 30% of attractions from violating operating hours.
AI.conclusion: Explicit spatiotemporal optimization combined with LLM generation makes multi-day itineraries substantially more feasible and efficient than generation alone.

title: MIRA: Mitigating Pole Geometry Bias in Recurrent Language Models
summary: We show that the Transformer's recurrent successors --- such as selective state-space models (SSMs), Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV), and Retentive Network (RetNet) --- can be characterized as infinite-impulse-response (IIR) systems. The zero--pole geometries of these IIR systems characterize the temporal modes they can represent. However, to trade parallelism, the algebraic structures of the parameterizations of these recurrent systems often give rise to poles constrained to the real axis, thereby inducing an architectural bias in their recurrent dynamics. To unify these recurrent architectures and eliminate their pole geometry bias, inspired by the lattice--ladder realization of general IIR systems, we present \textsc{Mira} (\textbf{M}odal \textbf{I}IR \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{A}rchitecture), a unified family of linear-time recurrent architectures for building large language models (LLMs) with a highly parallel algebraic structure. Each \textsc{Mira} block realizes a higher-order IIR system that represents temporal modes from token streams through a lattice--ladder structure, followed by a feed-forward network (FFN). This realization enables the model to represent the temporal modes associated with both real and complex-conjugate poles. We pretrain \textsc{Mira-S}, a 12-layer small-scale LLM with 0.14B parameters composed entirely of \textsc{Mira} blocks. Throughout the pretraining, \textsc{Mira-S} achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines, exhibits stronger context-window generalization beyond the training length, and attains higher throughput with a dedicated CUDA kernel.

AI.tldr: MIRA is a family of linear-time recurrent architectures built from higher-order IIR blocks with a lattice-ladder structure, removing the real-axis pole constraint of SSMs, RWKV and RetNet. The 0.14B-parameter model MIRA-S achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines.
AI.motivation: Recurrent successors of the Transformer, such as selective state-space models, RWKV and RetNet, are constrained to poles on the real axis for parallelism, which induces an architectural bias in their recurrent dynamics.
AI.method: Each MIRA block realizes a higher-order IIR system with a lattice-ladder structure that represents temporal modes from token streams, followed by a feed-forward network, which allows both real and complex-conjugate poles; the authors pretrain MIRA-S, a 12-layer, 0.14B-parameter model built entirely of MIRA blocks, with a dedicated CUDA kernel.
AI.result: During pretraining, MIRA-S achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines, shows stronger context-window generalization beyond the training length, and attains higher throughput.
AI.conclusion: Modal IIR recurrence removes the pole geometry bias while keeping a highly parallel algebraic structure, offering a unified family of recurrent LLM architectures.

title: Typed-Centrality Grounding for Agentic GraphRAG: A Symbolic Approach for Agentic Reasoning
comment: Preprint. 7 pages. Final version published in 2026 IEEE Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC), DOI: https://doi.org/10.1109/ISCC70364.2026.11739974
summary: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) represent two approaches for knowledge representation and reasoning over heterogeneous data. Recent research has explored their integration through Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) systems, which use KGs to provide structured context to LLMs. However, existing GraphRAG approaches treat KGs as homogeneous graphs and rely on textual similarity between the input prompt and the context, rather than using it as a source of deterministic knowledge. This work proposes an agent-based GraphRAG system that introduces a symbolic layer to integrate deterministic reasoning alongside text similarities. This approach is based on the definition of typed centralities for KGs, where centrality measures are computed separately for each specific KG's class. This information is used to construct a symbolic representation that is provided to the LLM as a deterministic source. The proposed system was mathematically validated and evaluated on a real-world POLE (Person, Object, Location, Event) dataset, comparing reasoning and information retrieval with and without the symbolic layer. The results indicate that the our approach leads to responses that are more consistent with the context, improving the generated outputs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an agent-based GraphRAG system with a symbolic layer built on typed centralities, computed separately for each knowledge graph class, which gives the LLM deterministic knowledge alongside text similarity. On a POLE dataset the responses are more consistent with the context.
AI.motivation: Existing GraphRAG approaches treat knowledge graphs as homogeneous and rely on textual similarity between prompt and context, rather than using the graph as a source of deterministic knowledge.
AI.method: Typed centrality measures are computed separately for each KG class and used to build a symbolic representation that is provided to the LLM as a deterministic source within an agent-based GraphRAG system; the approach was mathematically validated and compared with and without the symbolic layer on a real-world POLE (Person, Object, Location, Event) dataset.
AI.result: The results indicate that the approach leads to responses more consistent with the context and improves the generated outputs; the abstract reports no specific numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Integrating deterministic symbolic information with text similarity improves LLM outputs in GraphRAG-based reasoning and information retrieval.

title: Agentic AI for Healthcare Claim Denial Analysis: A Policy-Grounded Framework for Privacy Preservation
summary: In the healthcare sector, claim denials impose significant financial and administrative burdens, emphasizing the need for automated and trustworthy decision-support systems. This paper proposes a modular Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework for healthcare claim denial analysis, integrating specialized agents for denial risk prediction, risk factor identification, diagnosis-procedure-medication code relationship analysis, and counterfactual analysis. The framework integrates predictive analytics, graph-based learning, a Hybrid Contextual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in healthcare policy documents, and a dedicated HIPAA Compliance Agent to support privacy protection. Evaluated on a synthetic healthcare claims dataset, the framework achieved 98% traceability of reported numerical findings, validated 214 of 216 policy citations, and removed all 280 identified sensitive identifiers without modifying the underlying analysis. These findings pave the way for further research into Agentic AI as a framework for explainable, policy-aware, and privacy-preserving healthcare claim denial management.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a modular agentic AI framework for healthcare claim denial analysis that combines predictive analytics, graph learning, a policy-grounded RAG pipeline and a HIPAA Compliance Agent. On a synthetic claims dataset it achieved 98% traceability of reported numerical findings and removed all 280 identified sensitive identifiers.
AI.motivation: Claim denials impose significant financial and administrative burdens, and the sector needs automated decision-support systems that are both trustworthy and privacy-preserving.
AI.method: Specialized agents handle denial risk prediction, risk factor identification, diagnosis-procedure-medication code relationship analysis and counterfactual analysis; a Hybrid Contextual RAG pipeline is grounded in healthcare policy documents, and a dedicated HIPAA Compliance Agent supports privacy protection.
AI.result: On a synthetic healthcare claims dataset, the framework achieved 98% traceability of reported numerical findings, validated 214 of 216 policy citations, and removed all 280 identified sensitive identifiers without modifying the underlying analysis.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI grounded in policy and equipped with privacy controls is a promising direction for explainable, policy-aware and privacy-preserving claim denial management, and it warrants further research.

title: Definitions, Label Names, or Demonstrations? Auditing What Governs LLM Annotation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate social-science texts, but high accuracy does not establish that they apply researcher-supplied category definitions: predictions may instead reflect prior associations with category labels or labeled demonstrations. We introduce a counterfactual audit that reassigns definitions among output labels, distinguishing adherence to supplied definitions from preservation of a dataset's original mapping. Across three political-text datasets, models rarely follow reassigned definitions, and standard fine-tuning strengthens the original mapping without reliably increasing definition adherence. We then study retrieval-augmented annotation. Retrieving the nearest training examples generally outperforms retrieving examples separately within each category despite using fewer demonstrations. On the two tasks with substantial gains, direct \(k\)-nearest-neighbor classification recovers 74--93\% of the improvement, indicating that neighborhood labels provide much of the predictive signal. Relabeling fixed demonstrations redirects predictions, whereas aligning demonstrations with reassigned definitions substantially increases adherence to the new mapping. Thus, accuracy-improving interventions need not increase codebook adherence; definitions, category labels, demonstrations, retrieval, and training data should be aligned and validated jointly.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether LLM annotators follow researcher-supplied category definitions and finds that models rarely follow reassigned definitions. Nearest-example retrieval generally outperforms per-category retrieval, and k-nearest-neighbor classification recovers 74-93% of the improvement on the two tasks with substantial gains.
AI.motivation: High annotation accuracy does not establish that LLMs apply supplied category definitions, since predictions may instead reflect prior associations with category labels or labeled demonstrations, which matters for social-science annotation.
AI.method: A counterfactual audit reassigns definitions among output labels to separate adherence to supplied definitions from preservation of a dataset's original mapping, across three political-text datasets; the authors then study retrieval-augmented annotation and the effect of relabeling or aligning demonstrations.
AI.result: Models rarely follow reassigned definitions, and standard fine-tuning strengthens the original mapping without reliably increasing definition adherence; nearest-example retrieval generally outperforms per-category retrieval with fewer demonstrations; direct k-nearest-neighbor classification recovers 74-93% of the improvement on the two tasks with substantial gains; aligning demonstrations with reassigned definitions substantially increases adherence to the new mapping.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy-improving interventions need not increase codebook adherence, so definitions, category labels, demonstrations, retrieval and training data should be aligned and validated jointly.

title: ENGRAM: From Agent Experience to Weights through Verified Consolidation
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures
summary: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in this http URL.

AI.tldr: ENGRAM consolidates agent experience into model weights by separating training admission from memory release, using a demonstration-aware gate and a verification gate. Verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while staying close to retain-all performance, and ENGRAM also improves task performance.
AI.motivation: Consolidating stored experience into weights requires deciding which experience to train on and when external records can be released; admission based only on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, and removal right after training can discard guidance the model still needs.
AI.method: A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or on sufficient successful teacher demonstrations; the student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph; a verification gate compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes, and release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria.
AI.result: ENGRAM shows consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls across interactive and reasoning benchmarks; verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release; ENGRAM also reduces input-token usage and model calls.
AI.conclusion: Verified, selective release lets agents keep external guidance only for skills that fail verification, reducing retrievable experience without sacrificing performance.
