Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods either rely on inference-time correction around frozen models or train on limited circuit types without directly using simulation outcomes as training signals. A key bottleneck is that existing datasets do not provide sufficient task information for training LLMs on end-to-end specification-conditioned design. To fill this gap, we first construct a large-scale simulation-grounded dataset with 8,626 design tasks across 10 different types of analog circuits, where each task includes a textual description, labeled I/O ports, loading condition, target specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. Using this dataset, we present SAFTAC, a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to generate and revise analog circuit design. SAFTAC combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning, which progressively builds the capabilities required for analog circuit design and feedback-guided correction, with simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning, which further optimizes models using simulation-grounded rewards. We evaluate SAFTAC under single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback, showing improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% and 7.8%, respectively.

AI.tldr: SAFTAC is a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to generate and revise analog circuit designs, using a new dataset of 8,626 simulation-grounded design tasks across 10 analog circuit types. It improves over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% under single-pass generation and by 7.8% under two-pass generation with simulation feedback.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM methods either rely on inference-time correction around frozen models or train on limited circuit types without using simulation outcomes as training signals, and existing datasets lack the task information needed for end-to-end specification-conditioned design.
AI.method: Each dataset task includes a textual description, labelled I/O ports, loading condition, target specifications, a testbench and a reference netlist; SAFTAC combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning with feedback-guided correction and simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning that uses simulation-grounded rewards.
AI.result: SAFTAC improves over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% under single-pass generation and by 7.8% under two-pass generation with simulation feedback.
AI.conclusion: Using simulation outcomes as training signals and feedback lets open-source LLMs improve over a strong closed-source model on analog circuit design.

title: PINNeval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Standard for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 54 pages. Code: this https URL
summary: The Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) literature has produced a rapidly expanding catalogue of methods. We divide a PINN training pipeline systematically into four components and observe that many existing benchmarks study these components in isolation. These components are domain-importance adaptation, loss balancing, neural network architecture, and optimization scheme. Moreover, the studies set the surrounding and not considered components of the pipeline to a minimal default that is no longer representative of current best practice approaches. Conclusions drawn under such conditions may not transfer to competitive pipelines. In this work, we propose a new evaluation protocol that (1) treats the four components as an integrated system; (2) crucially requires competitive implementations of the components not under investigation; (3) specifies the metrics and reporting format; and (4) is accompanied by structured documentation that ensures the traceability of evaluations across studies. Based on this comprehensive protocol, we release PINNpipe, an innovative JAX package containing 18 different methods from the current literature as well as nine efficiently implemented benchmark problems. Using PINNpipe, we illustrate our evaluation protocol in relation to established benchmark studies and report results that challenge common assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an evaluation protocol for physics-informed neural networks that treats domain-importance adaptation, loss balancing, architecture and optimisation as an integrated system, and releases PINNpipe, a JAX package with 18 methods and nine benchmark problems. Applying the protocol, the authors report results that challenge common assumptions.
AI.motivation: Many PINN benchmarks study pipeline components in isolation with minimal default settings that no longer represent best practice, so their conclusions may not transfer to competitive pipelines.
AI.method: The protocol treats the four components as one system, requires competitive implementations of the components not under investigation, specifies metrics and reporting format, and is accompanied by structured documentation for traceability across studies.
AI.result: PINNpipe contains 18 methods from the literature and nine efficiently implemented benchmark problems; the authors illustrate the protocol in relation to established benchmark studies and report results that challenge common assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations that keep the surrounding pipeline at competitive settings are needed before conclusions about individual PINN components can be relied on to transfer.

title: Towards Label-Efficient Geospatial Foundation Model Adaptation via Positive-Unlabeled Learning for Building Damage Mapping
summary: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.

AI.tldr: PUMA is a positive-unlabeled framework for adapting geospatial foundation models to building damage mapping that needs annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. It is reported to be effective and robust on global disaster benchmarks and to map damage accurately in a real application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning does not guarantee label efficiency, and when weak supervision is used for building damage mapping, learning sufficiently discriminative representations becomes difficult.
AI.method: PUMA combines non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement, which mitigates the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, with latent-state-based label disambiguation that refines supervision reversibly without estimating class priors.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrate effectiveness and robustness, and a real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires shows accurate damage mapping under highly limited supervision.
AI.conclusion: Weakly supervised PEFT is presented as a label-efficient pathway from geospatial foundation models to real-world applications.

title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
comment: IAAI-27 (Oral)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.

AI.tldr: CascadeRec is a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a financial planning and analysis SaaS provider, escalating only requests likely to benefit from extra inference compute. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier it reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date.
AI.motivation: Running an expensive LLM reranker on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers recommendation quality.
AI.method: A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request, and a router escalates selected requests to a Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning or a larger model); the rollout is segment-gated.
AI.result: In a production A/B experiment running for over a month, inference cost fell by about 10%. On MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics, uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and escalating cold users can make the loss larger.
AI.conclusion: Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, motivating the segment-gated rollout used in production; the paper also reports lessons on inter-tenant load imbalance and LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.

title: Q-OIL: Optimistic Exploration in Learning from Human Interventions
comment: Project website: this https URL
summary: As robots are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably make mistakes. Human interventions provide valuable feedback for improving their behavior, enabling them to adapt online to new scenarios. However, studying human-in-the-loop robot learning is difficult: real-world experiments are slow and expensive, so most algorithm development relies on simulated human models. We show that common human modeling assumptions do not match how real people intervene in practice. Through analyzing intervention data from human participants, we find that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls, and that their corrective actions are often suboptimal. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, enabling realistic algorithm benchmarking and development in simulation. Building on these insights, we propose Q-OIL, a method that adds optimistic bonuses to intervention transitions in reinforcement learning and softly guides exploration toward human corrections. We find that decoupled critics are critical for stability because they prevent the bonuses from backing up to pre-intervention states. As a result, Q-OIL learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10-50% higher success in simulation and on real robots, and improving pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks. As we ground both evaluation and algorithms in realistic human behavior, this work provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.

AI.tldr: Q-OIL is a reinforcement learning method that adds optimistic bonuses to human intervention transitions, softly guiding exploration toward human corrections. It achieves 10-50% higher success than competitive baselines in simulation and on real robots and improves pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Human-in-the-loop robot learning is hard to study because simulated human models do not match real interventions, which occur when agent progress stalls and whose corrective actions are often suboptimal.
AI.method: The authors introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, and propose Q-OIL, which adds optimistic bonuses to intervention transitions and uses decoupled critics so the bonuses do not back up to pre-intervention states.
AI.result: Q-OIL learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10-50% higher success in simulation and on real robots, and improves pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks; the progress-based intervention model gives higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings.
AI.conclusion: Grounding both evaluation and algorithms in realistic human behaviour is presented as a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.

title: HaNDF: Object-Conditioned Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.

AI.tldr: HaNDF is an object-conditioned neural distance field that serves as a data-driven prior for plausible hand poses in the context of the object being manipulated. The abstract names pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion and physically plausible manipulation synthesis as applications.
AI.motivation: Unconditional generative priors model human pose well, but hands mostly interact with objects, so plausible hand poses must be modelled conditioned on the object under interaction.
AI.method: Plausible hand articulations are represented in the zero-level set of an object-conditioned neural distance field, using Riemannian geometry both to represent plausible hands on the field and to project a given pose onto it; the method can also optimise for the object under interaction.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations show that HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction. The abstract reports no specific numerical results.
AI.conclusion: HaNDF is presented as a flexible prior for hand-object interaction tasks.

title: s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL
summary: Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.

AI.tldr: s3 is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents learn for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organisation or roles. With matched budgets, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25x more coordination problems than the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Organisation in multi-agent systems usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed in advance that do not adapt to agent behaviour or task specifications.
AI.method: Agents learn to organise themselves through cooperative multi-agent RL, deciding for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read messages, with no predefined roles.
AI.result: Swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25x more coordination problems than the strongest baseline under matched training and inference budgets. In parallel exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points; agents also develop emergent complementary roles and generalise to bigger teams.
AI.conclusion: Organisation can emerge from a shared goal instead of being designed in advance, pointing toward capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.

title: From Geometry to Function: A Multi-Task LiDAR Benchmark Dataset for Semantic and Functional Parsing of Urban Facades
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 19 pages (8 main + supplementary), includes appendix. Project page: this https URL ; Code: this https URL
summary: Understanding building facades is central to urban digital twins, heritage modelling, and sustainable city analysis, yet existing LiDAR benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element. We introduce HFX3D, a large-scale urban facade benchmark of approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across four seasons, day and night, and varied weather. Each facade is annotated at three tiers, semantic, instance, and per-instance functional attributes, making it, to our knowledge, the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels. Annotations are produced by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation. We benchmark representative point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer architectures and find that semantic segmentation is already challenging under severe class imbalance, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder. The benchmark establishes a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding. Project page: this https URL ; code: this https URL

AI.tldr: HFX3D is a LiDAR benchmark of about 492 million points from 26 buildings in Halifax, annotated with semantic, instance and per-instance functional labels. Benchmarked architectures find semantic segmentation already challenging, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR facade benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element.
AI.method: Facades were captured across four seasons, day and night and varied weather, and annotated at three tiers (semantic, instance and per-instance functional attributes) by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation.
AI.result: Point-based, graph-based, convolutional and transformer architectures are benchmarked; semantic segmentation is challenging under severe class imbalance, and instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark is presented as a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding.

title: VoluCompose: Constructing Compact Volumetric Visual Representations for Medical Image Understanding
summary: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: VoluCompose is a training-free, model-agnostic framework that compresses volumetric visual tokens for medical vision-language models by grouping neighbouring slices and allocating tokens by attention entropy. It retains about 22.78% of visual tokens on average while reaching a mean relative quality of 121.68% against uncompressed references.
AI.motivation: Processing full volumes produces long, redundant visual-token sequences, and existing compression methods couple content selection with budget determination.
AI.method: A hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses Lorentz distance for token allocation, anchor selection and refinement; a capacity control module allocates more tokens when visual-encoder attention entropy is higher.
AI.result: Across nine calibrated settings on two tasks, three datasets and four backbones, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality-retention hypervolume among compared methods; its lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4%, against 15.0% to 70.5% for the compression baselines, and it stays robust at a 10% token budget.
AI.conclusion: Separating which visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate yields compact volumetric representations that keep quality against uncompressed references.

title: Scoring, Not Learning: Decomposing Catalog-Consolidation Gains in Web-Scraped Retail Product Recognition
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, was accepted by a computer vision conference workshop
summary: Retail product catalogs assembled from web image search are cheap to build and pervasively noisy: queries return packaging shots instead of products, and entries proliferate under names that cannot be distinguished visually. Consolidating such a catalog can look like an alternative to scaling the model. We show this is not a comparison between two ways of improving a recognizer, but between improving a recognizer and changing what counts as correct. We study a public archive of 165,769 cheese images across 1,824 query-named entries. A packaging filter and near-duplicate removal reduce it to a 998-class recognition set on one fixed, group-aware split. Canonicalizing entries to their base type (844 classes) raises top-1 accuracy by 4.0 points. Scoring the unchanged model against the merged label space, by summing its predicted probability within each canonical group, recovers +4.27 points with no retraining (+4.25 over six seeds). Retraining on the consolidated catalog then adds -0.10$\pm$0.53, +0.08$\pm$0.65 and -0.10$\pm$0.65 points at 28, 50 and 88 M parameters, indistinguishable from zero at every capacity ($\pm$ is the across-seed standard deviation). That component is specific, not mechanical: random merges with the identical size profile yield only +0.68 points, and the three backbones agree to within 0.1 points. But it is overwhelmingly category coarsening, not alias correction: across the 37 merged groups, type coarsenings supply 94% of the gain and alias collapses only 7%. We also detect no interaction between consolidation and backbone size: tripling backbone parameters is worth +1.50$\pm$0.57 points on the raw catalog and +1.42$\pm$00.44 on the canonical one, a within-seed interaction of -0.08 [-0.79,+0.63]. On this archive, the reported consolidation gain primarily reflects the evaluation label space, and separating that out costs one evaluation

AI.tldr: The paper argues that gains from consolidating a web-scraped cheese catalogue mainly reflect a change in the evaluation label space rather than a better recognizer. Scoring the unchanged model against merged canonical groups recovers +4.27 points with no retraining, while retraining on the consolidated catalogue adds nothing beyond seed noise.
AI.motivation: Consolidating a noisy web-image-search catalogue can look like an alternative to scaling the model, but the comparison may conflate improving a recognizer with changing what counts as correct.
AI.method: On 165,769 cheese images across 1,824 query-named entries, a packaging filter and near-duplicate removal give a 998-class set on one fixed group-aware split; entries are canonicalised to 844 base types, and the unchanged model is scored by summing its predicted probability within each canonical group, with retraining compared at 28, 50 and 88 M parameters.
AI.result: Canonicalisation raises top-1 accuracy by 4.0 points; group scoring with no retraining recovers +4.27 points (+4.25 over six seeds); retraining on the consolidated catalogue adds -0.10±0.53, +0.08±0.65 and -0.10±0.65 points at the three capacities; random merges with the same size profile yield only +0.68 points; type coarsenings supply 94% of the gain across 37 merged groups; no interaction with backbone size is detected.
AI.conclusion: On this archive the reported consolidation gain primarily reflects the evaluation label space rather than the recognizer; the abstract's final sentence is cut off in the input.

title: JEPAhead: From Inpainting to Causal Forecasting for Urban Driving
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures
summary: We fine-tune a pre-trained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting while keeping the encoder frozen. Using contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets, and group-level causal attention, the model forecasts eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass. On CARLA Town12, it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, compared with 55.3% for persistence, with greater gains at longer horizons and on tokens exhibiting greater change. It also outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters. Semantic analysis indicates driving-relevant information in predicted features: a fixed linear probe trained on real encoder tokens achieves 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes, versus 0.13 for persistence. Vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon. Pixel-space evaluation shows modest L1 gains but little improvement under LPIPS, motivating direct evaluation through latent and semantic measures alongside an oracle reconstruction reference. These findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.

AI.tldr: The paper fine-tunes a pretrained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting for urban driving, keeping the encoder frozen. On CARLA Town12 it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, against 55.3% for persistence.
AI.motivation: The predictor was trained for bidirectional inpainting, and the paper asks whether it can be adapted to forecast future driving scene states causally, which would be useful for driving perception.
AI.method: The model uses contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets and group-level causal attention to forecast eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass.
AI.result: Correct-future retrieval among 591 candidates is 69.0% versus 55.3% for persistence, with larger gains at longer horizons and on tokens with more change; the model outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters; a fixed linear probe scores 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes versus 0.13 for persistence; vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon; pixel-space L1 gains are modest and LPIPS improvement is small.
AI.conclusion: The findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.

title: FoleyForge: Free-form, Controllable, Rectified-flow Editing of Sound Effects
summary: We present FoleyForge, a generative model for instruction-based editing of sound effects. Given an input clip and a free-form instruction describing the desired change, it applies the edit while preserving the input's identity. A single model handles semantic, stylistic, and DSP-like changes. We introduce a data pipeline that guides an audio language model to author both DSP-based acoustic edits and similarity-preserving semantic edits, thus addressing the lack of publicly available audio editing data. Such data is then used to fine-tune a rectified-flow audio generation model, which we extend to expose attribute controls for loudness change, edit strength, and an input-derived contour envelope, each tunable via classifier-free guidance, yielding a more expressive editing model. FoleyForge achieves state-of-the-art instruction adherence at competitive audio quality and source faithfulness.

AI.tldr: FoleyForge is a rectified-flow generative model for instruction-based editing of sound effects that applies free-form edits while preserving the input's identity. It achieves state-of-the-art instruction adherence at competitive audio quality and source faithfulness.
AI.motivation: Publicly available audio editing data is scarce, and a single editing model must handle semantic, stylistic and DSP-like changes.
AI.method: A data pipeline guides an audio language model to author both DSP-based acoustic edits and similarity-preserving semantic edits; a rectified-flow audio generation model is fine-tuned on this data and extended with attribute controls for loudness change, edit strength and an input-derived contour envelope, each tunable via classifier-free guidance.
AI.result: The model achieves state-of-the-art instruction adherence at competitive audio quality and source faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: A single controllable model handles semantic, stylistic and DSP-like sound effect edits while keeping the source faithful.

title: An Educated Guess: Deriving Statistically Aligned Gradient Estimates for Zeroth-Order Optimisation
comment: 39 pages, 15 figures
summary: As novel hardware architectures are explored for the purposes of machine learning, including neuromorphic chips, asynchronous systems, and ASICs, effective learning algorithms are highly desirable. While backpropagation is the standard for differentiation on standard hardware, its requirement for global synchrony and exact differentiability limits the exploration of exotic algorithms on non-traditional substrates and devices. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation methods, such as SPSA and weight perturbation, offer a compelling alternative by estimating gradients through inference-only passes; however, these methods have historically suffered due to the `curse of dimensionality', where random perturbations become increasingly misaligned with the true gradient in high-dimensional spaces. In this work, we move beyond blind random noise by deriving zeroth-order search directions from activation geometry available during the forward pass. This leads to a family of Spectral Zeroth-Order methods, SZO-$\kappa$, whose directions solve local response-based gradient-guessing objectives under explicit stochastic assumptions. These methods explore feature-supported directions that are more likely to produce informative loss responses. Using multilayer and convolutional networks, we analyse gradient alignment, bias-variance structure, and training stability of these methods relative to standard perturbation baselines and backpropagation.

AI.tldr: The paper derives Spectral Zeroth-Order methods (SZO-kappa) whose search directions come from activation geometry in the forward pass, instead of blind random perturbations, to estimate gradients without backpropagation. It analyses gradient alignment, bias-variance structure and training stability against standard perturbation baselines and backpropagation.
AI.motivation: Backpropagation requires global synchrony and exact differentiability, limiting learning on neuromorphic, asynchronous and ASIC hardware, while zeroth-order methods such as SPSA and weight perturbation suffer from the curse of dimensionality because random perturbations become misaligned with the true gradient.
AI.method: The search directions solve local response-based gradient-guessing objectives under explicit stochastic assumptions, exploring feature-supported directions that are more likely to produce informative loss responses.
AI.result: The abstract reports analysis of gradient alignment, bias-variance structure and training stability on multilayer and convolutional networks, but states no specific numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Activation-geometry-guided zeroth-order directions are presented as a way to make inference-only gradient estimation more informative than random perturbation.

title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Evaluating Timing and Omission in Longitudinal AI Mental Health Support
summary: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support commonly focus on the clinical appropriateness of individual responses, potentially overlooking failures that emerge across extended interactions. As AI assistants accumulate memory of users' circumstances and prior disclosures, this raises an accountability question: Do AI chatbots provide appropriate support as users' needs evolve? We investigate by analyzing 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, examining how a memory-equipped assistant responds to suicidal ideation, self-harm, and anxiety crises across recovery trajectories and communication styles. We introduce the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (CARE) framework, developed with mental health professionals, to assess the timing and quality of advice, including omissions. Advice was less aligned with users' readiness after a crisis than in matched control stretches of the same conversation, largely because of premature recommendations, which were most common when recovery stalled. Revisiting a crisis reduced premature advice but not lagging advice, and users' communication style changed how often and when the assistant gave recommendations. Although explicitly unproductive advice was rare, the assistant frequently omitted clinician-expected support such as follow-up and planning for next steps. These findings show the limits of single response-level safety evaluation and the need to assess timing, omission, and consistency across users when holding AI systems accountable for longitudinal support.

AI.tldr: Analysing 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, the paper finds that a memory-equipped assistant often gives advice misaligned with users' readiness after a crisis, mostly through premature recommendations, and frequently omits clinician-expected support. The authors introduce the CARE framework to assess timing and omissions.
AI.motivation: Mental health evaluations of LLMs focus on the appropriateness of individual responses and can overlook failures that emerge across extended interactions, especially as assistants accumulate memory of users' circumstances.
AI.method: The authors simulate suicidal ideation, self-harm and anxiety crises across recovery trajectories and communication styles, and assess advice with the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (CARE) framework, developed with mental health professionals, comparing crisis stretches with matched control stretches of the same conversation.
AI.result: Advice was less aligned with readiness after a crisis than in matched controls, largely because of premature recommendations, which were most common when recovery stalled. Revisiting a crisis reduced premature advice but not lagging advice, and communication style changed how often and when recommendations were given. Explicitly unproductive advice was rare, while clinician-expected support such as follow-up and next-step planning was frequently omitted.
AI.conclusion: Response-level safety evaluation alone has limits, and timing, omission and consistency across users need assessing when holding AI systems accountable for longitudinal support.

title: How are viral trends different from educational and commercial uses of LLM image generation and editing? A privacy-preserving descriptive analysis
summary: Gemini's Nano Banana models, first introduced in late 2025, led to a shift in the capabilities and use of image generation and editing. We utilize Urania, a Google-developed framework for generating insights about LLM chatbot interactions with rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees, to analyze use cases and intents, techniques and ways of prompting, without ever looking at a single image or individual prompt. We select a subsample of 2.1M conversations in early 2026 which utilized Nano Banana models, into roughly 800 clusters in five categories: (1) Social & Viral Sharing, (2) Brand & Marketing Collateral, (3) Educational & Technical Information Media, (4) Product Visualizations & E-commerce, and (5) Architectural & Spatial Designs. We then compare these clusters on 21 features of use, measuring aspects of prompts' (a) editing techniques, (b) artistic style requests, (c) composition, and (d) chatbot interactions. This allows us to describe a baseline of how people are using image generation and editing tools for different use cases---(including growing and emergent use cases which were not possible before Nano Banana)---in a privacy-preserving manner.

AI.tldr: Using Urania, a differentially private analysis framework, the paper clusters about 2.1M early-2026 conversations involving Nano Banana image models into roughly 800 clusters in five categories and compares them on 21 features. It provides a privacy-preserving descriptive baseline of how people use image generation and editing for different purposes.
AI.motivation: Gemini's Nano Banana models, introduced in late 2025, shifted the capabilities and use of image generation and editing, and no privacy-preserving baseline of these use cases existed.
AI.method: Urania analyses use cases, intents, techniques and prompting styles without viewing any image or individual prompt; clusters are grouped into five categories (social and viral sharing, brand and marketing collateral, educational and technical media, product visualisation and e-commerce, architectural and spatial design) and compared on 21 features covering editing techniques, artistic style requests, composition and chatbot interactions.
AI.result: The abstract reports the cluster categories and the 21-feature comparison as descriptive output and does not state specific feature differences.
AI.conclusion: The analysis gives a baseline description of image generation and editing use across the five categories, including growing and emergent use cases that were not possible before Nano Banana.

title: Random Symbolic Boosting: A Geometric Approach to Symbolic Regression
summary: Symbolic models offer interpretability, but their construction through generational evolution can be computationally expensive. This article presents Random Symbolic Boosting (RSB), a method that constructs explicit additive symbolic models via boosting over populations of randomly generated syntax trees, eliminating the need for generational evolution. The idea combines two observations: high-dimensional spaces can be spanned by enough linearly independent vectors, and the semantics of syntax trees can be directly manipulated as such vectors. It is shown that, for Ordinary Least Squares, the boosting process guarantees a monotonic reduction of the training error for both regression and classification. Furthermore, an adaptive geometric early stopping mechanism is introduced. It is based on the angle between the prediction and target vectors, is independent of the problems scale, and requires no adjustments across tasks. Evaluated on a standard benchmark for symbolic regression, the method is located at the Pareto-optimal point between predictive accuracy and training time, ranking first on the real-world datasets. Additionally, it was tested on a large tabular classification benchmark with 200 problems, achieving competitive results.

AI.tldr: Random Symbolic Boosting builds explicit additive symbolic regression models by boosting over populations of randomly generated syntax trees, avoiding generational evolution. It guarantees monotonic training error reduction for ordinary least squares, ranks first on the real-world datasets of a symbolic regression benchmark, and is competitive on a 200-problem tabular classification benchmark.
AI.motivation: Symbolic models offer interpretability, but building them through generational evolution is computationally expensive.
AI.method: The method treats syntax tree semantics as vectors, using the observation that high-dimensional spaces can be spanned by enough linearly independent vectors, and adds an adaptive geometric early stopping rule based on the angle between prediction and target vectors that is independent of problem scale.
AI.result: For ordinary least squares, boosting guarantees monotonic reduction of training error for regression and classification; on a standard symbolic regression benchmark the method sits at the Pareto-optimal point between predictive accuracy and training time and ranks first on the real-world datasets; on a large tabular classification benchmark with 200 problems it achieves competitive results.
AI.conclusion: Random symbolic boosting is presented as an efficient alternative to evolutionary symbolic regression that keeps models interpretable.

title: AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay
comment: 26 pages, 14 figures. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: AtariBench is a controlled benchmark of 20 Atari 2600 games that tests whether vision-language models can perceive fast visual dynamics and make sequential decisions. Experiments show that state-of-the-art VLMs often fail to infer object motion, make brittle sequential decisions, and over-rely on textual interaction history.
AI.motivation: VLMs perform strongly on static visual understanding benchmarks, but their ability to act in dynamic environments is less well understood.
AI.method: The benchmark decouples fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed and requires sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. It adds a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores reliably signal competence, and studies how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance.
AI.result: State-of-the-art VLMs often fail to infer object motion and direction, show brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback.
AI.conclusion: AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making and provides a lightweight, rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that reason and act in dynamic environments.

title: Goals as a Representational Layer for Human-AI Collaboration
summary: Goals are central to how people, teams, and organizations structure their work. Yet, while generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly operate across a worker's context, information about why a person is pursuing a task, beyond local prompts and interactions, is typically missing. We argue that goals should become an explicit representational layer mediating interactions among people, AI systems, and organizations. Because human goals are hierarchical, partially latent, and dynamically evolving, such a layer must be multidimensional, both grounded in human articulation and inferred from available evidence, and continuously updated. A goal layer could connect immediate requests to broader outcomes, improve the organization and retrieval of relevant context, support reflection and coordination, and provide a foundation for training, aligning, and evaluating AI systems in terms of human-centered outcomes. We highlight these opportunities while identifying open challenges involving goal inference, socio-cognitive frictions, alignment, privacy, and governance.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that goals should become an explicit representational layer mediating interactions among people, AI systems and organizations. It outlines opportunities and open challenges for such a layer.
AI.motivation: Generative AI systems increasingly operate across a worker's context, but information about why a person pursues a task is typically missing beyond local prompts and interactions.
AI.method: The authors propose a multidimensional goal layer that is grounded in human articulation, inferred from available evidence and continuously updated, reflecting that human goals are hierarchical, partially latent and dynamically evolving.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experiments. It identifies opportunities such as connecting immediate requests to broader outcomes, improving retrieval of relevant context, supporting reflection and coordination, and providing a basis for training, aligning and evaluating AI systems.
AI.conclusion: A goal layer could make AI systems evaluable in terms of human-centered outcomes, but open challenges remain in goal inference, socio-cognitive frictions, alignment, privacy and governance.

title: CrowdDirector: Runtime Orchestration of Crowd Simulation through Natural-Language Directives
summary: Natural language offers an intuitive way to direct a virtual crowd while a simulation is running. Handwritten rules execute efficiently but cannot respond flexibly to varied instructions, whereas asking a large language model (LLM) to control the crowd at every update introduces repeated latency, cost, and the risk of unsupported actions. We present CrowdDirector, a framework that uses an LLM only when the user adds or changes an instruction. The LLM translates the request into a structured instruction, and a scene validator checks whether the entities and actions it references exist in the current Unity scene. Accepted instructions are stored and remain continuously active as the simulation is running. At each simulation tick, a graph neural network uses the current scene state and active instruction to choose an available action and target for each agent, while Unity handles movement, interactions, and animation. The network is trained offline on simulated scenarios, with LLM guidance on how agents should respond to instructions. Our evaluations show the scene validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgements more often than the LLM's own assessment, and on a behavioural benchmark CrowdDirector follows user instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls. It therefore provides a practical middle ground between fixed rules and continuous LLM control.

AI.tldr: CrowdDirector is a framework for runtime control of a Unity crowd simulation through natural-language instructions. It calls an LLM only when an instruction is added or changed, and a graph neural network chooses actions for agents at each simulation tick.
AI.motivation: Handwritten rules execute efficiently but cannot respond flexibly to varied instructions, while asking an LLM to control the crowd at every update adds latency, cost and the risk of unsupported actions.
AI.method: An LLM translates each request into a structured instruction, and a scene validator checks that the referenced entities and actions exist in the current Unity scene. A graph neural network, trained offline on simulated scenarios with LLM guidance on agent responses, selects an action and target for each agent per tick while Unity handles movement, interaction and animation.
AI.result: The scene validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgements more often than the LLM's own assessment. On a behavioural benchmark, CrowdDirector followed user instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls.
AI.conclusion: The approach is a practical middle ground between fixed rules and continuous LLM control of virtual crowds.

title: Conflux: Preventing Privilege Escalation with Principal Contexts and System-Level Evaluation
comment: 17 pages excluding references and appendix
summary: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals while acting externally. We formalise privilege escalation (PE) as the system-level security objective: an action may proceed only if every principal that influenced it would allow it. Model-level defences remain probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement. We present Conflux, a principal-context defence. Its kernel, ITES, derives authority from provenance and the organisation's existing access-control system and intersects the permissions of every influencing principal. We prove a conditional authority-confinement theorem: under complete mediation, no-laundering provenance, a known non-empty decision context, fresh permission checks, and action binding, the kernel admits no action that escalates privilege with respect to any recorded influencing principal. The theorem covers the represented value-influence fragment; control influence from tool, branch, recipient, or plan-step selection remains a refinement obligation. Conflux extends the kernel with independent policy ports, argument-aware authorisation, disclosure, consent, delegation, restriction, and exposure planning. We describe two system- level evaluators. SLED is a black-box evaluator: it exhaustively explores a declared finite model of a defence up to a bound. SLED-V is a white-box evaluator: it checks a serialisable intermediate representation against security and provenance properties. The evidence is bounded and partial. The appendix reports retained AgentDojo, SLED, and SLED-V results, including the limits of those runs. No result in this paper is an unbounded deployment guarantee.

AI.tldr: Conflux is a principal-context defence against privilege escalation in LLM agents, enforcing that an action may proceed only if every influencing principal would allow it. The paper proves a conditional authority-confinement theorem and reports bounded, partial evaluation results.
AI.motivation: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals when acting externally, and model-level defences are probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement.
AI.method: The kernel ITES derives authority from provenance and the organisation's existing access-control system and intersects the permissions of every influencing principal. Conflux extends it with independent policy ports, argument-aware authorisation, disclosure, consent, delegation, restriction and exposure planning. SLED is a black-box evaluator that exhaustively explores a declared finite model up to a bound, and SLED-V is a white-box evaluator that checks a serialisable intermediate representation.
AI.result: The theorem holds under complete mediation, no-laundering provenance, a known non-empty decision context, fresh permission checks and action binding, and covers the represented value-influence fragment; control influence remains a refinement obligation. The appendix reports retained AgentDojo, SLED and SLED-V results, including their limits.
AI.conclusion: The evidence is bounded and partial, and the paper makes no unbounded deployment guarantee.

title: Federated training performs as well as centralized for 3D Latent Diffusion for Diagnosis-Conditioned Brain MRI Synthesis
summary: Generative models of brain MRI are useful to understand brain conditions, and to enrich scarce and imbalanced neuroimaging data. However, training these models requires large, multi-site training sets, which is challenging. Federated learning (FL) allows for training deep learning models without sharing data. We show that training a 3D conditional latent model federatedly (where data is kept private at each site) performs similarly to centralized training (where all the data have been copied to a single site). We evaluate three metrics: conditional fidelity (how well generated MRIs perform in classification), diversity (how the generated images match the real data distribution, using MultiScale-SSIM), and realism (how close generated images are to real images, using Fréchet Inception Distance). Our results show that federated training is a viable route to develop multi-site generative models of brain MRI.

AI.tldr: Federated training of a 3D conditional latent diffusion model for diagnosis-conditioned brain MRI synthesis performs similarly to centralized training. The authors argue that federated learning is a viable route to multi-site generative models of brain MRI.
AI.motivation: Generative models of brain MRI can enrich scarce and imbalanced neuroimaging data, but training them normally requires large multi-site training sets, which is difficult to assemble.
AI.method: A 3D conditional latent model is trained federatedly, with data kept private at each site, and compared with centralized training in which all data are copied to a single site.
AI.result: Federated and centralized training perform similarly on conditional fidelity (how well generated MRIs perform in classification), diversity (MultiScale-SSIM) and realism (Fréchet Inception Distance).
AI.conclusion: Federated training is a viable way to develop multi-site generative models of brain MRI without sharing data.

title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness
comment: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026
summary: Can a network look stable at every layer and still be exponentially unstable as a whole? The Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a basic stability quantity appearing in optimization guarantees, generalization bounds, and robustness certificates. Deep networks naturally admit two such notions, input Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to data perturbations, and parameter Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to weight perturbations. We prove that, for deep networks with normalization layers, with batch normalization as the canonical example, both Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth and hence with parameter dimension, even under strong per-layer norm control such as $\|W_\ell\|_2\le 1$, and already for linear activations. Thus, a mechanism widely used to stabilize training can create severe worst-case instabilities that are invisible locally, i.e., from layerwise norm bounds alone. Parameter-Lipschitz explosion turns Lipschitz-dependent nonsmooth optimization guarantees into exponential-in-dimension bounds for deep normalized networks, while input-Lipschitz explosion makes worst-case Lipschitz-based generalization and robustness certificates vacuous. The latter also yields a concrete rank-separation mechanism for adversarial vulnerability. The theory predicts that perturbations introducing new singular directions should be amplified much more strongly than perturbations at the same noise level that remain within the input's original singular subspace. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support this prediction, showing that rank-creating perturbations cause substantially sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins than same-subspace perturbations.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that in deep networks with normalization layers, batch normalization being the canonical case, both input and parameter Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth even when every layer has norm at most 1. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 support a rank-separation account of adversarial vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Lipschitz constants underpin optimization guarantees, generalization bounds and robustness certificates, and layerwise norm control is usually assumed to keep the whole network stable, which the paper shows is not the case for normalized networks.
AI.method: The authors prove exponential growth bounds for deep networks with normalization layers, even under per-layer spectral norm control and linear activations, and analyse input-Lipschitz and parameter-Lipschitz explosion. They compare rank-creating perturbations with same-subspace perturbations at the same noise level.
AI.result: Rank-creating perturbations cause substantially sharper drops in accuracy, confidence and margins than same-subspace perturbations on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10.
AI.conclusion: Instabilities invisible from layerwise bounds can arise in normalized networks, turning Lipschitz-based optimization guarantees into exponential-in-dimension bounds, making robustness certificates vacuous, and giving a concrete mechanism for adversarial vulnerability.

title: Learning from How Users Interpret: Personalizing Recommendation Explanation Order
comment: Preprint
summary: Personalized explanations typically adapt their content or presentation based on preferences, interaction histories, or other user characteristics. We examine whether regularities inferred from prior textual interpretations can support personalization of explanation organization. In a controlled within participant study with 122 participants, prior interpretations were represented along three dimensions: information selection, relative salience, and relational organization. The relational dimension was partially operationalized through co mobilization. These representations were aggregated into fixed historical profiles and used to organize otherwise identical explanation sentences. Participants encountered four organization procedures: the OWN historical profile, the DONOR historical profile, a population profile called POP, and a language model procedure using the historical profile called PROFILE LLM. Post exposure objective comprehension was the primary outcome. OWN achieved 86.5 percent correct responses, compared with 66.0 percent for DONOR, 63.9 percent for POP, and 73.0 percent for PROFILE LLM. Mixed effects analyses showed higher comprehension with OWN than with each alternative procedure. No reliable overall condition effect was detected for recommendation acceptance. These findings indicate that historical profiles derived from prior interpretations can provide an actionable signal for personalizing explanation order while keeping explanatory content and wording fixed.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether explanation order can be personalized from users' prior textual interpretations while keeping content and wording fixed. Ordering by a user's own historical profile gave the highest comprehension among the compared procedures.
AI.motivation: Personalized explanations usually adapt content or presentation to preferences or interaction histories, but whether regularities in how people interpret prior text can personalize the organization of explanations is unclear.
AI.method: In a controlled within-participant study with 122 participants, prior interpretations were represented along information selection, relative salience and relational organization, aggregated into fixed historical profiles, and used to order otherwise identical explanation sentences. Four procedures were compared: OWN, DONOR, a population profile (POP) and a language model procedure using the historical profile (PROFILE LLM).
AI.result: Post-exposure comprehension was 86.5 percent for OWN, 66.0 percent for DONOR, 63.9 percent for POP and 73.0 percent for PROFILE LLM, and mixed-effects analyses showed higher comprehension with OWN than with each alternative. No reliable overall condition effect was detected for recommendation acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Historical profiles derived from prior interpretations provide an actionable signal for personalizing explanation order, while acceptance was not reliably affected.

title: Training Stability under Adaptive Curricula
summary: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approaches train reinforcement learning (RL) agents on diverse curricula that may evolve with their capabilities. While prior work has largely focused on how these curricula are constructed, we study whether their students remain trainable under the resulting distributions. Across multiple UED mechanisms, environment complexities, and extended training horizons, we identify recurring learner-side pathologies, including parameter growth, degraded value--outcome ordering, and loss of representational diversity, that accompany stagnation and performance degradation. These findings connect limitations in UED to optimization failures previously identified in conventional deep RL, while showing how adaptive curricula couple the learner's optimization state to its future training distribution. Controlled interventions show that mitigating selected pathologies improves learning. Stabilizing the learner improves long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum rule or increasing environment interaction. Our results establish learner trainability as a complementary design principle for UED. Effective curricula require students that remain capable of learning from the distributions they produce.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether learners remain trainable under adaptive curricula in unsupervised environment design (UED). It identifies recurring learner-side pathologies, and stabilizing the learner improves long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum rule.
AI.motivation: Prior UED work has focused on how curricula are constructed, not on whether the students remain trainable under the resulting training distributions.
AI.method: Across multiple UED mechanisms, environment complexities and extended training horizons, the authors identify pathologies including parameter growth, degraded value-outcome ordering and loss of representational diversity, and run controlled interventions that mitigate selected pathologies.
AI.result: Mitigating selected pathologies improves learning. Stabilizing the learner improves long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum rule or increasing environment interaction.
AI.conclusion: Learner trainability is a complementary design principle for UED, since effective curricula require students that can keep learning from the distributions they produce.

title: Not All Latents Are Equal: Importance-Weighted Latent Graph Generation
summary: Graph generation has shown tremendous effectiveness in modeling complex scientific tasks ranging from molecule generation to optimized circuit design. Most recent advancements have developed models that learn to denoise noisy graphs using either discrete diffusion or flow matching. However, discrete graph diffusion scales quadratically with the number of nodes, making it difficult to use such models on larger graphs. On the other hand, latent graph generation instead seeks to denoise noisy graph latents, which scale better to more nodes due to their lower dimension. However, in practice, latent graph generation models lag behind their discrete counterparts in performance. We study this problem, finding that it is caused by the unequal distribution of that different latent dimensions have on graph reconstruction. the impact. We observe that the vast majority of impact is contained in only a smaller number of latent dimensions. Since equal emphasis is placed on reconstructing the entire latent in the loss function, existing models are optimized to reconstruct information irrelevant to the downstream task. To tackle this problem, we propose Latent Importance Reweighting ({\bf LIR)} which weights each latent dimensions via it's importance to final graph reconstruction. Importance is calculated as the relative influence of a single latent unit on graph reconstruction, which is represented via the Jacobian of the decoder relative to the latent. Our method is model-agnostic and requires no additional model parameters or hyperparameters. Experiments show that LIR can boost performance and lead to faster training convergence when applied to two different autoencoders on various benchmark datasets. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Latent Importance Reweighting (LIR), which weights each latent dimension of a graph autoencoder by its influence on graph reconstruction, measured via the decoder Jacobian. It targets the gap in performance between latent graph generation and discrete graph diffusion.
AI.motivation: Discrete graph diffusion scales quadratically with node count, while latent graph generation scales better but lags behind in performance. The authors attribute the gap to a loss that weights all latent dimensions equally, although most of the impact on reconstruction sits in a small number of dimensions.
AI.method: The importance of a latent unit is its relative influence on graph reconstruction, represented by the Jacobian of the decoder with respect to the latent, and the loss reweights latent dimensions by this importance. The method is model-agnostic and adds no parameters or hyperparameters.
AI.result: LIR boosts performance and leads to faster training convergence when applied to two different autoencoders on various benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: Reweighting latent dimensions by their reconstruction importance is a simple, model-agnostic way to improve latent graph generation.

title: MotionDecipher: LLM-Assisted Clinical Interpretation of Human Motion Signals for Efficient Gait Analysis
comment: 33 pages, 19 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (IMWUT), Vol. 10, No. 4, Article 245, December 2026
summary: Clinical gait and motion analysis is widely used to guide targeted interventions for patients with neurological disorders, the outcome of which is typically a report with descriptions of joint movements and forces. Current practices rely on experts' manual effort, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide opportunities to address this problem, but translating human motion into clinical gait descriptions remains challenging because the quality of the context directly affects LLMs' reasoning capability over continuous motion signals. To tackle this, we introduce MotionDecipher, a novel framework bridging the semantic gap between motion data and clinical interpretations. Specifically, we made 3 key advancements: 1) a Human Motion Tokenizer that converts motion signals into domain-specific tokens for time- and frequency-informed gait interpretation; 2) a Meta Feature Selector that transforms tokens into Structured Representations; and 3) a Hybrid Context Constructor to determine the optimal demonstration-based prompt for In-Context Learning. We evaluated MotionDecipher on data collected at an accredited gait lab from 122 patients and 46 controls. Results show that MotionDecipher achieves 0.91 BERTScore (13% over GPT-5), while expert evaluation ranks MotionDecipher highest in Correctness, Completeness, and Conciseness compared to baselines, highlighting its promise for efficient gait analysis.

AI.tldr: MotionDecipher is an LLM-based framework that produces clinical gait descriptions from human motion signals using motion tokenization, structured representations and hybrid in-context prompting. It reports a BERTScore of 0.91, 13 percent above GPT-5.
AI.motivation: Clinical gait analysis relies on labour-intensive expert effort to produce reports, and translating continuous motion signals into clinical descriptions is hard because LLM reasoning depends on the quality of the context.
AI.method: A Human Motion Tokenizer converts motion signals into domain-specific tokens for time- and frequency-informed gait interpretation, a Meta Feature Selector transforms tokens into structured representations, and a Hybrid Context Constructor selects the optimal demonstration-based prompt for in-context learning.
AI.result: Evaluated on data from 122 patients and 46 controls at an accredited gait lab, MotionDecipher achieves a BERTScore of 0.91, 13 percent over GPT-5, and expert evaluation ranks it highest in correctness, completeness and conciseness compared with baselines.
AI.conclusion: The framework highlights the promise of LLM-assisted interpretation for efficient gait analysis.

title: What Matters for LLM Persona Simulation: Signal Form in Cold-Start E-Commerce Advertising
comment: Accepted at GenAIECommerce'26: The Third Workshop on Agentic and Generative AI for E-Commerce, co-located with RecSys 2026. 13 pages
summary: Estimating advertising performance in cold-start settings is challenging because historical logs are unavailable before launch. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential alternative by simulating persona-conditioned user responses, but it remains unclear which design choices actually drive LLM-based persona simulation. Using real Google Ads e-commerce campaign data across five demographic segments, we identify three signal-form dimensions that affect simulation quality: (i) a demographic anchor without noisy rich attributes, (ii) a relative qualitative banner-blindness signal rather than quantitative anchors, and (iii) prompt phrasing. On this campaign, our method attains an MAE of 24.9 and a MAPE of 26.1%, a 51.3% lower MAE than the best tested non-LLM baseline and 77.3% lower than an LLM configuration using explicit CTR anchors. Systematic ablations show that minimal demographic descriptions achieve lower mean error than richer persona configurations, while relative qualitative cues substantially outperform the tested quantitative anchors. We additionally compare these configurations with direct-prior and rule-based baselines and with alternative LLM configurations.

AI.tldr: On real Google Ads e-commerce campaign data, LLM persona simulation for cold-start advertising estimates works best with a minimal demographic anchor and relative qualitative cues rather than quantitative anchors. The best configuration reaches an MAE of 24.9 and a MAPE of 26.1 percent.
AI.motivation: Cold-start advertising performance cannot be estimated from historical logs, and it is unclear which design choices drive LLM-based persona simulation of user responses.
AI.method: Using real Google Ads campaign data across five demographic segments, the authors vary three signal-form dimensions: a demographic anchor without noisy rich attributes, a relative qualitative banner-blindness signal instead of quantitative anchors, and prompt phrasing. They run ablations and compare against direct-prior, rule-based and non-LLM baselines.
AI.result: The method attains an MAE of 24.9 and a MAPE of 26.1 percent, a 51.3 percent lower MAE than the best tested non-LLM baseline and 77.3 percent lower than an LLM configuration using explicit CTR anchors. Minimal demographic descriptions achieve lower mean error than richer persona configurations, and relative qualitative cues substantially outperform the tested quantitative anchors.
AI.conclusion: Signal form matters more than richer persona detail for LLM-based persona simulation in cold-start ad performance estimation, at least on this campaign.

title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
summary: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while smoothing the arrival of generated samples at the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Complete ASP improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. Within ASP, scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. ASP also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to about two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.

AI.tldr: ASP is an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous RL of LLMs that reduces padding, skewness and sorting bubbles in a single preprocessing pass. It improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times relative to MindSpeed-RL.
AI.motivation: Multi-instance rollout is needed to overcome the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference, but length heterogeneity, long-tail outputs and queue occupancy fluctuations cause rollout underutilization.
AI.method: ASP jointly addresses padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from training-queue fluctuations induced by length-sorted dispatch. It is integrated into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded.
AI.result: Complete ASP improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8 percent relative to MindSpeed-RL and by up to 62.5 percent relative to verl. Scheduling alone reduces mean iteration time by 10.9 percent, with no visible convergence degradation in the bounded-lag regime. In an internal telecom-domain workflow, the reported training period dropped from more than three months to about two months.
