AI.conclusion: ASP scales more robustly with additional generation resources than the baselines and has been used to produce a domain-enhanced model for telecom knowledge answering and tool calling.

title: The Relational Capacity Framework: A Lens for AI-Mediated Relationality
summary: A growing literature examines the impact of engaging with AI chatbots on our relationality: our ability to form relationships with others, maintain them through life's changes, and exit when needed. Currently, substantial work focuses on purpose-built AI companions (e.g. Replika, this http URL), with less work investigating socioemotional uses of the more widely-used general-purpose chatbots. In this paper, we present a 100-person investigation into how people engage general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs. Participants' AI uses varied, from practicing specific social skills to seeking additional bandwidth and information as they navigated their social contexts. To explain this heterogeneity, we provide 8 states that describe how AI expands or contracts relationality for people with different levels of skills, bandwidth, and information. We then present a unified conceptual model for the role of technology in mediating human relationality, the Relational Capacity Framework, and outline future research designing appropriate roles for AI in human connection.

AI.tldr: A 100-person study of how people use general-purpose AI chatbots for socioemotional needs yields eight states describing how AI expands or contracts relationality, which feed into a unified Relational Capacity Framework.
AI.motivation: Prior work on AI and relationality focuses on purpose-built AI companions, with less attention to socioemotional use of the more widely used general-purpose chatbots.
AI.method: The authors conducted a 100-person investigation into how people engage general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs, and used it to describe eight states that depend on people's skills, bandwidth and information.
AI.result: AI uses varied from practicing specific social skills to seeking additional bandwidth and information while navigating social contexts. The eight states describe how AI expands or contracts relationality for people with different levels of skills, bandwidth and information.
AI.conclusion: The Relational Capacity Framework offers a unified conceptual model of technology's role in mediating human relationality and outlines future research on designing appropriate roles for AI in human connection.

title: Who's Asking? Audience-Conditioned Privatization
summary: The abundance of user-generated conversational data makes the question of how to responsibly derive insights from confidential data without putting the individuals in it at risk ever more important. However, the majority of existing differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation (SDG) and anonymization approaches ignore the context of the data's downstream usage, which results in loss of important information. DP-SDG provides the same guarantee regardless of the recipient, and anonymization relies on predefined attribute categories. They both ignore the observation that an attribute that is harmless to one audience can be sensitive to another, and each audience typically needs only some attributes preserved. We propose Ext-Classify-Priv, a framework that (1) extracts the information types present in a corpus, (2) classifies which of them are private for a given audience following contextual integrity, and (3) protects only those attributes, using either anonymization or SDG with Feature-DP approaches. On Reddit data with 3 audiences, our audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release for every audience. On bioRxiv data, our SDG method improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1 and on the proprietary real estate data, our anonymization method improves MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959 over the best baselines.

AI.tldr: Ext-Classify-Priv extracts the information types in a text corpus, classifies which are private for a given audience under contextual integrity, and protects only those with anonymization or feature-DP synthetic generation. Audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release.
AI.motivation: Existing DP synthetic text generation and anonymization ignore the downstream usage of the data. DP-SDG gives the same guarantee regardless of recipient, and anonymization relies on predefined attribute categories, although an attribute harmless to one audience can be sensitive to another.
AI.method: The framework (1) extracts the information types present in a corpus, (2) classifies which of them are private for a given audience following contextual integrity, and (3) protects only those attributes, using either anonymization or SDG with Feature-DP.
AI.result: On Reddit data with 3 audiences, audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release for every audience. On bioRxiv data, the SDG method improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1, and on proprietary real estate data the anonymization method improves MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959 over the best baselines.
AI.conclusion: Protecting only the attributes that are private for a specific audience preserves more useful information than an audience-agnostic release, and this holds across the tested corpora.

title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety
summary: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.

AI.tldr: HomeLoop is a simulation framework and 20-task benchmark built on Isaac Sim for VLM-driven home robots that must coordinate with IoT devices and wearables in ambiguous hazard scenarios. The best of six evaluated VLMs scores 61.9 percent, and models show a pattern of over-reaction.
AI.motivation: Home robots must integrate with existing cameras, IoT devices and wearables and reason through ambiguous scenarios in which the same alert can have different causes, a setting not covered by existing evaluations.
AI.method: The benchmark combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors and hazards that evolve over time, with 20 tasks across five families. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost.
AI.result: The best of six open-weight and proprietary VLMs achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9 percent. Failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause.
AI.conclusion: HomeLoop is an extensible foundation for research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance and privacy-safety trade-offs, and it will be released with 2,100 home layouts, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.

title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle
summary: Can frontier general-purpose agents understand client intent, explore creative directions, execute revisions, and prepare production deliverables? We introduce DRAFT-Bench (Design Reliability Across Feedback and Tasks), a lifecycle-oriented evaluation of requirement elicitation, creative exploration, constrained editing, iterative revision, and production handoff. Its Requirement-to-Artifact framework links evolving requirements, protected properties, artifact versions, and delivery obligations. We compare native Codex/Astra and Claude Code across 35 design briefs under 43 conditions, alongside a separate 40-scenario RFQ track. Astra completes 43/43 design conditions and Claude 35/43. All scored core runs receive full structural credit, yet on the 28 core conditions scored for both systems, semantic checks flag violations in 11 for Astra and 5 for Claude; these are model judgments, not expert-confirmed failure rates. RFQ coverage is high, but success ordering changes across cohorts. SKU expansion, revision dependencies, and White ink files expose ambiguity among unmet obligations, missing inputs, and evaluator interpretations. These findings separate execution, requirement compliance, and professional acceptance. Unpaired tracks and different tools preclude claims of RFQ-to-delivery success, factory acceptance, or a pure model ranking.

AI.tldr: DRAFT-Bench evaluates frontier agents across the professional design lifecycle, from requirement elicitation to production handoff. Astra completes 43 of 43 design conditions and Claude 35 of 43, and semantic checks flag violations in a subset of core runs.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether general-purpose agents can understand client intent, explore creative directions, execute revisions and prepare production deliverables across the professional design lifecycle.
AI.method: The Requirement-to-Artifact framework links evolving requirements, protected properties, artifact versions and delivery obligations. Native Codex/Astra and Claude Code are compared across 35 design briefs under 43 conditions, alongside a separate 40-scenario RFQ track.
AI.result: Astra completes 43 of 43 design conditions and Claude 35 of 43. On the 28 core conditions scored for both systems, semantic checks flag violations in 11 for Astra and 5 for Claude, though these are model judgments rather than expert-confirmed failure rates. RFQ coverage is high, but success ordering changes across cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Execution, requirement compliance and professional acceptance are separable dimensions, and because the tracks are unpaired and use different tools, the results do not support RFQ-to-delivery success claims or a pure model ranking.

title: Ordered Policy Optimization
comment: 36 pages, 12 figures, 11 tables. Published in Proc. of the 40th Conference on Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.

AI.tldr: Ordered Policy Optimization (OPO) replaces PPO's fixed clipping range with sample-wise radii for the most extreme importance ratios in each minibatch. It keeps the objective first-order and reports strong performance on MuJoCo and Atari.
AI.motivation: PPO's single fixed clipping range fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme importance ratios from large but tolerable changes.
AI.method: In each minibatch, OPO sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive radii derived from a prescribed tail profile of desired target values. The resulting objective remains first-order and needs only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss.
AI.result: Experiments on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks show that the modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Reliable policy updates require controlling extreme ratios rather than only checking that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval, and this simple modification is a practical alternative to fixed clipping.

title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
comment: Accepted to AgenticAI4HPC 2026 (SC26 Workshops). 10 pages
summary: Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An automated output check drives the self-correction loop, complemented by an offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with three open-source LLMs. Our framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in all 18 model and direction combinations over a state-of-the-art baseline while consuming up to 52.4% fewer tokens, remaining consistent across models and directions without architectural modification.

AI.tldr: An agent-skill framework translates parallel scientific HPC codes among CUDA, OpenMP and SYCL using three coordinated agents and targeted repair skills. It attains higher verified correctness than a state-of-the-art baseline in all 18 model and direction combinations while using up to 52.4 percent fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Translating parallel scientific code between HPC frameworks is labour-intensive, and existing LLM pipelines use fixed sequential steps with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice.
AI.method: Translation, compilation diagnosis and execution validation are separated into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, which routes each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An automated output check drives self-correction, complemented by offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks.
AI.result: On 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP and SYCL with three open-source LLMs, the framework attains higher verified correctness than the baseline in all 18 model and direction combinations, consuming up to 52.4 percent fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: The framework remains consistent across models and directions without architectural modification, suggesting that targeted repair and separated responsibilities can make LLM-based code translation both more correct and more efficient.

title: LEF-JEPA: Denoising-Trained Latent Energy Fields for Spatial Representation Learning
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables. Includes supplementary material
summary: A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) that applies prediction supervision only at masked positions struggles to clearly capture object shapes and boundaries in its latent representations. We further observe that some existing methods improve spatial structure while also retaining rich variations in texture and color. However, preserving more low-level visual information does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action. This raises a key question: how can we strengthen the spatial structure in latent representations that supports prediction and action without over-encoding these details? We introduce LEF-JEPA, which learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and transfers this supervision to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint; the energy module is used only during pretraining and adds no inference overhead. To reduce the cost of energy optimization during pretraining, we further construct a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that allows low-energy-state search to be performed by specialized Ising solvers. On physical hardware, we validate the feasibility of achieving lower forward latency with fewer local updates. Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation protocol, both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in image classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.

AI.tldr: LEF-JEPA improves spatial structure in JEPA latent representations through target-guided latent recovery and a relative-energy constraint that is used only during pretraining. Both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 on CIFAR-10 for image classification, foreground segmentation and visual planning.
AI.motivation: A JEPA that applies prediction supervision only at masked positions struggles to capture object shapes and boundaries, and preserving more low-level texture and colour does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action.
AI.method: The method learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and transfers this supervision to the visual encoder via a relative-energy constraint, with the energy module used only during pretraining. To reduce the cost of energy optimization, a conditional Ising Hamiltonian lets specialized Ising solvers search for low-energy states, and lower forward latency is validated on physical hardware with fewer local updates.
AI.result: Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation protocol, both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in image classification, foreground segmentation and visual planning.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing spatial structure through an energy constraint that adds no inference overhead can yield representations better suited to prediction and action than retaining low-level visual detail.

title: Capital Efficiency, Isolation, Risk, and Ruin in Generative AI Inference Serving Infrastructure
summary: Generative AI serving is an extremely capital-intensive endeavor that demands rapid, step-change improvements in capital efficiency to prevent industry wide increases in the cost of capital from limiting growth plans. Keeping pace with the economic necessities will increasingly require infrastructure providers to confront operationally-inconvenient realities of production serving, including the extreme heterogeneity of generative AI request costs. We have explored workload isolation as a foundational, fleet-level lever for increasing capital efficiency. Isolation is the practice of intelligently grouping "like" requests before execution. Rather than exposing every replica to the full heterogeneous workload distribution, isolation deliberately reshapes the workload presented to the hardware by assigning requests with different cost characteristics to different portions of the fleet. Workload isolation on its own does not make expensive requests cheaper; it prevents a costly portion of the workload from unnecessarily determining the operating point and capital efficiency of the entire fleet. It additionally lays the foundational groundwork that can serve as a launching point for compounding gains via narrow-band optimizations (tailoring) and custom silicon designs while also informing up on pricing policy. This paper uses representative production data and experience to convey the motivation behind isolation as a fleet-level lever for increased capital efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that workload isolation, which groups like requests before execution, is a fleet-level lever for capital efficiency in generative AI inference serving. It uses representative production data and experience to convey the motivation.
AI.motivation: Generative AI serving is capital-intensive, and the extreme heterogeneity of request costs means that a costly portion of the workload can determine the operating point and capital efficiency of the entire fleet.
AI.method: Isolation groups requests with similar cost characteristics and assigns them to different portions of the fleet, reshaping the workload presented to the hardware. It lays groundwork for narrow-band tailoring, custom silicon and informed pricing policy.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results. It states that isolation on its own does not make expensive requests cheaper, but prevents them from setting the operating point of the whole fleet.
AI.conclusion: Workload isolation is a foundational lever for capital efficiency that can support later compounding optimizations, and the paper argues this from production data and operating experience.

title: FoundaRF: A Physics-Informed Foundation Model Framework for Radio-Frequency Passive Components
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
summary: Designing RF/mmWave passive components is a time-consuming process that relies heavily on expert knowledge and iterative EM simulations. Although recent ML surrogate models have shown great promise in accelerating passive design, they remain task-specific and lack generalization. This paper presents FoundaRF, a foundation model framework that unifies passive layout modeling across diverse layout structures and technologies. It combines a self-supervised encoder with adaptive layout processing and physics-aware decoders to enable few-shot transfer. Experiments across four semiconductor technologies show strong generalization to unseen structures, outperforming baselines with up to a 3.3x reduction in prediction error, reducing labeled-data requirements by up to fourfold, and substantially shortening design turnaround. FoundaRF establishes a scalable and data-efficient solution for RF/mmWave passive design automation.

AI.tldr: FoundaRF is a foundation model framework that unifies RF/mmWave passive component layout modeling across diverse structures and technologies and enables few-shot transfer. Across four semiconductor technologies it generalizes to unseen structures and reduces prediction error by up to 3.3x.
AI.motivation: Designing RF/mmWave passives relies on expert knowledge and iterative EM simulations, and existing ML surrogate models are task-specific and generalize poorly.
AI.method: A self-supervised encoder with adaptive layout processing and physics-aware decoders, built as a foundation model that enables few-shot transfer across layout structures and technologies.
AI.result: Across four semiconductor technologies it outperforms baselines with up to a 3.3x reduction in prediction error, reduces labeled-data requirements by up to fourfold, substantially shortens design turnaround, and shows strong generalization to unseen structures.
AI.conclusion: It establishes a scalable and data-efficient solution for RF/mmWave passive design automation.

title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection
summary: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether vision-language models can separate injected concepts from actual image content, a reality-monitoring problem. Only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts, and even then the source it reports is fragile.
AI.motivation: Introspection studies of language models are text-only, but VLMs must also keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see, which is the reality monitoring problem known from cognitive psychology.
AI.method: A paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently; on each trial the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what the thought is, so both concept identification and source attribution are scored.
AI.result: Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B identifies injected concepts reliably (35% vs. 3% for steering alone) with almost no false alarms. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports, and injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating multimodal self-reports requires checking both their content and their reported source.

title: Optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming: Complexity and Implementations
comment: Accepted for publication in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming
summary: Probabilistic Answer Set Programming (PASP) extends Answer Set Programming with the possibility of representing uncertain data. Among the possible available semantics, we focus here on the credal semantics. In this setting, prior work has focused exclusively on plain ASP programs, i.e., programs without optimization constructs. However, many real world tasks define optimality criteria over the possible solutions, which cannot be conveniently modeled with existing probabilistic ASP frameworks. In this paper, we close this gap and propose optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming, which extends PASP by also allowing weak constraints, which are the standard optimization construct of ASP. We define the semantics of such programs, study the computational complexity of the inference and most probable explanation tasks, and propose practical implementations based on Algebraic Model Counting and Answer Set Programming with Quantifiers. An empirical evaluation of the proposed approach on three real world tasks confirms the applicability of our framework.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming, which extends credal-semantics PASP with weak constraints so that optimality criteria over solutions can be modeled. It analyzes the complexity of inference and most probable explanation tasks and gives practical implementations.
AI.motivation: Prior probabilistic ASP work covers only plain programs without optimization constructs, so many real-world tasks that define optimality criteria cannot be conveniently modeled.
AI.method: Adds weak constraints, the standard ASP optimization construct, to PASP under the credal semantics; the implementations are based on Algebraic Model Counting and ASP with Quantifiers.
AI.result: The paper defines the semantics and studies the computational complexity of inference and most probable explanation tasks; an empirical evaluation on three real-world tasks confirms the framework's applicability.
AI.conclusion: The framework closes the gap for optimization-aware probabilistic ASP and is shown to be applicable in practice.

title: A Controlled Study of Models, Skills, Feedback, and Curriculum in Agentic Robotics
summary: Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and iteratively improve robot policies from simulated and real-world physical interactions. We study the self-learning loop of agentic robotics through a controlled simulation study spanning nine manipulation tasks, 631 different experiment configurations, and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The experiment data suggests that the bottleneck is often not the access to sufficient information, but interpreting it into the right policy update. Across these factors, a successful self-learning loop depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code to improve policies.

AI.tldr: A controlled simulation study of agentic robotics, in which coding agents iteratively improve robot policies, finds that the bottleneck is often interpreting feedback into the right policy update rather than access to information. A successful self-learning loop depends on attributing failures, reasoning about spatial geometry, and selectively restructuring code.
AI.motivation: Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and improve robot policies from physical interaction, but what makes the self-learning loop succeed is not well understood.
AI.method: A controlled simulation study across nine manipulation tasks, 631 experiment configurations and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure and curriculum.
AI.result: The data suggests the bottleneck is often not access to sufficient information but interpreting it into the right policy update. Success depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason about task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code.
AI.conclusion: Progress in agentic robot learning depends on how feedback is interpreted, not only on how much information is provided.

title: ToolDex: An Ego-Exo Human Demonstration Dataset for Creative Physical Tool Use
summary: Creative tool use is a fundamental human capability and an important step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. It requires agents to reason about object affordances, physical constraints, and manipulation strategies, especially when standard tools are unavailable. However, progress in this area is limited by the lack of real-world datasets that capture human tool-use behavior with sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity. Existing benchmarks are often simulation-based, focus on simplified interactions, or lack detailed observations and annotations. We introduce ToolDex, a large-scale egocentric-exocentric (ego-exo) human demonstration dataset for creative physical tool use. ToolDex captures scenarios in which humans select, adapt, and repurpose available objects as tools. Using synchronized egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras, the dataset provides high-fidelity multi-view observations and rich annotations for hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. Beyond data collection, we establish a benchmark suite characterizing three core capabilities: physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning. ToolDex provides a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and developing embodied agents that can adaptively use tools in complex real-world environments. Dataset visualizations and benchmarking results are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ToolDex is a large-scale egocentric-exocentric human demonstration dataset for creative physical tool use, in which humans select, adapt and repurpose objects as tools. It also establishes a benchmark suite covering tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning.
AI.motivation: Progress in creative tool use is limited by the lack of real-world datasets with sufficient scale, fidelity and diversity, since existing benchmarks are often simulation-based, simplified, or lack detailed observations and annotations.
AI.method: Synchronized egocentric cameras plus eight exocentric cameras capture high-fidelity multi-view observations, with rich annotations for hands, tools, target objects and their deformable interactions; a benchmark suite then characterizes three core capabilities.
AI.result: The abstract reports benchmarking results on physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning, but gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: ToolDex provides a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and for developing embodied agents that adaptively use tools in complex real-world environments.

title: Equidistribution of Solution Gradients in Physics-Informed Neural Networks via Coordinate Transformations
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) often struggle to approximate solutions with sharp gradients due to optimization difficulties and spectral bias. Motivated by the principle of gradient equidistribution from the stretching approach in grid generation, which redistributes solution gradients to reduce functional complexity, we propose Coordinate Transformation PINNs (CTPINNs), which incorporate learnable coordinate transformations to map the physical domain into a computational domain where the physical solutions become approximately affine, making them easier for neural networks to learn. We propose two constructions of the transformation: an explicit construction based on Majorants and an implicit construction based on invertable neural networks. Experimentally, the explicit construction can improve accuracy for PDEs with available explicit coordinate transformations, and the implicit construction can be combined with other advanced PINN models as an efficient plug-in module to improve performance across a range of challenging PDE benchmarks.

AI.tldr: CTPINNs are physics-informed neural networks that learn coordinate transformations mapping the physical domain to a computational domain where solutions become approximately affine, which eases learning of sharp gradients. Two constructions are proposed: an explicit one based on Majorants and an implicit one based on invertible neural networks.
AI.motivation: PINNs struggle to approximate solutions with sharp gradients because of optimization difficulties and spectral bias, and the gradient equidistribution principle from grid generation suggests redistributing gradients to reduce functional complexity.
AI.method: Learnable coordinate transformations; an explicit construction based on Majorants, and an implicit construction based on invertible neural networks that can be combined with other advanced PINN models as a plug-in module.
AI.result: The explicit construction improves accuracy for PDEs with available explicit coordinate transformations; the implicit construction improves performance across a range of challenging PDE benchmarks when used as a plug-in. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Learnable coordinate transformations are an effective way to handle sharp gradients in PINNs, with the implicit construction serving as an efficient plug-in module.

title: ProtoCouncil: Multi-Encoder Anatomical Prototypes for Prostate Cancer Detection in Micro-Ultrasound
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, Under Review
summary: Purpose: Micro-ultrasound ($\mu$US) is a promising modality for prostate cancer (PCa) detection, but identifying suspicious tissue depends heavily on clinical experience. Models trained on sparse, noisy core-level pathology offer little insight into their decisions and can fail under domain shift. Clinical use needs a traceable decision process and a flag for uncertain predictions. Methods: We introduce ProtoCouncil, in which three foundation encoders (MedSAM, DINOv3 and V-JEPA 2.1) learn case-based prototypes at three anatomical levels: whole gland, needle track and gland sectors. Prototypes are projected onto real training-core regions, and label-free fusion keeps every class logit as a bias plus an exact sum of prototype similarity contributions. Encoder disagreement triggers selective prediction. Results: In five-fold patient-level cross-validation (6,588 cores, 693 patients), ProtoCouncil reaches 82.9% AUROC for clinically significant PCa (csPCa, Grade Group $\geq$3), 4.3 points above the best previously published method. In zero-shot evaluation on two external cohorts, ProtoCouncil achieves higher all-cancer and csPCa AUROC than all previous methods. Nearest same-class exemplars match test-core tumor involvement better than random same-class cases. Externally, csPCa accuracy falls from 79% when encoders agree to 27% when two oppose the fused call. Abstaining on disagreement raises balanced accuracy by 7 and 15 points, while retaining 58% and 54% of the cores. Conclusion: ProtoCouncil grounds core-level predictions in exact similarity-based evidence from real, anatomically indexed training cases, which makes its reasoning interpretable. It achieves the highest csPCa AUROC across three cohorts and identifies unreliable predictions through encoder disagreement.

AI.tldr: ProtoCouncil is a multi-encoder prototype model for prostate cancer detection in micro-ultrasound that grounds predictions in real training-core prototypes and abstains when its encoders disagree. It reaches 82.9% AUROC for clinically significant prostate cancer in five-fold patient-level cross-validation.
AI.motivation: Models trained on sparse, noisy core-level pathology give little insight into their decisions and can fail under domain shift, while clinical use needs a traceable decision process and a flag for uncertain predictions.
AI.method: Three foundation encoders (MedSAM, DINOv3 and V-JEPA 2.1) learn case-based prototypes at whole-gland, needle-track and gland-sector levels; prototypes are projected onto real training-core regions, label-free fusion keeps each class logit as a bias plus an exact sum of prototype similarity contributions, and encoder disagreement triggers selective prediction.
AI.result: In five-fold patient-level cross-validation (6,588 cores, 693 patients) it reaches 82.9% AUROC for clinically significant prostate cancer, 4.3 points above the best previously published method. In zero-shot evaluation on two external cohorts it achieves higher all-cancer and clinically significant AUROC than all previous methods. Clinically significant accuracy falls from 79% when encoders agree to 27% when two oppose the fused call; abstaining on disagreement raises balanced accuracy by 7 and 15 points while retaining 58% and 54% of cores.
AI.conclusion: ProtoCouncil makes core-level predictions interpretable through exact similarity-based evidence from real, anatomically indexed training cases, achieves the highest clinically significant AUROC across three cohorts, and flags unreliable predictions through encoder disagreement.

title: UniRGBA: Unifying RGB and Alpha in Pretrained Video Diffusion Models
summary: Recent advances in video diffusion models have achieved remarkable photorealistic RGB synthesis, yet generating videos with a native alpha channel remains an open challenge. Existing approaches often rely on matting-style data and non-native RGBA designs, causing them to specialize in real-object scenes and to degrade severely on visual-effect content whose semi-transparency is spatially non-local and non-elliptical. We present UniRGBA, a unified framework whose key insight is that RGBA generation does not require a dedicated alpha encoder or complex latent-space restructuring---a minimal, targeted extension of the existing RGB pathway is sufficient. UniRGBA-VAE extends a causal video VAE to 4-channel RGBA via zero-initialized channel expansion, symmetric selective layer unfreezing (5% trainable), and a six-term progressive reconstruction loss anchored by a KL reference loss that prevents latent drift, followed by a two-stage schedule that introduces a lightweight GAN objective. We then apply standard DoRA to the pretrained DiT, reusing the unified 4-channel latent without any alpha-specific architectural changes. On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, UniRGBA substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA reconstruction while preserving RGB fidelity. For generation, UniRGBA outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA text-to-video tasks and matches or surpasses the original pretrained Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics, demonstrating that native alpha support can be integrated without compromising the underlying RGB prior or the model's architectural versatility.

AI.tldr: UniRGBA extends a pretrained video diffusion model to generate videos with a native alpha channel through a minimal, targeted extension of the RGB pathway, without a dedicated alpha encoder. It outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA reconstruction and text-to-video while preserving RGB quality.
AI.motivation: Existing RGBA video generation relies on matting-style data and non-native RGBA designs, so it specializes in real-object scenes and degrades on visual-effect content whose semi-transparency is spatially non-local and non-elliptical.
AI.method: UniRGBA-VAE extends a causal video VAE to four channels via zero-initialized channel expansion, symmetric selective unfreezing of 5% of layers, and a six-term progressive reconstruction loss with a KL reference loss, followed by a two-stage schedule that adds a lightweight GAN objective; standard DoRA is then applied to the pretrained DiT.
AI.result: On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, UniRGBA substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA reconstruction while preserving RGB fidelity. For generation it outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA text-to-video and matches or surpasses the original Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics.
AI.conclusion: Native alpha support can be integrated into a pretrained video diffusion model without compromising the RGB prior or the model's architectural versatility.

title: GlobalPuzzle: Globally Informed Genetic Search for Eroded Jigsaw Puzzle Reassembly
comment: 22 pages (10 pages main paper and 12 pages supplementary material), 16 figures
summary: Jigsaw puzzle reassembly remains a highly challenging task, particularly when piece boundaries are irregularly eroded to simulate damage to cultural artifacts. On the GAP benchmark, existing methods achieve a perfect assembly accuracy of only 0.3% on $5 \times 5$ puzzles, whereas humans can solve jigsaw puzzles with remarkably high accuracy. Humans typically approach puzzle solving by identifying potentially adjacent pieces, evaluating the current assembly, and iteratively performing complex operations such as adding pieces, replacing incorrectly placed pieces, and moving entire connected groups of pieces. However, existing methods face a fundamental limitation: approaches that leverage global visual information typically predict piece arrangements directly, making it difficult to explicitly perform such complex iterative operations, while search based methods can rearrange pieces but primarily rely on pairwise boundary compatibility, lacking global visual information to evaluate and guide the search process. To bridge this gap, we propose GlobalPuzzle, a jigsaw puzzle reassembly framework that integrates global canvas level evaluation, action guidance, and genetic search. By incorporating global visual information into the evaluation and optimization of candidate assemblies, GlobalPuzzle aims to resolve ambiguous adjacency relationships that are difficult to determine from irregularly eroded piece boundaries alone, enabling flexible, globally informed reconstruction.

AI.tldr: GlobalPuzzle is a jigsaw reassembly framework for eroded pieces that combines global canvas-level evaluation, action guidance and genetic search. It aims to resolve ambiguous adjacencies that pairwise boundary compatibility alone cannot.
AI.motivation: On the GAP benchmark existing methods reach only 0.3% perfect assembly accuracy on 5x5 puzzles; methods that use global visual information predict arrangements directly and struggle with iterative operations, while search-based methods rely on pairwise boundary compatibility and lack global visual information.
AI.method: Integrates global canvas-level evaluation, action guidance and genetic search, incorporating global visual information into the evaluation and optimization of candidate assemblies, with operations such as adding pieces, replacing misplaced pieces and moving connected groups.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results; it only states that the framework aims to resolve ambiguous adjacency relationships that are hard to determine from irregularly eroded boundaries alone.
AI.conclusion: The approach aims to enable flexible, globally informed reconstruction of eroded jigsaw puzzles.

title: Training-Free Active Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) is usually studied in a fully unsupervised regime, where adaptation relies on pseudo-labels, confidence scores, or entropy computed by the model itself. This is a severe restriction on hard shifted samples: the model is asked to repair its own uncertain predictions without any external evidence. At the other extreme, supervised online adaptation assumes labels can directly train or correct the model. We study the intermediate deployment regime between these two extremes. In Active Test-time Adaptation for VLMs (Active VLM-TTA), a pretrained VLM may spend an explicit labeling budget on selected test samples, but the prediction for the current sample must be emitted before its label can be used; queried labels are therefore costed, delayed evidence for future samples rather than free correction for the present one. Under this future-only constraint, the central question is how to reuse sparse labels conservatively. We instantiate this setting with ACTive VLM-TTA for Online Retrieval (ACTOR), a training-free plug-in module that routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query, and memory-based correction using a consistency-and-reliability check over previously queried labels. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and a domain-transfer benchmark based on ImageNet, ACTOR consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead. Our implementation is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ACTOR is a training-free plug-in for active test-time adaptation of VLMs, where a limited labeling budget can be spent on test samples but the labels only help future predictions. It routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query and memory-based correction, and consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines.
AI.motivation: Fully unsupervised TTA for VLMs relies on the model's own uncertain predictions, while supervised online adaptation assumes labels can directly correct the model; the intermediate regime, with costly and delayed labels, is less studied.
AI.method: ACTOR (ACTive VLM-TTA for Online Retrieval) routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query and memory-based correction, using a consistency-and-reliability check over previously queried labels.
AI.result: Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and a domain-transfer benchmark based on ImageNet, ACTOR consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Conservative reuse of sparse, delayed labels through a training-free module can improve VLM test-time adaptation under an active labeling budget.

title: When Routine Operations Break Architectural Pattern Relationships in LLM Agent Harnesses
summary: LLM agent harnesses distribute tool mediation, state management and safety guardrails across native services, independently written plugins and configuration. Routine operations can change the runtime order or retained state that architectural pattern relationships require, without any code change. We study five relationships associated with the Guardrail Enforcement Point, Autonomy Controller and Blackboard patterns across five released harnesses, analysing a main sample of fourteen independently written plugins. Using PatternOps, our assessment procedure, we trace requirements from pattern descriptions, provider documentation and deployment profiles to the providers that realise them and the records that decide them. We then compare alternative allocations under supported operations. Such operations broke relationships silently: after a plugin was reapplied or an allow rule saved, policy stopped evaluating edits while every plugin stayed active, and a prohibited edit executed. Which alternatives qualified depended on the requirement. Allocations that kept the required order, or kept or rebuilt the needed state, held on their tested paths and operation sequences, while others prevented prohibited effects but missed edits rejected elsewhere. In these harnesses, a pattern relationship is a property of the running system and its history, so architects should evaluate it against the decision paths, state lifetimes and operation sequences their deployments use.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that routine operations in LLM agent harnesses, such as reapplying a plugin or saving an allow rule, can silently break architectural pattern relationships without any code change, and a prohibited edit executed in one case. Pattern relationships must therefore be evaluated against decision paths, state lifetimes and operation sequences.
AI.motivation: Harnesses spread tool mediation, state management and safety guardrails across native services, independently written plugins and configuration, so routine operations can change the runtime order or retained state that pattern relationships require.
AI.method: Studies five relationships tied to the Guardrail Enforcement Point, Autonomy Controller and Blackboard patterns across five released harnesses, with a main sample of fourteen independently written plugins; PatternOps traces requirements to the providers and records that realize them and compares alternative allocations under supported operations.
AI.result: Supported operations silently broke relationships: after a plugin was reapplied or an allow rule saved, policy stopped evaluating edits while every plugin stayed active, and a prohibited edit executed. Allocations that kept the required order, or kept or rebuilt the needed state, held on their tested paths, while others prevented prohibited effects but missed edits rejected elsewhere.
AI.conclusion: In these harnesses a pattern relationship is a property of the running system and its history, so architects should evaluate it against the decision paths, state lifetimes and operation sequences their deployments use.

title: AdaAlloc: Adaptive Visual Token Allocation for Long-Video Question Answering
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.

AI.tldr: AdaAlloc is a training-free framework for long-video question answering that adaptively splits a fixed visual-token budget between a global video overview and high-resolution local evidence. It improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Under strict visual-token budgets, uniform sampling keeps temporal coverage but obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval works over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes and before-after relations.
AI.method: Recasts long-video reasoning as visual-token allocation: plans a global/local allocation policy, uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments, refines them into a compact temporal memory, and sets frame sampling density and resolution accordingly, combining sparse low-resolution global frames with denser high-resolution local frames.
AI.result: Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive allocation of visual tokens between global context and local detail is an effective, training-free way to improve long-video question answering under a fixed budget.

title: SPDMX: Large-Scale Open Stem Audio From Symbolic Music
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, 1 table
summary: Large public datasets have driven recent progress in machine learning, from text and vision to speech and general audio. Music remains an outlier, as copyright blocks redistribution of training audio, while many modern tasks need individual stems rather than mixtures. Existing multitrack resources trade off realism, scale, and licensing, while synthetic alternatives rely on proprietary VSTs or naive open rendering that yields weak stems. We introduce SPDMX, a listening-guided rendering of public-domain PDMX scores into an openly-licensed stem corpus with aligned scores and an open render pipeline: $253{,}982$ songs, $490{,}159$ mono stems, and $5{,}469$ song-hours at $44.1$ kHz under CC BY 4.0, with paired MIDI and identifiers linking to PDMX metadata. $88{,}403$ songs ($34.8\%$; $2{,}734$ song-hours) provide multitrack supervision. To our knowledge, this is the largest openly-licensed synthetic multitrack subset by song-hours, enabling source separation, stem-conditioned synthesis, MIDI-to-audio, transcription, and joint symbolic-audio modeling. We release the corpus, metadata, and open pipeline for reuse on other symbolic collections. Demos and experimental notes are on the project page.

AI.tldr: SPDMX is an openly licensed synthetic stem corpus rendered from public-domain PDMX scores, containing 253,982 songs, 490,159 mono stems and 5,469 song-hours under CC BY 4.0. Of these, 88,403 songs provide multitrack supervision.
AI.motivation: Copyright blocks redistribution of music training audio, and existing multitrack resources trade off realism, scale and licensing, while synthetic alternatives rely on proprietary VSTs or naive open rendering that yields weak stems.
AI.method: A listening-guided rendering of public-domain PDMX scores into stems at 44.1 kHz, with aligned scores, paired MIDI, identifiers linking to PDMX metadata, and an open render pipeline for reuse on other symbolic collections.
AI.result: The corpus has 253,982 songs, 490,159 mono stems and 5,469 song-hours; 88,403 songs (34.8%; 2,734 song-hours) provide multitrack supervision. The authors describe it as the largest openly licensed synthetic multitrack subset by song-hours.
AI.conclusion: Releasing the corpus, metadata and pipeline enables source separation, stem-conditioned synthesis, MIDI-to-audio, transcription and joint symbolic-audio modeling.

title: Circuit Theory-Informed AI for Condition Monitoring in Power Electronics
comment: The manuscript has been accepted for publication in the Proceedings of 2026 IEEE Design Methodologies Conference (DMC 2026)
summary: Artificial intelligence for power electronics is evolving toward a deeper comprehension of system intrinsic behaviors and dynamics. As a novel integration of neural computation and electric circuits, spike-based neuromorphic computing offers promising potential in high energy efficiency and adaptability for data-driven applications. Building on the latency-coding principles, this article proposes a framework for data-light condition monitoring that relies solely on three-phase AC current measurements. The AC current signals are encoded as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which are inherently compatible with spiking neural networks that can effectively facilitate the estimation of device parameters. Case studies are presented to validate the performances, while constraints and further optimizations are also evaluated and discussed, and future extensions of the methodology are provided.

AI.tldr: A data-light framework for condition monitoring of power electronics encodes three-phase AC current measurements as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which feed spiking neural networks that estimate device parameters.
AI.motivation: AI for power electronics needs a deeper understanding of system behavior, and spike-based neuromorphic computing offers high energy efficiency and adaptability for data-driven applications.
AI.method: Using latency-coding principles, AC current signals are encoded as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which are compatible with spiking neural networks that estimate device parameters; only three-phase AC current measurements are required.
AI.result: The abstract reports case studies validating performance, with constraints and further optimizations also evaluated, but gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The abstract presents the approach as a data-light monitoring framework validated by case studies and identifies constraints and extensions for future work.

title: Learning Generative Dynamics for 3D Molecule Generation via Sequential Neuro-Symbolic Constraints
summary: Diffusion models have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for generating 3D molecules. Despite showing remarkable promise, they learn atomic distributions implicitly from data, without explicitly encoding physicochemical rules into their generative dynamics. Consequently, generated samples can be statistically plausible yet chemically invalid. To address this problem, we propose Sequential Neuro-Symbolic Constrained Diffusion (SensDiff), a framework that integrates symbolic rules into generative modeling, enabling the model to internalize scientific priors during training. Central to SensDiff is the observation that the diffusion trajectory of 3D molecule generation exhibits a coarse-to-fine evolution: valid molecules arise by first mitigating macroscopic geometric conflicts and then refining structures toward microscopic chemical consistency through iterative denoising. Accordingly, SensDiff mirrors this dynamic by sequentially enforcing constraints with adaptive weighting during training, progressively steering generation toward valid molecular geometries. Moreover, SensDiff translates domain knowledge into interpretable generative controls, grounding opaque neural denoising in scientific principles. Experiments on molecular benchmarks and real-world constrained generation tasks confirm that SensDiff consistently improves chemical validity while adhering to physicochemical rules and user-specified targets. The code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SensDiff is a constrained diffusion framework for 3D molecule generation that enforces symbolic physicochemical rules in sequence during training, matching the coarse-to-fine evolution of the denoising trajectory. It improves chemical validity while adhering to physicochemical rules and user-specified targets.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models learn atomic distributions implicitly from data, so generated samples can be statistically plausible yet chemically invalid.
AI.method: Sequential Neuro-Symbolic Constrained Diffusion enforces constraints in order during training with adaptive weighting, first mitigating macroscopic geometric conflicts and then refining toward microscopic chemical consistency, and translates domain knowledge into interpretable generative controls.
AI.result: Experiments on molecular benchmarks and real-world constrained generation tasks show consistent improvements in chemical validity while adhering to physicochemical rules and user-specified targets. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Integrating symbolic scientific priors into diffusion training grounds generation in physicochemical principles and yields more valid molecular geometries.

title: FIND: Frequency Invariance Disentanglement for Test-Time Adaptation in LiDAR 3D Detection
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection (L3OD) is a fundamental 3D perception task, yet its performance is often compromised by domain shifts arising from diverse sensor configurations and environmental conditions. Existing Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods primarily leverage self-supervision in the spatial domain, yet they frequently confound semantic content with domain style due to the sparse, non-Euclidean nature of point clouds. To overcome this limitation, we propose FIND (Frequency INvariance Disentanglement), a novel TTA framework that precisely disentangles domain-invariant content from domain-specific interference within the frequency domain. Our methodology utilizes B-Spline fitting to construct locally adaptive filters integrated into a dual-stream architecture: an Invariant Stream extracts robust features to guide pseudo-labeling, while a Specific Stream enforces consistency against domain perturbations. By combining invariance-driven alignment with stability-guided regularization, our approach dynamically extracts robust domain-invariant features while suppressing domain-specific interference. Extensive experiments on cross-dataset adaptation and robust corruption benchmarks demonstrate that FIND significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FIND is a test-time adaptation framework for LiDAR 3D object detection that disentangles domain-invariant content from domain-specific interference in the frequency domain, using B-Spline-based locally adaptive filters in a dual-stream architecture. It significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on cross-dataset adaptation and corruption benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Domain shifts from diverse sensor configurations and environments degrade LiDAR 3D detection, and existing spatial-domain self-supervised TTA methods confound semantic content with domain style in sparse, non-Euclidean point clouds.
AI.method: B-Spline fitting builds locally adaptive filters inside a dual-stream architecture: an Invariant Stream extracts robust features to guide pseudo-labeling, and a Specific Stream enforces consistency against domain perturbations; invariance-driven alignment is combined with stability-guided regularization.
AI.result: The abstract states that FIND significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on cross-dataset adaptation and robust corruption benchmarks, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-domain invariance disentanglement dynamically extracts domain-invariant features while suppressing domain-specific interference, improving robustness of LiDAR 3D detection under domain shift.

title: SIFR: Stable Signed Flow Reinforcement
summary: Reward-based fine-tuning of flow models requires effectively promoting high-reward and suppressing low-reward samples, while maintaining training stability over many rounds of iterative updates. Iterative reward fine-tuning provides a simple starting point, but the positive reward weights give no explicit unfitting signal, and repeated reweighting concentrates the distribution and causes collapse. We propose Stable Signed Flow Reinforcement (SIFR), which replaces the reward weights by signed advantages to supply the missing unfitting signal, and constrains the velocity drift from a reference model to stabilize the updates, with a Lagrange multiplier that adapts the regularization strength to a prescribed drift budget. We further show that existing flow RL methods fall within this framework: they implicitly minimize the signed loss, differing in their regularization choices. We validate SIFR on SD3.5 Medium (2.5B) and FLUX.2 Klein (9B) and scale it to Cosmos 3 Super Text2Image (64B): across all 12 backbone--reward pairs with preference and rule-based rewards, it matches or exceeds existing methods, reaches their peak rewards much faster, and keeps improving over long training where they plateau or collapse.

AI.tldr: SIFR is a reward fine-tuning method for flow models that uses signed advantages to push down low-reward samples and constrains velocity drift from a reference model with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier. It matches or exceeds existing methods across 12 backbone-reward pairs and keeps improving over long training where others plateau or collapse.
AI.motivation: Iterative reward fine-tuning of flow models gives positive reward weights with no explicit unfitting signal, and repeated reweighting concentrates the distribution and causes collapse.
AI.method: Replaces reward weights with signed advantages and constrains velocity drift from a reference model, with a Lagrange multiplier adapting the regularization strength to a prescribed drift budget; the authors show that existing flow RL methods fall within this framework as implicit minimizers of the signed loss that differ in regularization.
AI.result: Validated on SD3.5 Medium (2.5B) and FLUX.2 Klein (9B) and scaled to Cosmos 3 Super Text2Image (64B); across all 12 backbone-reward pairs with preference and rule-based rewards it matches or exceeds existing methods, reaches their peak rewards much faster, and keeps improving over long training where they plateau or collapse.
AI.conclusion: SIFR gives a stable update rule that places existing flow RL methods in one framework and scales to a 64B-parameter text-to-image model.

title: On the Limits of Execution Traces for Repairing Assertion Failures in LLM-Generated Code
comment: Under review at 2027 2nd International Conference on Advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
summary: Iterative repair returns a failed program's error to a large language model (LLM) and asks it to fix it. After iterative repair, the remaining failures are mostly assertion failures: with four Qwen2.5 models, they make up 79% of residual failures on BigCodeBench, all on HumanEval and 93% on LiveCodeBench. We argue, through an information view of the feedback, that an assertion failure says little about where the fault lies. We propose Breakpoint Debugging (BPD), which returns the failed program annotated inline with its variables' runtime values. We take the tasks that iterative repair failed to fix with five repair attempts and compare two ways of spending five further generations on them: BPD, and resampling. On BigCodeBench, BPD repairs 26.7% of these tasks against 22.4%, and its advantage grows with model size. On HumanEval, BPD outperforms resampling but only slightly, and on LiveCodeBench, fresh sampling repairs more (6.5% against 4.9%). Furthermore, BPD reduces unchanged-code resubmissions from 28% to 8% on BigCodeBench. Using only the first failing test's trace, it outperforms tracing all failing tests while using fewer tokens than both all-trace BPD and plain iterative repair. On LiveCodeBench, BPD gives no gain even on the public tests, so a visible failing input is not enough for a trace to help. These results match the information view: a trace helps only when the test exposes a failing input, and the fault is an implementation slip; otherwise, a repair loop should resample rather than trace.

AI.tldr: Breakpoint Debugging (BPD) returns failed LLM-generated programs annotated with runtime variable values and helps repair assertion failures only when a visible failing input exposes the fault. The paper argues that an assertion failure says little about where the fault lies.
AI.motivation: After iterative repair, assertion failures make up most residual failures (79% on BigCodeBench with four Qwen2.5 models, and all of them on HumanEval, and 93% on LiveCodeBench), and an assertion failure says little about where the fault lies.
AI.method: BPD annotates the failed program inline with its variables' runtime values and is compared with resampling, using five further generations on tasks that five repair attempts failed to fix; a variant uses only the first failing test's trace.
AI.result: On BigCodeBench BPD repairs 26.7% of these tasks against 22.4% for resampling, with its advantage growing with model size. On HumanEval it outperforms resampling only slightly; on LiveCodeBench fresh sampling repairs more (6.5% vs. 4.9%). BPD cuts unchanged-code resubmissions from 28% to 8% on BigCodeBench, and tracing only the first failing test outperforms tracing all failing tests while using fewer tokens. On LiveCodeBench BPD gives no gain even on public tests.
AI.conclusion: A trace helps only when the test exposes a failing input and the fault is an implementation slip; otherwise a repair loop should resample rather than trace.

title: BOXBOX: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Long-Running Performance Optimization
comment: 47 pages, 22 figures, 12 tables, including appendices. Project page: this http URL
summary: Automated harness optimization improves agents by learning from trajectories and task feedback. Existing offline methods use reference answers to optimize harnesses for reuse on held-out tasks. However, many real-world tasks are open-ended, while long runs expose new difficulties that offline-optimized harnesses may not address. To study harness optimization in these settings, we introduce PerfRace, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and investigate whether agents can use task-specific experience to recursively improve their harnesses during an ongoing task. To this end, we introduce BOXBOX, which enables agent-triggered harness revision and kernel-managed hot reloading while preserving execution context. We evaluate BOXBOX on PerfRace under matched test-time budgets, comparing it with Frozen Harness, offline Harness Evolution, and Harness Scaling. BOXBOX achieves higher speedup with more efficient use of task time and model cost, reaching a Speedup@4h of 1.70x, compared with 1.54x for the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: BOXBOX lets agents trigger harness revisions during a long-running task, with kernel-managed hot reloading that preserves execution context, and improves long-running performance optimization on the PerfRace benchmark. It reaches a Speedup@4h of 1.70x against 1.54x for the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Offline harness optimization uses reference answers and suits reusable tasks, but many real-world tasks are open-ended, and long runs expose new difficulties that offline-optimized harnesses may not address.
AI.method: Introduces PerfRace, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and BOXBOX, which enables agent-triggered harness revision and kernel-managed hot reloading while preserving execution context.
AI.result: Under matched test-time budgets, compared with Frozen Harness, offline Harness Evolution and Harness Scaling, BOXBOX achieves higher speedup with more efficient use of task time and model cost, reaching a Speedup@4h of 1.70x against 1.54x for the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Agents can use task-specific experience to recursively improve their harnesses during an ongoing task, outperforming offline harness optimization under matched budgets.

title: HMMF-Net: A Lightweight Hierarchical Multi-Frame Multimodal Fusion Network for Accurate Fish Feeding Intensity Assessment
comment: 47 pages, 10 figures, 15 tables
summary: Automated fish feeding intensity assessment (FFIA) is important for precision aquaculture and feed cost optimization. However, unimodal methods are vulnerable to acoustic noise and visual disturbances, while existing multimodal frameworks often rely on computationally intensive 3D convolutions or Transformers, limiting their use on edge devices. To address these limitations, we propose HMMF-Net, a lightweight multimodal architecture that combines early multi-frame visual encoding and multi-axis acoustic modeling through a hierarchical bidirectional messenger cross-modal fusion (BMCF) mechanism. The visual branch captures temporal variations in feeding behavior by stacking temporally distant frames as a multi-channel input to an adapted 2D EfficientNetB0 backbone. The acoustic branch employs adaptive multi-axis residual units (AMARU) to extract temporal, frequency, and local time-frequency representations from log-mel spectrograms. BMCF progressively exchanges information between the two modalities at intermediate representation levels through compact messenger tokens, reducing the computational overhead of dense cross-modal attention. Evaluated on the AV-FFIA dataset using five-fold cross-validation, HMMF-Net achieves 96.77% accuracy and 96.88% F1-score on the held-out test folds, with 3.987M parameters and 1.002 GFLOPs. Compared with the best-performing visual configuration (95.49% accuracy), HMMF-Net reduces the classification error by 28.38%. Deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano using TensorRT with FP32 precision maintains comparable accuracy, with an inference time of 11.54 ms per 2-second sample and a model size of 18.81 MB. These results demonstrate that HMMF-Net combines effective multimodal representation learning with computational efficiency, enabling accurate and practical FFIA on resource-constrained edge platforms.

AI.tldr: HMMF-Net is a lightweight multimodal network for fish feeding intensity assessment that fuses multi-frame visual input with log-mel acoustic features through messenger-token cross-modal fusion. It reaches 96.77% accuracy on AV-FFIA with 3.987M parameters and runs on a Jetson Orin Nano.
AI.motivation: Unimodal methods are vulnerable to acoustic noise and visual disturbances, while existing multimodal frameworks rely on computationally intensive 3D convolutions or Transformers that limit use on edge devices.
AI.method: A 2D EfficientNetB0 visual branch takes temporally distant frames stacked as a multi-channel input; an acoustic branch with adaptive multi-axis residual units (AMARU) models temporal, frequency and local time-frequency representations of log-mel spectrograms; hierarchical bidirectional messenger cross-modal fusion (BMCF) exchanges information between the modalities through compact messenger tokens.
AI.result: Five-fold cross-validation on AV-FFIA gives 96.77% accuracy and 96.88% F1 with 3.987M parameters and 1.002 GFLOPs; against the best visual configuration (95.49% accuracy) it reduces classification error by 28.38%. TensorRT FP32 deployment on a Jetson Orin Nano keeps comparable accuracy, with 11.54 ms per 2-second sample and an 18.81 MB model.
AI.conclusion: HMMF-Net combines effective multimodal representation learning with computational efficiency, enabling accurate and practical feeding intensity assessment on resource-constrained edge platforms.

title: FondueQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating Parametric Compensation in Multi-Hop QA
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show remarkable performance based on parametric knowledge, i.e., their ability to recall facts and associations internalized in a model's weights. However, studying this capability on established multi-hop benchmarks may be complicated by benchmark contamination, as many of these benchmarks have been publicly available long enough to plausibly appear in modern pretraining corpora. As a result, correct answers under missing evidence may reflect either general parametric knowledge or memorization of benchmark-specific instances. To study how models use internal knowledge when retrieval evidence is incomplete, we introduce FondueQA, in which every required multi-hop fact is uniquely localized to a designated evidence document. This enables controlled document-level evidence ablations to study parametric compensation under incomplete retrieval. Our empirical evaluation reveals that parametric compensation strongly depends on both entity popularity and the structural role of missing evidence. Generally, models compensate more successfully for facts involving popular entities. On FondueQA, we show that bridging evidence can be more useful than the answer-bearing document itself. Moreover, models may recall a missing fact in isolation but fail to use it under partial evidence, particularly when the context contains plausible competing entities, which can reduce Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points.
