AI.tldr: FondueQA is a multi-hop QA benchmark where each required fact is uniquely localized to one evidence document, which enables controlled evidence ablations to study how LLMs compensate with parametric knowledge when retrieval is incomplete.
AI.motivation: Established multi-hop benchmarks may be contaminated by pretraining data, so correct answers under missing evidence may reflect memorization of benchmark instances rather than general parametric knowledge.
AI.method: FondueQA maps every required multi-hop fact to a designated evidence document, and document-level evidence ablations then measure parametric compensation under incomplete retrieval.
AI.result: Parametric compensation depends strongly on entity popularity and on the structural role of the missing evidence; models compensate more successfully for popular entities; bridging evidence can be more useful than the answer-bearing document; plausible competing entities can reduce Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Models may recall a missing fact in isolation yet fail to use it under partial evidence, so incomplete retrieval exposes limits in how models combine parametric knowledge with context.

title: AudioSphere: Towards Self-Supervised Spatial Audio Representation Models
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Recent audio embedding models learn representations that transfer across clip- and frame-level tasks, yet they operate almost exclusively on single-channel signals and are blind to spatial structure. Spatial audio models capture that structure but rely on clip-level supervision or contrastive objectives, yielding embeddings unsuitable for frame-level tasks like sound event detection and localization (SELD). We argue this dichotomy is not fundamental: patch-level spatial self-supervision can jointly learn acoustic and spatial features at both temporal granularities. We introduce AudioSphere, a multi-channel masked autoencoder trained on Ambisonics recordings that reconstructs both spectral content and directional cues via a joint spatiotemporal masking strategy that masks both time-frequency patches and intensity vectors. AudioSphere supports frame-level predictions while producing strong clip-level representations via aggregation. Alongside the model, we release RealSELD, a standardized benchmark for evaluating frozen backbones on real-world multi-channel SELD. AudioSphere enables, for the first time, SELD with a frozen self-supervised backbone, while matching or exceeding prior self-supervised audio embedding models on clip-level classification tasks spanning environmental sound, speech, and music, and on frame-level sound event detection. All code and data are available at this https URL and this https URL.

AI.tldr: AudioSphere is a multi-channel masked autoencoder for Ambisonics audio that learns spectral and spatial features at frame and clip levels, and it comes with RealSELD, a benchmark for evaluating frozen backbones on real multi-channel SELD.
AI.motivation: Audio embedding models are single-channel and blind to spatial structure, while spatial audio models rely on clip-level supervision or contrastive objectives, which yields embeddings unsuitable for frame-level tasks such as sound event detection and localization.
AI.method: A joint spatiotemporal masking strategy masks both time-frequency patches and intensity vectors, so the model reconstructs spectral content and directional cues, supports frame-level predictions, and produces clip-level representations via aggregation.
AI.result: AudioSphere enables SELD with a frozen self-supervised backbone and matches or exceeds prior self-supervised audio embedding models on clip-level classification across environmental sound, speech and music, and on frame-level sound event detection.
AI.conclusion: Patch-level spatial self-supervision can learn acoustic and spatial features jointly at both temporal granularities, so the clip-level versus frame-level dichotomy is not fundamental.

title: Diversity-Aware Client Selection for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning
comment: 4 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at SNCNW 2026
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw data, making it attractive for privacy-sensitive and bandwidth-constrained applications. A practical challenge in deploying FL is reducing communication overhead while maintaining model performance under heterogeneous, non-IID data distributions. Selecting which subset of clients participates in each training round offers a principled way to address both challenges simultaneously, yet its impact on data diversity and representativeness remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate three client selection strategies, Power-of-Choice, Fisher information, and Centered Kernel Alignment, evaluating them not only by accuracy and convergence, but through the lens of participation diversity using the Gini coefficient and KL divergence. Under non-IID conditions, restricting participation to 15% of clients per round achieves significant communication savings, and when selection promotes diverse and balanced contributions, it also improves generalization over biased alternatives. This work provides a systematic and reproducible analysis demonstrating that diversity-focused client selection renders communication efficiency and model quality complementary rather than competing objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper compares three client selection strategies for federated learning and shows that selecting diverse participants can make communication savings and model quality improve together under non-IID data.
AI.motivation: Choosing which clients join each round reduces communication overhead, but its effect on data diversity and representativeness under heterogeneous non-IID distributions is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Power-of-Choice, Fisher information and Centered Kernel Alignment selection by accuracy, convergence and participation diversity, measured with the Gini coefficient and KL divergence.
AI.result: Restricting participation to 15 percent of clients per round gives significant communication savings under non-IID conditions, and selection that promotes diverse and balanced contributions improves generalization over biased alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Diversity-focused client selection makes communication efficiency and model quality complementary rather than competing objectives, according to a systematic and reproducible analysis.

title: A Stochastic Latent Variable Generalization of Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
comment: WACV 2027
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) predict the latent embedding of a target signal from a context signal, with an auxiliary variable z conditioning the predictor. Despite its prominent role in the original JEPA blueprint, the content of z has been carried by a fixed deterministic token in every prior instantiation, collapsing the genuinely multi-modal distribution over plausible completions to a point estimate. We present S-JEPA, which realises z as a proper stochastic latent variable for masked image prediction: a learned posterior infers z from context and target during training, while a learned context-conditioned prior approximates the distribution of plausible completions at inference, with no decoders and no reconstruction. In its deterministic limit the objective reduces to the I-JEPA loss in functional form, generalising that objective rather than strictly containing the I-JEPA model. Our central finding is that stochasticity adds capabilities, error-correlated predictive uncertainty and diverse completions, at no cost to representation quality: under matched architectures and schedules S-JEPA improves over the deterministic I-JEPA baseline and exceeds LeJEPA at matched architecture, while additionally producing spatially structured uncertainty maps and semantically diverse completions, neither of which the deterministic predictor produces.

AI.tldr: S-JEPA makes the auxiliary variable of JEPA a stochastic latent, learned as a posterior during training and as a context-conditioned prior at inference, for masked image prediction without decoders or reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Prior JEPA instantiations fix the auxiliary variable z to a deterministic token, which collapses the multi-modal distribution of plausible completions to a single point estimate.
AI.method: A learned posterior infers z from context and target during training, and a learned prior approximates the distribution of plausible completions at inference; no decoder or reconstruction loss is used, and the deterministic limit reduces to the I-JEPA loss in functional form.
AI.result: Under matched architectures and schedules, S-JEPA improves over the deterministic I-JEPA baseline and exceeds LeJEPA at matched architecture without loss of representation quality, and it additionally yields spatially structured uncertainty maps and semantically diverse completions.
AI.conclusion: Stochasticity adds capabilities such as error-correlated predictive uncertainty and diverse completions, and the framework generalises the I-JEPA objective rather than strictly containing the I-JEPA model.

title: Robust Deep Prototype Classifiers via Lipschitz Training
summary: Robustness and interpretability are interrelated and desirable properties of machine learning models. A model that changes its prediction under imperceptible perturbations behaves inconsistently with human-recognizable features and, hence, is not interpretable. Prototype-based classifiers such as Generalized Learning Vector Quantization address both at once. They are interpretable by construction because they make the decision by comparing the input to the prototypical example; and their hypothesis margin yields a closed form robustness certificate. However, on high-dimensional data, these shallow models need deep embedding networks to achieve high accuracy, and this voids the robustness certificate. The margin is a statement about distances in the embedding space, and an unconstrained network can map an arbitrarily small input perturbation to arbitrarily large attacks in the embedding space. We close this gap with a theorem: if the embedding network is locally L-Lipschitz around a point, and the classifier is {\epsilon}-robust around its embedding, then the full model is {\epsilon}/L-robust in the input space. Based on this, we propose a Lipschitz training scheme to achieve L-Lipschitz properties for embedding networks. We evaluate three classification heads (linear, linear Support Vector Machine, and GLVQ) crossed with two embedding networks (standard and Lipschitz-constrained) on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Imagenette-160, under FGS, PGD and C\&W attacks. The evaluation results show that combining a prototype-based head with a Lipschitz-constrained embedding provides the strongest robustness. This suggests that the Lipschitz constraint provides an additional robustness benefit in addition to the advantage provided by the prototype-based head. Since the Lipschitz constraint is enforced by sampling rather than by construction, the reported robustness is empirical rather than certified.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a Lipschitz-continuous embedding network carries the margin-based robustness of prototype classifiers into input space, and proposes a Lipschitz training scheme whose robustness is empirical rather than certified.
AI.motivation: Prototype classifiers such as GLVQ are interpretable and have a closed-form robustness certificate, but the deep embedding networks needed for high-dimensional data void that certificate, since an unconstrained embedding can amplify small input perturbations.
AI.method: A theorem states that if the embedding network is locally L-Lipschitz and the classifier is epsilon-robust in embedding space, the full model is epsilon/L-robust in input space; three heads (linear, linear SVM, GLVQ) are crossed with standard and Lipschitz-constrained embeddings and tested under FGS, PGD and C&W attacks.
AI.result: On MNIST, CIFAR-10 and Imagenette-160, a prototype head combined with a Lipschitz-constrained embedding gives the strongest robustness across the attacks.
AI.conclusion: The Lipschitz constraint adds robustness beyond the benefit of the prototype head, but because it is enforced by sampling rather than by construction, the reported robustness is empirical, not certified.

title: Reliable Prerequisite-Aware Learning Path Recommendation under Uncertain Knowledge Structures: Long-Horizon Evaluation and Cross-Dataset Validation
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Under review at Computers & Education: Artificial Intelligence (Elsevier)
summary: Learning-path recommendation often depends on knowledge and prerequisite structures whose reliability is uncertain, while high accuracy in predicting the next resource does not necessarily establish reliable long-horizon path behaviour. This study develops a reliability-oriented prerequisite-aware framework that jointly examines immediate next-resource ranking, uncertain prerequisite structures, hard, soft and hybrid constraint semantics, graph robustness, and autoregressive path generation under course-level confirmatory evaluation and independent cross-dataset validation. Development used 3,187 MOOCCubeX courses, followed by a frozen confirmatory evaluation on 541 held-out courses and 37,747 transitions. The primary MOOCCubeX task is structural and course-prefix-conditioned rather than learner-personalised. Junyi provides independent structure-/hierarchy-aware external validation, uses hierarchy metadata rather than an explicit prerequisite graph and is not a zero-shot transfer setting. On the frozen MOOCCubeX evaluation, XGBoost pairwise was the strongest observed immediate ranker, with mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.9048, whereas the proposed prerequisite-aware graph model achieved 0.7707. In the controlled graph-variant development ablation, the no-graph condition produced the strongest immediate ranking result, and immediate prediction showed strong dependence on permitted title/path-similarity information. Autoregressive evaluation exposed path properties not captured by one-step ranking. On Junyi, Markov achieved the strongest observed MRR of 0.4453, compared with 0.3954 for the proposed graph model, with metric-specific differences across ranking measures. Overall, immediate predictive accuracy, prerequisite-structure reliability, and long-horizon path quality should be treated as complementary rather than interchangeable evaluation dimensions in educational recommendation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a prerequisite-aware learning-path framework and finds that immediate next-resource accuracy, prerequisite-structure reliability and long-horizon path quality are distinct, with a simpler ranker outperforming the proposed graph model on immediate ranking.
AI.motivation: Learning-path recommendation depends on prerequisite structures of uncertain reliability, and high accuracy in predicting the next resource does not establish reliable long-horizon path behaviour.
AI.method: A prerequisite-aware graph framework is assessed under hard, soft and hybrid constraint semantics, graph robustness and autoregressive path generation, using MOOCCubeX development data (3,187 courses), a frozen confirmatory set of 541 held-out courses with 37,747 transitions, and Junyi as independent structure-aware validation.
AI.result: On the MOOCCubeX evaluation XGBoost pairwise was the strongest immediate ranker with MRR 0.9048, against 0.7707 for the proposed graph model; on Junyi, Markov reached MRR 0.4453 versus 0.3954 for the proposed model, with metric-specific differences.
AI.conclusion: Immediate predictive accuracy, prerequisite-structure reliability and long-horizon path quality should be treated as complementary rather than interchangeable evaluation dimensions in educational recommendation.

title: When Feedback Becomes a Backdoor: Tracing Backdoor Skill Formation in Text-Space Skill Optimization
comment: Accepted as a poster at the Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. OpenReview: this https URL
summary: Reference answers are a supervision channel in text-space Skill optimization, which produces reusable text artifacts called Skills that guide future agent behavior. Poisoning those answers can induce a persistent trigger-conditioned rule without giving the attacker access to the model, optimizer, or Skill file. We study this reference-feedback poisoning in SkillOpt by tracing an attacker-supplied trigger--payload mapping from reflection to held-out activation. In SearchQA, where the payload replaces a short answer, the natural attack retains an exact rule in all three seeds; each final Skill emits the payload on 200/200 triggered questions and 0/200 clean questions. In seed 42, removing the rule eliminates activation, and an in-run comparison shows similar clean accuracy to benign SkillOpt (169/200 versus 171/200). In SpreadsheetBench, where the payload requires an additional workbook edit, no natural run retains an exact rule across three seeds. Diagnostic interventions locate two successive bottlenecks: the Analyst abstracts away required literals, and, once literal preservation is enabled, edit-budget ranking can remove exact edits before candidate construction. Poisoned references can therefore create persistent backdoors, but exposure alone does not ensure that the induced rule is formed, selected, and retained.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether poisoned reference answers in text-space skill optimization (SkillOpt) produce persistent trigger-conditioned backdoor rules in the Skill artifacts that guide agents.
AI.motivation: Reference answers are a supervision channel in Skill optimization, so an attacker could implant a persistent rule without access to the model, the optimizer or the Skill file.
AI.method: The authors trace an attacker-supplied trigger-payload mapping from reflection to held-out activation in SkillOpt, testing SearchQA, where the payload replaces a short answer, and SpreadsheetBench, where the payload also requires a workbook edit, with diagnostic interventions on the Analyst and on edit-budget ranking.
AI.result: In SearchQA the attack keeps an exact rule in all three seeds, and each final Skill emits the payload on 200/200 triggered and 0/200 clean questions; in seed 42 clean accuracy is 169/200 against 171/200 for benign SkillOpt. In SpreadsheetBench no natural run keeps an exact rule across three seeds, and two successive bottlenecks are located.
AI.conclusion: Poisoned references can create persistent backdoors, but exposure alone does not ensure that the induced rule is formed, selected and retained.

title: HiMEM: Hippocampus-Inspired Memory Consolidation, Pruning, and Composition for Vision-Language-Action Models in 3D Scenes
summary: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

AI.tldr: HiMEM is a hippocampus-inspired memory system for vision-language-action models that consolidates episodic memories into semantic ones, prunes redundant episodes and composes memories, raising the average success of pi_0 on LIBERO from 91.88 to 98.20 percent.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA memory mechanisms store episodic memories full of redundant scene layout, object configuration and robot-state detail, which obscures generalizable manipulation principles and hinders cross-task transfer in complex 3D scenes.
AI.method: Three mechanisms are proposed: consolidation synthesizes episodic experiences into a compact set of semantic memories; episodic pruning removes episodes whose content is already captured by semantic memories; and memory composition jointly uses multiple episodic and semantic memories for complex tasks.
AI.result: On LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, HiMEM improves the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88 percent to 98.20 percent on LIBERO and is effective across different VLA backbones.
AI.conclusion: Consolidation and pruning increase effective memory capacity, which supports long-horizon task execution and cross-scenario generalization.

title: Mitigating Covariate Shift in Behavioral Cloning via Robust Stationary Distribution Correction
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures, NeurIPS 2024, Code: this https URL
summary: We consider offline imitation learning (IL), which aims to train an agent to imitate from the dataset of expert demonstrations without online interaction with the environment. Behavioral Cloning (BC) has been a simple yet effective approach to offline IL, but it is also well-known to be vulnerable to the covariate shift resulting from the mismatch between the state distributions induced by the learned policy and the expert policy. Moreover, as often occurs in practice, when expert datasets are collected from an arbitrary state distribution instead of a stationary one, these shifts become more pronounced, potentially leading to substantial failures in existing IL methods. Specifically, we focus on covariate shift resulting from arbitrary state data distributions, such as biased data collection or incomplete trajectories, rather than shifts induced by changes in dynamics or noisy expert actions. In this paper, to mitigate the effect of the covariate shifts in BC, we propose DrilDICE, which utilizes a distributionally robust BC objective by employing a stationary distribution correction ratio estimation (DICE) to derive a feasible solution. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method through an extensive set of experiments covering diverse covariate shift scenarios. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in improving the robustness against the shifts, outperforming existing offline IL methods in such scenarios.

AI.tldr: DrilDICE is an offline imitation learning method that mitigates covariate shift in behavioral cloning when expert data comes from arbitrary state distributions, using a distributionally robust BC objective built on stationary distribution correction estimation.
AI.motivation: Behavioral cloning is vulnerable to covariate shift, which becomes more pronounced when expert datasets are collected from biased or incomplete, non-stationary state distributions and existing offline IL methods can then fail substantially.
AI.method: DrilDICE uses a distributionally robust BC objective and a DICE-style stationary distribution correction ratio estimation to derive a feasible solution, targeting shifts from state distribution mismatch rather than dynamics changes or noisy expert actions.
AI.result: Experiments over diverse covariate shift scenarios show improved robustness to the shifts and outperformance of existing offline IL methods in those scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The approach is an effective way to make offline imitation learning robust to covariate shift caused by arbitrary state data distributions.

title: Can LLMs Debug Robots by Editing Their Weights?
summary: A language model can repair a robot policy's lexical instruction grounding by editing just 65 token-embedding rows. We bring weight-space programming to robot foundation policies: GPT-6 Astra reads weights and uses a CPU workspace and budgeted simulator feedback, without gradient updates or new demonstrations. Three independent sessions on $\pi_{0.5}$ all improve success on 765 held-out paraphrases; the best raises success from 86.3\% to 92.0\% (48 repairs, four regressions; exact paired $p=1.31\times10^{-10}$). Among the 335 instructions containing edited tokens, success rises from 74.3\% to 87.5\%; the other 430 episodes have zero outcome changes. Matched random-direction edits do not help. Full replacement using the editor's own lexicon explains much of the gain but produces more regressions; its direct difference from the editor is not significant at 0.05. Across 13 further robot sessions, the editor declines 12 candidates; the sole retained edit does not show a significant held-out gain. Separately, benchmark metadata lowers FastWAM success from 70.0\% to 48.6\%, while the evaluated VLA's aggregate rate is unchanged. The evidence supports precise lexical repair, not general acquisition of missing robot capabilities.

AI.tldr: A language model repairs a robot foundation policy's lexical instruction grounding by editing just 65 token-embedding rows, improving success on held-out paraphrases without gradient updates or new demonstrations.
AI.motivation: The paper tests whether weight-space programming can repair robot foundation policies, and it separates precise lexical repair from the general acquisition of missing robot capabilities.
AI.method: GPT-6 Astra reads the weights, works in a CPU workspace and uses budgeted simulator feedback to propose token-embedding edits, with matched random-direction edits and full replacement using the editor's own lexicon as comparisons.
AI.result: Across three independent sessions on pi_0.5, the best raises success on 765 held-out paraphrases from 86.3 to 92.0 percent (48 repairs, four regressions; exact paired p = 1.31e-10); among the 335 instructions containing edited tokens success rises from 74.3 to 87.5 percent, and matched random edits do not help. Across 13 further sessions the editor declines 12 candidates, and benchmark metadata lowers FastWAM success from 70.0 to 48.6 percent.
AI.conclusion: The evidence supports precise lexical repair rather than general acquisition of missing robot capabilities.

title: SPSC: Zero-Shot Cross-Subject EEG-to-Image Reconstruction via Semantic Preservation and Subspace Calibration
summary: Pretrained vision-language models and diffusion generators have driven rapid progress in brain-to-image generation, while EEG-based reconstruction is still constrained by low signal-to-noise ratio and cross-subject semantic shifts. Zero-shot cross-subject reconstruction poses even greater challenges: EEG semantic embeddings learned from source subjects deviate from the manifold of image embeddings of the unseen target subject, particularly when neither target labels nor target image embeddings are available. To address this issue, we introduce the Semantic Preservation and Subspace Calibration (SPSC) framework, which first uses Object Mask Contrastive Regularization (OMCR) with object identity for backend training, and then constructs Subspace Candidate Gate (SCG) to achieve label-free semantic correction for target subjects during inference. Specifically, OMCR regularizes the conditioning space with object-level positive samples to preserve object-level feature neighborhoods within the reconstruction prior and low-level branch, while SCG exploits training image prototypes and batch statistics of unlabeled target EEG to select candidates for each task within subspaces of image prototypes. Under the leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) setting across ten subjects on the THINGS-EEG dataset, SPSC improves the cross-subject reconstruction from 0.552 to 0.713 on CLIP and from 0.612 to 0.745 on Alex.5. These significant gains indicate that the semantically calibrated conditions can better support generation for the target subjects under label-free inference.

AI.tldr: SPSC is a zero-shot cross-subject EEG-to-image reconstruction framework that preserves object semantics during training and calibrates EEG embeddings of unseen subjects at inference without target labels.
AI.motivation: EEG semantic embeddings learned from source subjects deviate from the manifold of image embeddings of an unseen target subject, especially when neither target labels nor target image embeddings are available.
AI.method: Object Mask Contrastive Regularization (OMCR) uses object identity to regularize the conditioning space in backend training, and the Subspace Candidate Gate (SCG) uses training image prototypes and batch statistics of unlabeled target EEG to select candidates within prototype subspaces at inference.
AI.result: Under leave-one-subject-out evaluation across ten subjects on THINGS-EEG, cross-subject reconstruction improves from 0.552 to 0.713 with CLIP and from 0.612 to 0.745 with Alex.5.
AI.conclusion: Semantically calibrated conditions better support image generation for target subjects under label-free inference.

title: Artificial Shoppers and Attention Competition
summary: We study how AI shopping interfaces affect price competition, platform profit, and consumer welfare. A platform hosts two of three products of different quality. Without AI, consumers compare the hosted pair under salience distortion and overweight whichever attribute, price or quality, stands out. Under assistance, an AI assistant recommends the two products with the highest true utility, leaving consumers to make the same distorted comparison. Under delegation, an AI agent selects the best product, subject to purchase approval. Both modes access all products and know consumers' preferences; firms price strategically. First, assistance can soften competition despite expanded product access. The middle-quality firm may forgo low-valuation consumers because attracting them requires cutting the price paid by higher-valuation consumers as well. Relative to no AI with the same assortment, assistance lowers both hosted prices under the high- and low-quality pair but can raise both under the high- and middle-quality pair. Second, we identify an alignment paradox: some consumers can become worse off than without AI even though their best option remains recommended and becomes cheaper. Salience can induce a switch to a lower-quality product whose quality loss exceeds the saving relative to the original purchase. The assistant ranks products accurately but does not optimize the shortlist for consumers' realized welfare. Third, assistance can raise both platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus with the high- and middle-quality pair; delegation can do so with the high- and low-quality pair. Fourth, among AI designs, the platform weakly prefers delegation with the high- and middle-quality pair wherever all compared pricing equilibria exist. Yet this preferred design can yield lower platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus than the no-AI optimum.

AI.tldr: A model of a platform hosting three products shows that AI shopping assistance and delegation can soften price competition, create an alignment paradox in which some consumers are worse off than without AI, and shift platform profit and consumer surplus depending on the product pair.
AI.motivation: Consumers compare hosted products under salience distortion, so an AI shopping interface that ranks products accurately need not maximize realized consumer welfare, and its effect on price competition and platform profit is unclear.
AI.method: The platform hosts two of three products under three regimes: no AI, assistance (the AI recommends the two highest true-utility products) and delegation (the AI selects the best product subject to purchase approval), with firms pricing strategically and both AI modes knowing consumer preferences.
AI.result: Assistance can lower or raise hosted prices depending on the quality pair; some consumers become worse off despite a cheaper recommended option; assistance or delegation can raise both platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus for different pairs; the platform weakly prefers delegation with the high- and middle-quality pair, yet that design can yield lower profit and surplus than the no-AI optimum.
AI.conclusion: The alignment paradox arises because the assistant ranks products accurately but does not optimize the shortlist for realized consumer welfare, so the platform's preferred AI design need not be welfare-maximizing.

title: DataHelix: A CPU-GPU Co-Scheduling Data Plane for Multimodal Model Training
summary: Multimodal model training breaks the loose coupling between data loading and model execution assumed by conventional training pipelines. Large per-sample variation in decoding cost, token/latent count, and tensor size causes both CPU preprocessing time and GPU compute time to vary substantially across data-parallel ranks (training processes). In synchronous training, these two sources of heterogeneity interact tightly: GPU execution determines how long the input pipeline has to prepare the next batch, while delayed preprocessing in any rank in turn stalls all GPUs at synchronization. As a result, optimizing CPU throughput or GPU load balance in isolation cannot eliminate pipeline bubbles. We present DataHelix, a metadata-first CPU-GPU co-scheduling data plane for multimodal training. DataHelix jointly reasons about preprocessing demand and GPU execution progress, treating each GPU compute window as the readiness budget for the next batch and coordinating preprocessing across ranks to minimize deadline misses rather than CPU makespan. To avoid expensive data movement, placement is decided while samples remain lightweight descriptors, before decoding and collation amplify them into large tensors. Descriptor-level token-latent-aware batching performs coarse pre-balancing, while cost-gated collective rebalancing corrects residual skew only when its expected benefit exceeds transfer cost. Across 11 video and multimodal workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, DataHelix reduces mean deadline-miss rate by 67.8% and mean p95 input-wait latency by 87.0%, while achieving 2.72x geometric-mean throughput over rank-local DataLoaders and 1.82x over a Ray actor pool under the same CPU budget.

AI.tldr: DataHelix is a metadata-first CPU-GPU co-scheduling data plane that places multimodal training samples and coordinates preprocessing across data-parallel ranks against GPU readiness deadlines, reducing input-pipeline stalls.
AI.motivation: Per-sample variation in decoding cost and tensor size makes CPU preprocessing and GPU compute vary across ranks, so optimizing CPU throughput or GPU load balance in isolation cannot eliminate pipeline bubbles in synchronous training.
AI.method: Each GPU compute window is treated as the readiness budget for the next batch, and placement is decided on lightweight descriptors before decoding; descriptor-level token-latent-aware batching pre-balances the load, and cost-gated collective rebalancing corrects residual skew only when its expected benefit exceeds the transfer cost.
AI.result: Across 11 video and multimodal workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, DataHelix reduces mean deadline-miss rate by 67.8 percent and mean p95 input-wait latency by 87.0 percent, achieving 2.72x geometric-mean throughput over rank-local DataLoaders and 1.82x over a Ray actor pool under the same CPU budget.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating preprocessing with GPU execution progress, rather than optimizing either side in isolation, is what removes pipeline bubbles in multimodal training.

title: SmartBloch-Agent: An Agentic Framework for Automated MRI Sequence Design and Optimization
summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequences organize radiofrequency excitation, gradient encoding, and signal acquisition, determining magnetization evolution and image formation. Sequence research requires translating imaging objectives into executable protocols meeting physical and acquisition constraints, refined via physical simulation, signal reconstruction, and scientific evaluation. Sequence construction, physical verification, parameter search, and assessment involve many tools and manual decisions, limiting automation from objective to verifiable sequence. We develop SmartBloch-Agent, an integrated framework for automated MRI sequence design and optimization. Given objectives and scientific constraints in natural language, an AI agent interprets goals, plans tasks, orchestrates tools, and makes feedback-informed decisions, drawing on a construction module and optimizers for structural design and parameter search. Our GPU-accelerated SmartBloch engine supplies physical computation for both stages, so the framework configures, per sequence and objective, event validation, Full-Bloch magnetization evolution, signal acquisition, image reconstruction, and scientific evaluation, and closes the loop without external MRI simulators. Results return to the agent to guide sequence revision, parameter optimization, and candidate selection, and the design files carry simulation, reconstruction, and evaluation evidence, forming an output package for a real-scanner workflow. Experiments show the framework automatically designs and optimizes MRI sequences for varied objectives and constraints, refines candidates with physical feedback, and improves several parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction. SmartBloch-Agent unifies objectives, design, physical execution, and evaluation into a continuous workflow for end-to-end automation of MRI sequence research.

AI.tldr: SmartBloch-Agent is an AI agent framework that turns natural-language MRI objectives into executable pulse sequences, using a GPU-accelerated Full-Bloch simulation engine for physical evaluation and feedback-driven optimization without external MRI simulators.
AI.motivation: Designing an MRI sequence requires translating imaging objectives into protocols that meet physical and acquisition constraints, but construction, verification, parameter search and assessment involve many tools and manual decisions, which limits automation.
AI.method: An AI agent interprets the goals, plans tasks and orchestrates a construction module, optimizers and the SmartBloch engine, which performs event validation, Full-Bloch magnetization evolution, signal acquisition, image reconstruction and scientific evaluation in a closed loop.
AI.result: Experiments show that the framework designs and optimizes MRI sequences for varied objectives and constraints, refines candidates with physical feedback, and improves several parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Unifying objectives, design, physical execution and evaluation into one continuous workflow offers end-to-end automation of MRI sequence research, with design files that serve as output packages for a real-scanner workflow.

title: DexDICE: Reconciling Safety and Performance via Dual-Expert Offline Imitation Learning
comment: NeurIPS 2026. 55 pages, 13 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Ensuring high returns while providing strong safety guarantees in offline imitation learning (IL) is a fundamental challenge: existing approaches either rely on explicitly specified cost functions, which are difficult to design for complex real-world safety constraints, or require expert demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing, which are often too costly to collect. We introduce dual-expert imitation learning, which leverages two complementary data sources: (i) safety-compliant demonstrations that faithfully follow safety guidelines but may be suboptimal, and (ii) performance-oriented demonstrations that achieve high returns but may violate safety guidelines. To address this problem, we propose DexDICE (Dual-expert offline imitation learning via stationary DIstribution Correction Estimation). Instead of conventional distribution constraints, DexDICE combines DICE-style offline learning with safe support constraints, enabling agents to exploit high-return behaviors while remaining within safety-compliant regions. We prove that the ideal solution satisfying this constraint exactly has zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability. We evaluate DexDICE on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and validate it on a real-world mobile-robot navigation task trained directly from human teleoperation demonstrations, where it substantially outperforms baselines and remains robust to data scarcity and quality degradation.

AI.tldr: DexDICE is an offline imitation learning method that learns from two complementary datasets, safety-compliant but possibly suboptimal demonstrations and high-return but possibly unsafe ones, by combining DICE-style learning with safe support constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing offline IL either needs explicit cost functions, which are hard to design for complex real-world safety constraints, or expert demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing, which are costly to collect.
AI.method: Instead of conventional distribution constraints, DexDICE combines DICE-style offline learning with safe support constraints, so the agent can exploit high-return behaviours while staying within safety-compliant regions.
AI.result: The authors prove that the ideal solution satisfying the constraint has zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability; on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and a real-world mobile-robot navigation task trained from teleoperation, DexDICE substantially outperforms baselines and remains robust to data scarcity and quality degradation.
AI.conclusion: Dual-expert imitation learning reconciles safety and performance without requiring demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing.

title: Logit Laundering: Evading Data-Use Auditing in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to ACM CCS 2026
summary: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.

AI.tldr: Logit Laundering is an inference-time evasion framework that reshapes an LLM's output logits to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals, so watermark-based data-use auditing fails to detect unauthorized training while downstream utility is preserved.
AI.motivation: Watermark-based data-use auditing has been studied mainly from the defender's side, and the adversarial case, in which a non-compliant provider trains on unauthorized copyrighted data and evades detection, has received limited systematic investigation.
AI.method: A logit reshaping module suppresses watermark-induced statistics using a plug-and-play statistical bias estimator, and a confidence-aware scaling module calibrates suppression strength by next-token prediction confidence; model parameters are left unchanged and manipulation happens only in logit space.
AI.result: Logit Laundering evades various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals while preserving model utility on downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: The work argues for more robust auditing methods that can guard against such evasion behaviour.

title: Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures
summary: Policy entropy is widely used to diagnose exploration and collapse in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), yet its magnitude does not consistently track reasoning performance across optimization objectives. We argue that this ambiguity arises because global token entropy conflates uncertainty in successful and failed trajectories, diversity across correct solution strategies, and variation among realizations of the same strategy. We introduce \textbf{Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation (RCEA)}, a hierarchical diagnostic framework that separates complete-trajectory entropy from average token entropy, conditions uncertainty on verifier outcome and process validity, measures correct-solution-mode retention, and connects these population-level quantities to local covariance-driven updates. In controlled sweeps over six RLVR objectives at two model scales, entropy trajectories do not induce a stable ordering of reasoning accuracy. Token entropy is higher for verifier-failed than successful trajectories under both broad separately aggregated estimates and a common-question paired analysis, whose confidence intervals exclude equality at 10 of 12 displayed endpoints. A local covariance approximation predicts the direction of adjacent-checkpoint entropy change in 95.5\% of nonfailed transitions; a reward-stratified endpoint proxy further shows that positive chosen-token covariance is more tail-concentrated within failed prefixes. Every reportable trained endpoint exhibits some contraction in independently audited correct-solution-mode breadth, whose positive association with large-\(k\) coverage remains exploratory. These results show that entropy collapse should be diagnosed by which uncertainty is removed, rather than by global entropy alone.

AI.tldr: RCEA is a diagnostic framework showing that global token entropy in RLVR conflates uncertainty over successful and failed trajectories, so entropy collapse should be diagnosed by which uncertainty is removed rather than by total entropy alone.
AI.motivation: Policy entropy is widely used to diagnose exploration and collapse in RLVR, but its magnitude does not consistently track reasoning performance across optimization objectives.
AI.method: RCEA separates complete-trajectory entropy from average token entropy, conditions uncertainty on verifier outcome and process validity, measures correct-solution-mode retention, and connects these population-level quantities to local covariance-driven updates, in controlled sweeps over six RLVR objectives at two model scales.
AI.result: Entropy trajectories do not induce a stable ordering of reasoning accuracy; token entropy is higher for verifier-failed than for successful trajectories, with confidence intervals excluding equality at 10 of 12 displayed endpoints; a local covariance approximation predicts the direction of adjacent-checkpoint entropy change in 95.5 percent of nonfailed transitions; every trained endpoint shows some contraction of correct-solution-mode breadth.
AI.conclusion: Entropy collapse should be diagnosed by which uncertainty is removed, rather than by global entropy alone.

title: FusionCLIP: Multimodal Contrastive Pretraining for Fusion Plasma Diagnostics
summary: Visible-light videos and multivariate diagnostic signals provide complementary observations of tokamak discharges. However, existing fusion pretraining methods, primarily learn representations by reconstructing or predicting observations, leaving the correspondence between these modalities underexplored. Representation learning is further challenged by the fact that plasma-related regions occupy only part of each video frame and diagnostic variables have substantially different sampling rates. We propose FusionCLIP, a multimodal contrastive pretraining framework. Spatiotemporal Stability Selection retains informative visual tokens, while a Temporal Query Encoder integrates asynchronous diagnostic signals using their observation timestamps. Contrastive learning then aligns the two modality representations. We construct EAST Multimodal Diagnostics (EAST-MMD), comprising 1307 EAST discharges, and evaluate the model on three independently fine-tuned tasks: disruption prediction, edge-localized mode (ELM) classification, and $H_{98}$ regression. FusionCLIP achieves an aggregate score of 89.07\%, exceeding the best general-purpose pretraining configuration and an in-domain contrastive pretraining configuration without Spatiotemporal Stability Selection by 6.27 and 2.12 percentage points, respectively. Ablations and attention visualizations further support the contributions of its key components.

AI.tldr: FusionCLIP is a contrastive pretraining framework that aligns visible-light videos with asynchronous diagnostic signals from tokamak discharges, evaluated on disruption prediction, edge-localized mode classification and H98 regression.
AI.motivation: Existing fusion pretraining mainly reconstructs or predicts observations and leaves cross-modal correspondence underexplored, and plasma regions cover only part of each frame while diagnostic variables have very different sampling rates.
AI.method: Spatiotemporal Stability Selection retains informative visual tokens, a Temporal Query Encoder integrates asynchronous diagnostic signals using their observation timestamps, and contrastive learning aligns the two modality representations; the EAST Multimodal Diagnostics dataset (EAST-MMD) has 1307 EAST discharges.
AI.result: FusionCLIP reaches an aggregate score of 89.07 percent, exceeding the best general-purpose pretraining configuration and an in-domain contrastive configuration without Spatiotemporal Stability Selection by 6.27 and 2.12 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Ablations and attention visualizations support the contribution of each key component to multimodal pretraining for fusion plasma diagnostics.

title: Mosaic:montage-agnostic self-distilled graph learning for subject-independent ieeg seizure detection
summary: Intracranial EEG provides high signal-to-noise ratio and spatial resolution for detecting epileptic activity, but patient-specific electrode placement leads to substantial variation in channel count and montage across subjects. This heterogeneity limits the generalization of existing detectors under subject-independent evaluation. We propose MOSAIC (MOntage-agnostic Self-distilled Adaptive Inter-channel Connectivity learning), a lightweight graph-learning framework for subject-independent iEEG seizure detection. MOSAIC pairs a shared convolutional channel encoder with a patient-agnostic channel-attention module that infers a weighted inter-channel adjacency matrix from the encoded features, requiring no fixed montage graph. An exponential moving average self-distillation objective regularizes each prediction toward a slowly updated per-patient teacher. Across four public iEEG corpora (SWEC-ETHZ long- and short-term, Mayo, FNUSA), MOSAIC outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in F2 and Cohen's $\kappa$ while learning more stable inter-channel adjacencies, demonstrating that self-distilled connectivity learning transfers across unseen implantations.

AI.tldr: MOSAIC is a lightweight montage-agnostic graph-learning model that infers inter-channel adjacency from intracranial EEG features and uses self-distillation to detect seizures in subjects not seen in training.
AI.motivation: Patient-specific electrode placement makes channel count and montage vary across subjects, which limits the generalization of existing iEEG seizure detectors under subject-independent evaluation.
AI.method: A shared convolutional channel encoder is paired with a patient-agnostic channel-attention module that infers a weighted inter-channel adjacency matrix without a fixed montage graph, and an exponential moving average self-distillation objective regularizes each prediction toward a slowly updated per-patient teacher.
AI.result: Across four public iEEG corpora (SWEC-ETHZ long- and short-term, Mayo and FNUSA), MOSAIC outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in F2 and Cohen's kappa while learning more stable inter-channel adjacencies.
AI.conclusion: Self-distilled connectivity learning transfers across unseen implantations, supporting montage-agnostic seizure detection.

title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
comment: Code : this https URL Website : this https URL
summary: Lloyd's k-means algorithm is a long-running standard for clustering, with applications in data analysis, retrieval, quantization and data curation. In this paper, we introduce an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates, powered by modern deep learning machinery and new insights. We also establish scaling laws on how decay rate and batch size impact final performance. This gives us a formulaic rule to fix them for multiple problem sizes and embedding datasets, without the need for any hyperparameter sweep. The resulting clustering algorithm, coined e-means, is much faster than Lloyd k-means and converges to lower losses, frequently even beating k-means++. On a wide array of embeddings datasets, it beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, which translates to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations. As an example, e-means partitions DINO10B, a dataset of 10 billion DINO embeddings, into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.

AI.tldr: e-means is a mini-batch k-means variant that uses an exponential moving average update with decay and batch-size settings given by scaling laws, reaching lower loss than Lloyd k-means in a small fraction of the epochs.
AI.motivation: Lloyd's k-means is a long-standing clustering standard, but its speed and final loss can be improved for large embedding datasets without a hyperparameter sweep.
AI.method: An exponential moving average optimization procedure for mini-batch k-means, with scaling laws that relate decay rate and batch size to final performance and give a formulaic rule for setting both across problem sizes and embedding datasets.
AI.result: On a wide range of embedding datasets, e-means reaches the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, a 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedup over state-of-the-art k-means implementations, and it partitions a 10-billion-embedding dataset into 16 million clusters in 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.
AI.conclusion: e-means offers a much faster, lower-loss clustering method that frequently beats k-means++ without hyperparameter tuning.

title: V-STORM: A Structure-Aware Grounded Chain of Thought Dataset for Faithful and Fine-Grained Spatio-Temporal Video Reasoning
comment: 9 Pages, 5 figures
summary: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal this http URL address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal this http URL this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal this http URL reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: V-STORM is a framework that turns videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs and derives Grounded Chain of Thought annotations from validated evidence paths, releasing a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark. It finds that MLLMs can localize relevant spatio-temporal cues yet fail to compose them into correct multi-step reasoning, and fine-tuning on V-STORM improves answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness.
AI.motivation: MLLMs still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal video reasoning, and existing data construction and evaluation pipelines lack granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.
AI.method: Videos are converted into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs, from which Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) is derived along validated evidence paths so that each reasoning step is traceable to structured, verifiable evidence.
AI.result: The authors build a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both with GCoT annotations, and show that current MLLMs often localize evidence but fail at evidence composition; fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: Answer-only evaluation hides a localization-versus-composition bottleneck, and V-STORM supervision is an effective way to train faithful, evidence-grounded video reasoning.

title: Active Learning of Robust Models
summary: In many domains from species identification to cancer diagnosis, labelling data to train predictive models remains costly. In these settings, it is advantageous to intelligently select data points to label to achieve the maximum information gain, this is the motivation behind the study of active learning. In addition to the high costs of acquiring data in such domains, there is the added complexity of data distribution shifts that can occur between training and deployment. For example, the features of cancerous skin cells taken in one country may be different in another region of the world. These two challenges - efficient labelling of data, and learning models robust to distribution shifts have been studied separately but not together, even though these challenges often co-occur in real-life settings. We identify failure modes of standard active learning approaches when the distribution of data at deployment is different from the distribution in which the data is sampled for labelling. We propose a new strategy for efficiently learning classifiers that generalise under specific forms of distribution shift, namely subpopulation shift. Drawing on work in learning from heterogeneous data, we aim to train models that perform well across subpopulations of the data, through active learning. To handle this challenging setting, we exploit the fact that many datasets include metadata about data collection that can serve as a noisy proxy for each sample's underlying subpopulation. We demonstrate how to leverage these noisy labels during active learning selection, and demonstrate empirically that our approach improves classifier accuracy across subpopulations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies active learning under subpopulation shift, where the deployment distribution differs from the sampling distribution, and proposes a selection strategy that uses noisy subpopulation metadata to train classifiers that perform well across subpopulations. Experiments show improved classifier accuracy across subpopulations.
AI.motivation: Standard active learning fails when deployment data differ from the data sampled for labelling, and robustness to distribution shift and efficient labelling have been studied separately even though they often co-occur in practice.
AI.method: The authors exploit collection metadata as a noisy proxy for each sample's subpopulation and use these noisy labels during active learning selection, drawing on learning from heterogeneous data to train models that perform well across subpopulations.
AI.result: The approach is demonstrated empirically to improve classifier accuracy across subpopulations; the abstract does not name datasets or baselines.
AI.conclusion: Joint treatment of label efficiency and subpopulation robustness is feasible, and cheap, noisy collection metadata can guide active selection toward robust classifiers.

title: Multimodal Training with Knowledge Traction for Video Anomaly Detection
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures, 8 tables
summary: The task of weakly supervised video anomaly detection is challenging. Existing approaches mainly model video frame features and determine whether anomalies are present based on their magnitudes. In this work, we propose a novel method that incorporates external knowledge into training to improve model performance, robustness, and generalization. We leverage textual prompts and a large language model (LLM) to establish prior information for the specific task, and employ dictionary learning to normalize and compress this information. Moreover, during experiments, we observed inconsistencies in the textual descriptions extracted from similar video frames by image caption models. To address this, we devise a method that leverages an LLM and auxiliary information to ensure consistency in the textual descriptions of similar frames within a video. Finally, we introduce a feature processing approach that incorporates prior knowledge and cross-modal attention mechanisms. This approach learns the relationships and characteristics among different modalities to construct more accurate and reliable feature representations, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a weakly supervised video anomaly detection method that injects external knowledge from textual prompts and an LLM, with dictionary learning for compression, LLM-based caption consistency, and cross-modal attention. The authors report that the method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing weakly supervised video anomaly detection methods rely mainly on frame feature magnitudes, and image caption models produce inconsistent descriptions for similar frames.
AI.method: Textual prompts and an LLM supply task-specific prior information, which dictionary learning normalizes and compresses; an LLM with auxiliary information enforces consistent captions across similar frames; a feature processing step combines the prior knowledge with cross-modal attention.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches in experiments, without giving specific numbers or datasets.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating LLM-derived prior knowledge and cross-modal attention improves the accuracy, stability and generalization of weakly supervised video anomaly detection.

title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

AI.tldr: TT-MBRL encodes the memory of episode observations into world model parameters by running gradient descent at test time, so the agent learns a distinct world model per episode. It reports state-of-the-art results on the 3D Memory Maze benchmark and maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Model-based RL agents still fail to surpass human performance on tasks requiring long-term memory and planning, and architecture-based approaches rely on contextual memory alone.
AI.method: Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning uses gradient descent at test time to write episode observations into world model parameters, giving each episode its own world model in addition to contextual memory.
AI.result: A proof of concept on a simplified 2D variant called Memory Maze 2D shows consistent gains across world model architectures; in 3D it achieves new state-of-the-art results on Memory Maze; it also maintains strong performance on DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.
AI.conclusion: Test-time adaptation of world model parameters is an effective route to long-term memory in MBRL that goes beyond architecture design, without sacrificing performance on standard benchmarks.

title: Breaking the Privacy Promise: Gradient Inversion Attacks on Federated Low-Rank Adapted Vision Transformers
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been increasingly adopted to fine-tune pretrained models with low computational cost and is therefore also preferred in the federated learning paradigm to reduce computational and communication overhead. In this work, we investigate the sparsely explored problem of the risk of private data leakage in LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers (ViTs), where low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server with access to individual client updates. We show that quality of reconstruction is limited by two coupled ambiguities: reduced information in LoRA gradients and missing spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. To address this, we propose a spatially anchored generative inversion framework that incorporates server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings into ViT blocks during fine-tuning at clients. The resulting positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, providing additional positional cues, while the generative prior keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold, reducing duplicate-data and patch-permutation artifacts, {which produce similar gradients as those produced when the target client images are used}. Adding our proposed spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45, and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, as well as PSNR gains of 7.83 and 11.74 dB on high-resolution CelebA and CARS datasets, respectively, in the FedSGD setting. Such gains in reconstructed image quality metrics are also maintained at higher batch sizes and in FedAvg settings. These results indicate that LoRA-based PEFT does not, by itself, prevent data leakage in FL, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can help in exposing private information.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that gradient inversion attacks can reconstruct private client images from LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers in federated learning, and proposes spatial anchoring with server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings plus a generative prior to improve reconstruction. It concludes that LoRA-based PEFT does not by itself prevent data leakage in FL.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is favored in federated learning for its low cost, but the privacy risk of LoRA-adapted ViTs is sparsely explored, and low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server.
AI.method: The server prescribes trainable positional embeddings that are inserted into ViT blocks during client fine-tuning, so the positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, and a generative inversion prior (GIAS) keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold.
AI.result: Adding spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45 and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, and gives PSNR gains of 7.83 dB on CelebA and 11.74 dB on CARS in FedSGD; gains persist at higher batch sizes and under FedAvg.
AI.conclusion: LoRA-based PEFT is not a privacy safeguard in federated learning, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can expose private information more effectively.

title: Differentially Private GraphRAG: Protecting Relation Connectivity and Semantics
summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) connects information across documents through entity relationships to support relational reasoning. However, black-box access to GraphRAG systems can enable adversaries to reconstruct knowledge graphs and recover both structural connectivity between entities and the semantics of their relationships. Existing defenses lack formal privacy guarantees and provide limited protection against such reconstruction attacks. We propose RelGuard, the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG, which provides formal privacy guarantees by mitigating connectivity leakage and protecting relations and their semantic meaning through relation removal. We formalize relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which bounds the distinguishability of mechanism outputs according to the semantic distance between alternative relations while accounting for relation removal. Building on this definition, we develop a four-step defense mechanism that sanitizes source documents before GraphRAG indexing by perturbing relation predicates or removing their associated connectivity using the exponential mechanism. Experiments across three GraphRAG systems and two targeted reconstruction attacks demonstrate that RelGuard provides stronger protection against reconstruction attacks than four existing defense mechanisms while better preserving downstream utility.

AI.tldr: RelGuard is a differentially private defense for GraphRAG that sanitizes source documents before indexing by perturbing relation predicates or removing relations, under a formal relation-DP definition. It outperforms four existing defenses against two reconstruction attacks across three GraphRAG systems while preserving utility better.
AI.motivation: Black-box access to GraphRAG lets adversaries reconstruct knowledge graphs, including entity connectivity and relation semantics, and existing defenses lack formal privacy guarantees.
AI.method: The authors define relation differential privacy, which bounds output distinguishability by the semantic distance between alternative relations while accounting for relation removal, and implement a four-step mechanism that uses the exponential mechanism to perturb predicates or remove connectivity.
AI.result: Across three GraphRAG systems and two targeted reconstruction attacks, RelGuard gives stronger protection than four existing defense mechanisms while better preserving downstream utility.
AI.conclusion: Formal relation-level privacy can mitigate both connectivity leakage and semantic leakage in GraphRAG without the utility loss of prior heuristic defenses.

title: Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures. Equal contribution. Code and results will be released
summary: Robots increasingly choose actions by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences, in model-predictive control or best-of-$N$ selection; we measure what this does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic labels and blind labels from the two authors, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76%: with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from, while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97. On plate-slide human labels are exploited less than synthetic ones, and on window-open search helps. True return roughly follows how far the planner's weights move from its proposals ($\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}}$) for both weighting rules we test, and best-of-$N$ with a verifier from synthetic labels falls below a single noisy action. We prove that $\chi^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, that no positive gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own, and that an episode's return splits exactly into per-step terms, of which the guarantee covers the selection terms. Calibrated from 100 proposal pairs ranked by true return (an oracle) on start states the evaluation never uses, this rule is the safest fix we test: with each of five independent sets it succeeds in every arm run and keeps on average 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on plate-slide and drawer-open, though it is cautious where search helps. Calibration from a person's comparisons cannot detect a bias the scorer learned from that person; correcting for the pairs people cannot tell apart, or a second person, limits the damage.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that sampling-based control (MPPI search and best-of-N selection) against a reward model learned from human preferences exploits the learned reward, cutting true return by up to 76% on several robot tasks. It proves a chi-squared-regularized MPPI rule with a temperature calibrated from scorer error is worst-case optimal, and reports that this rule is the safest fix tested.
AI.motivation: Robots increasingly select actions by searching against reward models learned from human preferences, but the effect of this search on the true objective is unmeasured, and held-out label accuracy does not reveal the exploitation.
AI.method: The authors compare MPPI search strengths and best-of-N selection on HalfCheetah, Hopper, Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide, and window-open, using crowd-sourced, synthetic and blind labels, and analyze the result with a chi-squared-regularized MPPI whose temperature is set by the scorer's error spread on proposals.
AI.result: Harder search reduces true return by up to 76%, with drawer-open succeeding in 0 of 20 runs under human labels versus 10 of 10 for the cloned policy; held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97. The calibrated rule keeps 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on plate-slide and drawer-open across five independent calibration sets, though it is cautious where search helps.
AI.conclusion: Reward learned from preferences can be exploited by planners, and regularization calibrated from oracle-ranked proposal pairs limits the damage, but calibration from a person's comparisons cannot detect that person's own bias.

title: SURE:Spatiotemporal Uncertainty Representation for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Learning
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have become a promising paradigm for end-to-end robot control, but their effectiveness still depends heavily on large volumes of demonstration data. In manipulation tasks, this dependence is compounded by structured spatiotemporal uncertainty in the action space: multiple nearby actions or trajectories may successfully solve the same task, while semantically equivalent demonstrations often unfold at different speeds. Standard pointwise supervision treats each demonstrated action as an exact target, imposing an unnecessary learning burden under such uncertainty. We present SURE, a data-efficient VLA training framework that explicitly models both spatial and temporal uncertainty. SURE augments a VLA backbone with a lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder that captures spatial uncertainty through local correlations among neighboring action bins. It further introduces Soft-DTW alignment supervision to accommodate local timing variations between predicted and demonstrated action chunks. Together, these two components reduce sensitivity to demonstrator-specific poses and execution timing, enabling more data-efficient action learning. We evaluate SURE on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks. Even with only 10% of the demonstration data or 20% of the training steps, SURE achieves manipulation success rates that match or surpass baseline VLAs.

AI.tldr: SURE is a data-efficient VLA training framework that models spatial uncertainty with a transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder and temporal uncertainty with Soft-DTW alignment supervision. With only 10% of the demonstration data or 20% of the training steps, it matches or surpasses baseline VLAs on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: VLA policies depend heavily on large demonstration sets, and pointwise supervision treats each demonstrated action as an exact target even though multiple nearby actions succeed and demonstrations differ in speed.
AI.method: A lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder captures local correlations among neighboring action bins to represent spatial uncertainty, and Soft-DTW alignment supervision tolerates local timing differences between predicted and demonstrated action chunks.
AI.result: Evaluated on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation, SURE with 10% of demonstrations or 20% of training steps achieves success rates that match or surpass baseline VLAs.
AI.conclusion: Modeling action-space uncertainty explicitly reduces sensitivity to demonstrator-specific poses and execution timing, which makes VLA learning more data-efficient.

title: Verifier Noise Is a Temperature: Testing Tilt Predictions in Finite-Budget LLM-Guided Search
