comment: 34 pages, 5 figures. Pre-registered predictions, code and data checksums are described in Appendix C
summary: LLM-guided search loops propose a modified candidate, score it, and keep it if it scores better. When both candidates are re-scored at every comparison, as in the minibatch acceptance gates of prompt optimizers, keep-if-better is a reversible Markov chain if the score difference is logistic and the mutation operator is reversible, and its stationary law is the mutation equilibrium tilted by exp(beta f). For any continuous symmetric noise difference the same tilt is the stationary law of a small-step diffusion limit, with beta = 4F'(0); for a minibatch gate beta grows with the square root of the minibatch size. Caching the incumbent's score instead inflates the recorded score. We test the tilt as a prediction for LLM-guided program search, committing each prediction from calibration data before the search runs. The level after 150 steps rises with the minibatch size in six of seven settings, but its predicted value fails: on bin packing, search attains 62-88% of the predicted gain when the proposer edits the parent and 109-119% when it writes new heuristics. The attained fraction falls with the parent-child quality correlation of unselected mutation; a registered test on two new settings confirmed the direction, but not the quantitative agreement after a correction. Further registered tests found that runs started from a good program kept losing quality over 300 steps, more so from starts that search had selected, by a margin that passed its registered rule narrowly. Runs from different starts had not reached a common level, so whether the tilt describes the stationary law of LLM editing remains open. A registered test in prompt optimisation on frozen task-model scores failed: search exceeded the tilt, and the bin-packing relation did not transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper frames keep-if-better LLM-guided search with re-scored candidates as a Markov chain whose stationary law is the mutation equilibrium tilted by exp(beta f), and tests this tilt as a pre-committed prediction. The tilt predicts the level after 150 steps poorly on bin packing, where search attains 62-88% or 109-119% of the predicted gain depending on the proposer, and the prediction does not transfer to prompt optimisation.
AI.motivation: Prompt optimizers and LLM-guided program search accept mutations by noisy re-scored comparisons, and it is unknown whether the resulting stationary distribution has a tractable form that predicts search outcomes.
AI.method: The authors derive a tilt under logistic or continuous symmetric noise, with beta equal to 4F'(0) and growing with the square root of minibatch size in minibatch gates, then commit predictions from calibration data and test them on bin packing and new settings with registered tests.
AI.result: The level after 150 steps rises with minibatch size in six of seven settings, but the quantitative prediction fails on bin packing; the attained fraction falls with the parent-child quality correlation, and runs from good starts keep losing quality over 300 steps. A registered test in prompt optimisation on frozen task-model scores failed, with search exceeding the tilt.
AI.conclusion: Whether the tilt describes the stationary law of LLM editing remains open, since runs from different starts did not reach a common level and the bin-packing relation did not transfer.

title: Empirical Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in SSH Infrastructure
summary: With the anticipated arrival of Q-day, quantum computers threaten current cryptographic schemes for encryption and digital signatures. In response, major content delivery networks and cloud service providers are already adopting Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The current state-of-the-art focuses on benchmarking the operational performance of implementing PQC, but the real-world adoption status remains under-researched. This work utilizes large-scale SSH fingerprint data from a proprietary scanning tool to analyze PQC adoption across 1.52 million hosts and 27,012 entities. Our study shows that the PQC transition in the SSH protocol is underway but highly polarized: 45.2% of SSH hosts on port 22 support PQC, while 54.8% remain classical-only. At the entity level, 39.9% have enabled PQC on at least one host, whereas 60.1% have no PQC support. By correlating PQC adoption with industry, geography, and organizational size (digital and financial), this study provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of PQC adoption status in SSH infrastructure.

AI.tldr: A large-scale measurement of SSH hosts finds that post-quantum cryptography adoption is underway but polarized: 45.2% of hosts on port 22 support PQC, and 39.9% of 27,012 entities have enabled PQC on at least one host. The study also correlates adoption with industry, geography and organization size.
AI.motivation: CDNs and cloud providers are adopting PQC ahead of Q-day, but prior work benchmarks PQC performance rather than measuring real-world deployment status.
AI.method: The authors analyze large-scale SSH fingerprint data from a proprietary scanning tool covering 1.52 million hosts and 27,012 entities, and correlate PQC support with industry, geography, and digital and financial organizational size.
AI.result: 45.2% of SSH hosts on port 22 support PQC and 54.8% are classical-only; at the entity level 39.9% have PQC on at least one host and 60.1% have no PQC support.
AI.conclusion: The SSH PQC transition is in progress but highly uneven across hosts and entities, and the study gives a comprehensive empirical baseline of PQC adoption in SSH infrastructure.

title: Empirical Assessment of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in TLS
summary: Anticipating Q-day security concerns, major CDNs and cloud providers are migrating to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). While existing literature benchmarks PQC performance, empirical research evaluating real-world adoption data remains scarce. We present an empirical assessment of PQC deployment across seven critical protocols (HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAP-SSL, POP3-SSL, TELNETS, and RDP) using 10,000 target IP addresses per protocol. At the origin-server level, PQC algorithm support reaches 9.1% for HTTPS and 7.39% for LDAPS, while falling below 1% for all other evaluated protocols. At the entity level, PQC support is 11% for HTTPS and 5.4% for LDAPS, while the remaining protocols have less than 5% of entities supporting PQC on the hosted servers. We further correlate these adoption trends against organizational digital and financial footprint, and industry sectors, yielding a multi-dimensional empirical assessment of PQC deployment. Finally, at the domain level, we perform a comparative analysis of PQC adoption in Cloudflare-hosted domains against baseline Cloudflare datasets. Collectively, our findings provide critical insights into the current state of PQC readiness over Transport Layer Security (TLS).

AI.tldr: An empirical scan of PQC deployment across seven TLS-based protocols finds that adoption is concentrated in HTTPS and LDAPS, with all other protocols below 1% at the origin-server level. The study also compares Cloudflare-hosted domains against Cloudflare baseline datasets.
AI.motivation: Major CDNs and cloud providers are migrating to PQC, but empirical data on real-world PQC adoption across protocols is scarce, and prior work mainly benchmarks performance.
AI.method: The authors probe 10,000 target IP addresses per protocol across HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAP-SSL, POP3-SSL, TELNETS and RDP, correlate adoption with organizational digital and financial footprint and industry sectors, and run a domain-level comparison for Cloudflare-hosted domains.
AI.result: PQC algorithm support reaches 9.1% of origin servers for HTTPS and 7.39% for LDAPS and is below 1% for the other protocols; at the entity level it is 11% for HTTPS and 5.4% for LDAPS, with under 5% of entities for the rest.
AI.conclusion: PQC readiness over TLS is low outside HTTPS and LDAPS, and the findings give a multi-dimensional snapshot of current PQC deployment.

title: ICare-DT: a digital twin for continuous forecasting of intensive care patients
summary: Digital twins of intensive care patients should update forecasts from new data and predict treatment responses, but few studies test whether routine records support either. We propose ICare-DT, a Transformer-based twin that updates a latent patient state hourly from new measurements without retraining. We trained it on 140,473 eICU-CRD stays to forecast vital signs crossing their training-set means. On test data, later forecasts beat the twin's own hour-6 forecasts of the same windows in all 12 settings (+0.073 to +0.153 AUROC). On validation data, controls that withheld or swapped the new hours traced the gain to the patient's own measurements. Without refitting, the model kept its gain on a second database (8 of 9 settings, +0.025 to +0.114 AUROC) in a prespecified evaluation of the previously analyzed MIMIC-IV test split. Refitted within MIMIC-IV, a twin state fine-tuned on clinical endpoints gave gradient boosting a significant gain for acute kidney injury (+0.0035 AUROC; hypotension +0.0010, not significant). To test response prediction, we built a benchmark that replaces the treatments in real records with simulated doses and injects responses of known size, visible only at measurement times. Ridge models supervised with injected effects recovered them from real records only through frequently measured variables (heart rate) read at their measurement times. We asked standard learners to predict these effects for a dosing regime no patient had received. No standard learner outperformed predicting zero effect at an out-of-support query. When told how the simulated responses were generated, a separate learner recovered the effects from the same records without seeing their true values (R2 0.30 to 0.40 at one effect size). Routine records support forecasts that improve with each patient's new data, and our benchmark is a testbed for models that learn how responses are generated.

AI.tldr: ICare-DT is a Transformer-based digital twin that updates a latent ICU patient state hourly without retraining and forecasts vital-sign threshold crossings, with gains that persist on a second database. A benchmark with injected treatment responses shows that standard learners cannot predict effects for unseen dosing regimes, while a learner told how responses were generated recovers them with R2 of 0.30 to 0.40.
AI.motivation: Digital twins of intensive care patients should update forecasts with new data and predict treatment responses, but few studies test whether routine records support either.
AI.method: The Transformer twin updates a latent patient state from new hourly measurements without retraining; the authors train it on 140,473 eICU-CRD stays and build a benchmark that replaces real treatments with simulated doses and injects responses of known size visible only at measurement times.
AI.result: On test data, later forecasts beat the twin's own hour-6 forecasts in all 12 settings (+0.073 to +0.153 AUROC); without refitting, gains hold on MIMIC-IV in 8 of 9 settings (+0.025 to +0.114 AUROC); for acute kidney injury a refitted twin state gives gradient boosting +0.0035 AUROC, while hypotension is not significant; no standard learner beats predicting zero effect at an out-of-support query.
AI.conclusion: Routine ICU records support forecasts that improve with each patient's new data, and the benchmark is a testbed for models that must learn how treatment responses are generated, a task standard learners do not yet solve.

title: Safety Is $Π_1$, Provability Is $Σ_1$: One Framework for the Hugging Face Breach and OpenAI's Mathematical Proofs
summary: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face in July 2026, and the same company released more than seven hundred AI-generated manuscripts of mathematical proofs in October 2026. The first event is read as a failure in security, while the second is read as a success in mathematics. We read both through the hybrid framework of our paper (Kim and Kang, 2026, arXiv:2611.01914), in which coding, proving, and learning from data are derivations by one and the same deductive mechanism, distinguished by the kinds of premises from which they are derived. Under this framework, the AI systems behind the two events ran the same loop, in which a statistical proposer produces candidate exploits or proofs and a deductive verifier settles each one by a derivation. What separates the events is the logical form of the statement wanted by each of the two domains, security and mathematics. The safety of a program is a $\Pi_1$ statement, for it says that no exploit exists, which is not assured by any finite list of tests that have been passed by the program. By contrast, the provability of a sentence is a $\Sigma_1$ statement, for it says that a proof exists, which is assured by a single instance, namely a proof that has been checked by the deductive verifier. The theorem behind both is Turing's Undecidability Theorem: the halting set is $\Sigma_1$ but not decidable, so its complement is $\Pi_1$ and not $\Sigma_1$, which is to say that membership has a finite witness but non-membership has none. We prove that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier does not change this undecidability result, however good the proposer is. We then discuss what does assure safety and where the residual risk goes.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI safety is a Pi1 statement and provability is a Sigma1 statement, and uses this to read a security breach and a set of AI-generated mathematical proofs under one hybrid deductive framework. It proves that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier leaves Turing's undecidability result unchanged, however good the proposer is.
AI.motivation: The same company's AI systems produced a security breach and hundreds of mathematical proof manuscripts, which are read as a security failure and a mathematical success, and no unified logical account of the two outcomes exists.
AI.method: Within the hybrid framework of the authors' earlier paper, coding, proving and learning are derivations by one deductive mechanism, and the authors analyze the logical form of safety (no exploit exists, a Pi1 statement) and provability (a proof exists, a Sigma1 statement) using the halting set and its complement.
AI.result: The authors prove that a statistical proposer attached to a deductive verifier does not change the undecidability result, however good the proposer is; the abstract states no empirical numbers.
AI.conclusion: Safety cannot be assured by any finite list of passed tests, and the proposer-verifier loop cannot overcome undecidability; the paper then discusses what does assure safety and where residual risk goes.

title: When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Replication package: this https URL
summary: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like this http URL and this http URL, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, a third more than with the corrected command; in the other cases, we could not detect a difference. Although agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, none repaired the underlying instruction file. Correcting the instructions eliminated operations on obsolete paths, while removing them prevented most. Our findings show that task success alone can hide the costs of documentation debt, highlighting the need to evaluate agent behavior beyond final outcomes.

AI.tldr: A study of documentation debt in coding agents finds that agents follow stale repository instruction files when they are relevant to the task, adding tool calls, and that task success alone hides this cost. The stale-instruction test with Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, roughly a third more than with the corrected command.
AI.motivation: Repository instruction files read by coding agents such as Claude Code can fall behind the code, and evaluations that check only task success can miss the cost this stale guidance adds to every later session.
AI.method: The authors take three real stale instructions from open-source repositories (a test command, a code location and a component-addition procedure) and have agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under stale, corrected and removed versions, analyzing 732 trajectories from two models at the level of tool calls.
AI.result: Agents followed stale guidance when relevant, sometimes even when correct information was available elsewhere; on the stale test command Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, and no detectable difference appeared in the other cases; no agent repaired the instruction file, and correcting the file eliminated operations on obsolete paths while removing it prevented most.
AI.conclusion: Task success can hide documentation debt costs, so agent evaluations should look beyond final outcomes, and maintainers should correct or remove stale instructions.

title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks
summary: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: FiLSim is a scalable GNN framework for graph similarity (Graph Edit Distance and Maximum Common Subgraph) that uses a simplified GNN pipeline, remains accurate on graphs with over 150,000 nodes, and scores all test pairs within seconds on one GPU. The authors also release four large-scale datasets with reliable GED labels created by sequential graph editing.
AI.motivation: GNN-based approaches to graph similarity have been evaluated mainly on small graphs, and GED and MCS are NP-hard, so scalability to large graphs is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors propose FiLSim, a simplified GNN pipeline, and a sequential graph-editing strategy that constructs large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels for evaluating scalability.
AI.result: FiLSim is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four new large-scale datasets; it stays accurate on graphs with more than 150,000 nodes, where baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: A simplified GNN pipeline can stay competitive on standard benchmarks while scaling to very large graphs, and the new datasets provide a testbed for scalability.

title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
summary: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

AI.tldr: LLM agent teams synthesize and formally verify quantum programs in a Lean library, producing order-of-magnitude improvements on several scientific applications. The reported gains include 1.4x on parallel search, 290x on quantum arithmetic, and 11x, 8x and 2.5x on simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug metabolism.
AI.motivation: Quantum algorithm progress depends on slow expert collaboration, and quantum algorithms can usually be evaluated classically only on restricted or small instances, which limits automated discovery.
AI.method: The authors build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which LLM agents synthesize programs against formal specifications and verify correctness and cost, while agent teams share results through wikis and organized conferences.
AI.result: Results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations for fusion, photochemistry and drug metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively.
AI.conclusion: Combining human and AI effort under formal proof lets researchers design quantum algorithms that current classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

title: Grasp-TAGS: Task-Aware Grasp Selection via Critic Distillation for Prehensile Loco-Manipulation
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures
summary: Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. Therefore, we propose Grasp-TAGS, a task-aware grasp selection framework for goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement. We train a unified PPO-based reinforcement learning policy across multiple initial grasp configurations and distill the learned critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only the candidate grasp configuration and goal information. At inference time, we select the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility for the downstream policy to complete the task, before even making a contact. Experiments demonstrate that Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over both fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, achieving an average success rate of 89.84% compared with 79.87% for the best-performing single-grasp policies, an improvement of 9.97 percentage points. Grasp-TAGS also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects. For more qualitative results, refer to the supplementary webpage: this https URL

AI.tldr: Grasp-TAGS trains a PPO policy across multiple initial grasps and distills its critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that picks the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility before contact. It reaches an average success rate of 89.84% on goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement, versus 79.87% for the best single-grasp policy.
AI.motivation: Loco-manipulation performance depends strongly on the initial grasp, yet existing learning methods usually assume a fixed or predefined grasp, even though different stable grasps lead to very different manipulation outcomes.
AI.method: A unified PPO-based policy is trained over multiple initial grasp configurations, and its learned critic is distilled into a grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only grasp configuration and goal information.
AI.result: Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, with 89.84% average success versus 79.87% for the best single-grasp policy (a 9.97 percentage point gain), and it also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware grasp selection before contact is an effective way to improve large-object rearrangement performance over fixed-grasp policies.

title: GRAC: Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning for Surgical Scene Description
comment: 20 Pages and 4 Figures
summary: Purpose: Surgical operative reports support procedural documentation, surgical training, performance assessment, and workflow review. However, extracting meaningful information often requires extensive manual review and clinical expertise. Automated surgical scene descriptions could reduce this burden by leveraging recurring surgical activities and prior knowledge. Methods: We propose GRAC (Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning), a framework that represents surgical scenes as graphs capturing relationships among instruments, actions, and anatomical structures. Given an input scene graph, GRAC learns to retrieve relevant graph-caption pairs from training data. It compares instrument-tissue interactions between retrieved examples and the input scene, using comparison features to condition retrieved-caption representations during generation. Results: On the EndoVis-18 benchmark, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.88, compared with 4.23 for SGT and 3.36 for the strongest conventional Transformer baseline. Exact instrument-action-target triplet-set accuracy reached 52.6%, compared with 32.7% for SGT and 26.2% for the strongest conventional baseline. These results demonstrate improvements in language quality and factual agreement. On TORS, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.06, compared with 3.80 for the strongest baseline. Conclusion: GRAC demonstrates that combining structured surgical scene representations with retrieved examples improves surgical scene captioning and produces more contextually meaningful descriptions.

AI.tldr: GRAC is a graph-based retrieval-augmented captioning framework that represents surgical scenes as graphs and retrieves graph-caption pairs to condition caption generation. It achieves a CIDEr-D of 5.88 on EndoVis-18, compared with 4.23 for SGT and 3.36 for the strongest Transformer baseline, and also improves on TORS.
AI.motivation: Surgical operative reports require heavy manual review, and automated scene descriptions could reduce this burden by exploiting recurring surgical activities and prior knowledge.
AI.method: GRAC encodes instrument, action and anatomy relationships as scene graphs, retrieves relevant graph-caption pairs from training data, and uses comparison features of instrument-tissue interactions to condition the retrieved-caption representations during generation.
AI.result: On EndoVis-18, GRAC reaches a CIDEr-D of 5.88 (SGT 4.23, strongest conventional Transformer 3.36) and exact instrument-action-target triplet-set accuracy of 52.6% (SGT 32.7%, strongest conventional baseline 26.2%); on TORS it reaches a CIDEr-D of 5.06 versus 3.80 for the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Combining structured surgical scene representations with retrieved examples improves both language quality and factual agreement in surgical scene captioning, yielding more contextually meaningful descriptions.

title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
comment: Videos and code available at: this https URL
summary: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

AI.tldr: AMP1 is a reference harness in which a generalist AI model commands manipulators directly, achieving 85.6% zero-shot success on RoboLab-120 without demonstrations or task-specific training, compared with 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. It succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials and gains further from a persistent memory store across episodes.
AI.motivation: Robot manipulation research centers on specialist policies trained on demonstrations, and the paper asks whether generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably.
AI.method: The authors analyze agentic manipulation policies, in which a generalist model adapts its actions as the task unfolds, and present AMP1, a harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual and mobile manipulation, optionally with a memory representation carried across episodes.
AI.result: AMP1 reaches 85.6% zero-shot success on RoboLab-120 (49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies) and succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials across twelve tasks and three robots, cutting failure rates 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines; the memory-augmented harness lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual tasks by 4.6x versus zero-shot deployment.
AI.conclusion: Agentic manipulation policies are more general and robust than specialist policies, and cross-episode memory allows learning from experience, offering a foundation for robot manipulation.

title: Dynamic GPU Voxel Grids and Voxel-sequential Processing in NanoVDB
summary: We introduce two fundamental advances to the NanoVDB data structure: dynamic GPU-native topological updates, and a voxel-sequential access paradigm that dramatically accelerates point-wise and stencil-based operators on sparse grids. NanoVDB's linearized memory layout has delivered strong GPU performance, and the Index-Grid concept introduced in the fVDB framework [Williams et al 2024] provided topology/data separation and optimal compactness of storage in sparse machine learning workloads. However, all these prior iterations of NanoVDB assume a static topology that has precluded use of this data structure in simulation and dynamic geometric processes. We eliminate this limitation by introducing a suite of dynamic topology operators -- morphological dilation, grid merging, pruning, and cross-resolution coarsening and refinement. These operators use bit-parallel algorithms to reconstruct grids containing hundreds of millions of voxels in just a few milliseconds. We also introduce a voxel-sequential access paradigm and data structure for GPU kernels operating on sparse data. We stream active voxels as a flat linear sequence, minimizing or eliminating the need for tree traversal in the process. This achieves compute density and regularity that allow even complex stencil-based operators to approach peak memory bandwidth, with minimal storage overhead. Together, these contributions remove the read-only constraint from NanoVDB, establishing it as a high-performance primary representation for dynamic GPU simulation and geometry manipulation. We evaluate the efficacy of our newly introduced operators in benchmarks sourced from applications such as 3D reconstruction, fluid simulation, and large-scale mesh voxelization.

AI.tldr: The paper extends NanoVDB with dynamic GPU-native topology operators and a voxel-sequential access paradigm that streams active voxels as a flat sequence, removing the read-only limitation of the format. The operators rebuild grids with hundreds of millions of voxels in a few milliseconds, and stencil operators approach peak memory bandwidth.
AI.motivation: Earlier NanoVDB versions assume static topology, which rules out simulation and dynamic geometric processing on GPUs.
AI.method: The authors add morphological dilation, grid merging, pruning, and cross-resolution coarsening and refinement, implemented with bit-parallel algorithms, and introduce a voxel-sequential data structure that streams active voxels as a flat linear sequence to reduce tree traversal.
AI.result: The operators reconstruct grids with hundreds of millions of voxels in a few milliseconds, and voxel-sequential stencil operators approach peak memory bandwidth with minimal storage overhead; the paper evaluates on 3D reconstruction, fluid simulation and large-scale mesh voxelization.
AI.conclusion: The changes make NanoVDB a high-performance primary representation for dynamic GPU simulation and geometry manipulation, not only a read-only format.
